questions.question: A 28-year-old sex worker presented with a painless ulcer on her vulva. On examination, inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. Which of the following methods has been used to demonstrate the causative agent as per the given image?
questions.explanation:
A painless genital ulcer with inguinal lymphadenopathy with the presence of spiral organisms on microscopy is suggestive of syphilis. It is caused by Treponema pallidum, demonstrated by dark-field microscopy.

Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It uses reflected light and has a higher resolving power than the light microscope. Dark-field microscopy is the the most specific and sensitive technique to visualize Treponema pallidum when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present.

Other options:

Option B: Phase contrast microscopy improves the contrast to delineate structures within cells. A dark image is formed on a light background.

Option C: Fluorescent microscopy uses fluorescent dyes like auramine-rhodamine to appreciate Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites.

Option D: The electron microscope, invented by Ernst Ruska, helps in appreciating viral structures. It has a very high resolving power.

questions.question: Which among the following statements is false?
options: Muramic acid is present in prokaryotes
Mitotic division is present in eukaryotes
Multiple linear chromosomes present in eukaryotes
questions.answer: C. 80S ribosome is present in prokaryotes
questions.explanation:
80S ribosome is present in eukaryotes, while 70S ribosome is present in prokaryotes.

80S ribosome has subunits 60S and 40S, while 70S has subunits 50S and 30S.

questions.question: Which of the following methods will not help you visualize the bacterial cell wall?
questions.explanation:
The cell wall of bacteria cannot be seen with simple stains or direct light microscopy.

The bacterial cell wall is present outside the plasma membrane and confers strength and shape to the cell. It is composed of peptidoglycans. The cell wall can be demonstrated by the following methods:

• Plasmolysis

• Microdissection

• Reaction with specific antibodies

• Mechanical rupture of the cell

• Differential staining procedures (E.g. Chance's method)

• Electron microscopy

• Fluorescence microscopy

questions.question: In which of the following phases of the bacterial growth curve does sporulation occur?
questions.explanation:
Sporulation occurs in the stationary phase of the bacterial growth curve, which is marked as C in the image.

The bacterial growth curve is obtained when a batch of bacteria is seeded in a liquid medium and incubated. It consists of 4 distinct phases:

1. Lag phase (A) - The bacteria adapt to a new environment. They synthesize and accumulate enzymes and metabolic intermediates required for multiplication. Thus, there is no increase in cell number but cell size increases. Maximum cell size is obtained towards the end of this phase.

2. Log or exponential phase (B) - The bacteria start dividing and their numbers increase exponentially with time. Cells are smaller and stain uniformly. The growth rate is constant.

3. Stationary phase (C) - There is depletion of nutrients and accumulation of toxic products. Thus, cell division reduces and a state of equilibrium is attained, where the number of new cells formed equals the number that die. Growth rate is zero. Sporulation occurs during this phase. Many bacteria produce secondary metabolic products such as exotoxins and antibiotics.

4. Death phase or the phase of decline (D) - Growth rate is negative. The population decreases due to cell death from nutritional exhaustion, toxin accumulation and the action of autolytic enzymes. Involution forms are common.

questions.question: Which organism has the following cell wall structure?
questions.explanation:
The presence of teichoic acid and lipoteichoic acid with a thick peptidoglycan layer is a feature of gram-positive bacteria.

The cell wall of bacteria provides shape and ridigity to the bacterial cell. It is composed of peptidoglycans.

Gram positive
Gram negative

Teichoic acid, lipoteichoic acid
Present
Absent

Thickness (Peptidoglycan)
Thicker
Thinner

Variety of amino acids
Few
Several

Aromatic and sulfur-containing amino acids
Absent
Present

Lipopolysaccharides and outer membrane
Absent
Present

Other options:

Option C: The cell wall of fungi consists of chitin, mannan, and polysaccharides (glucan).

Option D: The cell wall of mycobacteria have mycolic acid, which is responsible for acid fastness.

questions.question: Which of the following methods of sterilization involves exposure to 100 °C for 20 minutes on 3 successive days?
questions.explanation:
The method of sterilization that involves exposure at 100°C for 20 minutes for 3 successive days is called tyndallization or intermittent sterilization.

Tyndallization, which utilizes steam, was used for sterilization of media containing gelatin, egg, serum, or sugar. This method may not kill spores of certain anaerobes and thermophiles. Autoclaving has replaced this method now.

Other options:

Option A: Autoclaving involves heating at 121°C for 15 minutes at a pressure of 15psi. This is the used for intruments, linen, laboratory ware.

Option C: In pasteurization, milk is heated at either 63°C for 30 minutes (the holder method) or at 72°C for 15–20 seconds (the flash process), followed by cooling quickly to 13°C or lower.

Option D: Heating an article at 80–85 °C for 30 minutes on 3 consecutive days is called inspissation.

questions.question: Which of the following works by disrupting the cell membrane?
questions.explanation:
Lysol works by disrupting the cell membrane.

Lysol is a phenol compound, which is obtained by distillation of coal tar. Phenols cause cell membrane damage and inactivate membrane-bound oxidases and dehydrogenases. This causes lysis and release of cell contents. Low concentrations of phenol can precipitate proteins. They are not inactivated by organic matter and are thus useful disinfectants.

The mechnisms of action of other disinfecting agents are:

1. DNA damage

• Ionizing radiation

• Ultraviolet light

• Hydrogen peroxide

• DNA reactive chemicals like acriflavin.

2. Protein modification

• Alcohol

• Chlorine

• Iodine

• Heavy metals (e.g. thiomersal)

• Hydrogen peroxide

• Formaldehyde

• Glutaraldehyde

• Ethylene oxide

• Acids and alkalis

questions.question: Which of the following methods is used in the test shown below?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows antibiotic sensitivity testing which uses the lawn culture method.

Lawn or carpet culture is the method in which a uniform surface growth of bacterium is present on the medium. It is used for antibiotic sensitivity testing (disc method) and bacteriophage typing. Stab culture (option D) is used for demonstration of gelatin liquefaction and oxygen requirements of bacterium, for maintenance of stock cultures. Streak culture (option A) is routinely used for the isolation of bacteria in pure culture from clinical specimens. Stroke culture (option C) is used for providing pure growth of bacterium for slide agglutination and other diagnostic tests. Other methods of culture include:

• Liquid culture - These are preferred for inocula containing antibiotics and other inhibitory substances.

• Pour plate culture - It gives an estimate of viable bacterial count in a suspension.

questions.question: In which of the following organisms will the following phenomenon not be observed in?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows Quellung reaction (halo around the bacteria) and is seen in capsulated bacteria. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not capsulated, therefore Quellung reaction will not be observed in it.

In Quellung reaction, a suspension of a capsulated bacterium is mixed with its specific anticapsular serum and examined under the microscope. The anticapsular antibodies bind to the capsule and thus the capsule becomes very prominent and appears swollen. Capsulated organisms can be remembered with the following mnemonic:

Some - Streptococcus pneumoniae

Killers - Klebsiella pneumoniae

Have - Haemophilus influenzae

Nice - Neisseria meningitidis

Capsules - Cryptococcus neoformans

questions.question:
Given are a few case scenarios. The etiological agents of which of the following are microaerophilic?

1. Endoscopic biopsy from a businessman with epigastric pain showing positive urease test.

2. Gram-negative, small, spirally curved rod-like, motile bacilli isolated from a patient with diarrhea.

3. Gram-negative curved bacilli with 'fish-in-stream' appearance isolated from a child with rice-water diarrhea.

4. Nasopharyngeal swab from a child with paroxysmal cough showing 'mercury drop' colonies.

5. Sputum from a farmer, cultured on LJ medium showing dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies.
questions.explanation:
The aetiological agents of 1 and 2 are microaerophilic.

The given case scenarios are:

1. A businessman with epigastric pain and positive urease test has peptic ulcer disease, caused by Helicobacter pylori. It is microaerophilic.
2. Diarrhea caused by Gram-negative, small, spirally curved rod-like, motile bacilli describes Campylobacter jejuni. It is microaerophilic.
3. Rice-water diarrhea and Gram-negative curved bacilli with 'fish-in-stream' appearance describes cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae. It is a facultative anaerobe.
4. Nasopharyngeal swab from a child with paroxysmal cough showing 'mercury drops' colonies describes Bordetella pertussis. It is an obligate aerobe.
5. Dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies on LJ medium describes Mycobacerium tuberculosis. It is an obligate aerobe.

Microaerophilic organisms grow best in low oxygen tension (2-10% oxygen).

Note: Mycobacteria, such as M. bovis, can grow at oxygen tensions ranging from atmospheric to microaerophilic conditions. However, M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe.

questions.question: The given image shows a culture medium with lactose fermenting and non-lactose fermenting bacteria. Which of the following is not a component of the culture medium?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows MacConkey agar. Cysteine is not a constituent of MacConkey agar.

MacConkey agar is a differential or indicator medium. Lactose-fermenting organisms (Eg: E. coli) produce a pink color, and non-lactose fermenting organisms (Shigella sp., Salmonella sp.) do not change the color. Contents of MacConkey agar include peptone, lactose, agar, neutral red and sodium taurocholate (Mnemonic- PLANT). MacConkey agar is also a selective medium i.e. the bile salts (sodium taurocholate) and dyes (neutral red) inhibit the growth of Gram-positive organisms and Gram-negative cocci.

questions.question: Which of the following is an enrichment medium?
questions.explanation:
The image 'A' represents alkaline peptone water, which is an enrichment medium used for Vibrio cholerae.

The other images represent:

Image B- Blood agar with P. aeruginosa colonies

Image C- Loeffler's serum slope, which is used to isolate C. diphtheriae

Image D- Chocolate agar with F. tularensis colonies

Enrichment media suppress the growth of commensal bacteria and allow for the growth of certain organisms. These media are used for samples with mixed flora e.g. stool. They are always liquid media, like alkaline peptone water. Other examples include tetrathionate broth and selenite-F broth for Salmonella sp. and Shigella sp.

Enriched medium are those media to which additional nutrients such as blood, serum, or egg are added. They're used to grow bacteria with specific nutritional requirements. Examples include blood agar to test the hemolytic property of bacteria, chocolate agar for isolation of H. influenzae and Loeffler's serum slope for isolation of C. diphtheriae.

questions.question: A microbiologist observes the following growth on a blood agar plate. Which of the following will not be the etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows a swarming type of growth on the agar plate. It will not be caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Swarming is the growth of motile bacteria in the form of a thin film on solid culture media. It is exhibited by the following:

• Gram-positive bacilli - Clostridium tetani (option A), Bacillus cereus (option D)

• Gram-negative bacilli - Proteus mirabilis (option C), Proteus vulgaris

• Gram-negative halophilic bacteria- Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Swarming can be inhibited by increasing the concentration of agar (6%), alcohol, sodium azide, boric acid, chloral hydrate, sulfonamide, and surface-active agents.

questions.question: Which of the following principles is primarily used in polymerase chain reaction?
options: It can amplify small amounts of DNA
It can amplify small amounts of RNA
questions.answer: B. It can amplify small amounts of DNA
questions.explanation:
The primary principle used in polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the amplification of small amounts of DNA.

PCR is an automated process in which a single or a few copies of a DNA piece is amplified to generate of thousands to millions of copies of that particular DNA sequence. There are 3 basic steps are involved in PCR:

• DNA extraction from microorganism

• Amplification of extracted DNA - Denaturation (95°C), Primer annealing (55°C), Extension (72°C)

• Gel electrophoresis of the amplified product

PCR is used in rapid diagnostic tests for infections (e.g. HIV DNA), forensic investigations etc. The founder of PCR is Karry B Mullis.

questions.question:
Which of the following describes the reverse transcriptase enzyme used in RT-PCR correctly?

(RT-PCR - Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction)
questions.explanation:
The enzyme involved in RT-PCR is reverse transcriptase (RT) which has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity.

In reverse transcription-polymerase chain reation (RT-PCR), reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from the RNA template. RT-PCR can be used for the demonstration of poliovirus RNA, causing paralytic poliomyelitis, in CSF. It can also be used for the detection of viruses from nasopharyngeal swabs (SARS-CoV2, H1N1).

In real-time RT-PCR, fluorescent dyes or DNA probes are used to quantify the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. So, it can be used to quantify viral loads in HIV, hepatitis B, etc., and is also called quantitative PCR (qPCR).

questions.question: What are jumping genes known as?
questions.explanation:
Jumping genes are also called transposons.

Transposons are genetic elements that can move between chromosomal and extra-chromosomal DNA molecules. Insertion of a transposon leads to acquisition of new characteristics by the recipient DNA. Transposons contain several genes, including those necessary for their migration from one genetic locus to another. They may contain genes for specialised functions like antibiotic resistance. However, they do not contain genes for their replication.

Jumping genes were discovered by Barbara McClintock and she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1983 for the same.

Other options:

Options A and B: The cytoplasmic carriers of genetic information are termed plasmids or episomes.

Option D: A cosmid is a type of hybrid plasmid that contains a Lambda phage cos sequence. (Cos sites + plasmid = cosmids).

questions.question: An orthopedician is performing the following procedure to visualize the anterior cruciate ligament in a patient. Which of the following will be used to sterilise the instrument used?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows arthroscopy being performed. Arthroscopes are sterilized using plasma sterilization which utilises hydrogen peroxide.

In plasma sterilisation, radiofrequency energy is applied to create an electromagnetic field through which hydrogen peroxide vapours are passed. This generates plasma which contains free radicals of hydrogen and oxygen. Plasma denatures all organisms and is used sterilize arthroscopes and ureteroscopes. Sterilization control is monitored by Geobacillus stearothermophilus and Bacillus atrophaeus.

Option A: Ethylene oxide has both microbicidal and sporicidal activity. It is used for sterilisation heat-sensitive equipment like heart-lung machines, respirators, suture materials etc. Sterilization control is monitored by Bacillius atrophaeus and Bacillus subtilus.

Option B: Gamma rays cause breakage of DNA. It destroys spores and vegetative cells, but is not effective against viruses. It is referred to as cold sterilisation and is used in commercial plants to sterilize plastics, syringes, swabs. Sterilization control is monitored by Bacillus pumilius.

Option D: Ultraviolet rays are used to sterilise biosafety cabinets, entryways, operation theatres and laboratories.

questions.question: While assessing the quality of drinking water in a village, you detect the presence of coliform bacilli by the multiple tube technique. Following this, you decide to perform the Eijkman test. What is this test also known as?
questions.explanation:
Eijkman test is also known as differential coliform test.

Drinking water should be free of any pathogenic microorganisms. The presence of coliform bacteria in the water may indicate faecal pollution, while the detection of E.coli confirms it.

The presumptive coliform test is done by the multiple tube technique. Following this, the Eijkman test is done to confirm the presence of E. coli. They can grow at 44°C (faecal thermotolerant bacilli), ferment lactose and cause indole and gas production.

Option A: Presumptive coliform count detects the probable number of coliform bacilli in water. It can be positive due to the presence of organisms other than E.coli also.

Option C: Colony counts provide an estimate of the general bacterial purity of water.

Option D: Methylene blue reduction test is used to assess the bacterial contamination of milk.

questions.question: Faecal contamination of a water source is suspected by the mayor of a municipal corporation. He asks you to test the water for evidence of recent contamination. The presence of which of the following organisms would suggest this?
questions.explanation:
Recent fecal contamination of water is suggested by the presence of enterococcus (fecal streptococci).

Clostridium perfringens may be present for a long duration. If it is present in water, it suggests that contamination is not recent.

If Escherichia coli is detected, it is definitive proof of fecal contamination. However, it is non-specific for suggesting the duration of the contamination.

questions.question: Which of the following tests is not used for bacteriological examination of milk?
questions.explanation:
Pasteurization is not used for the bacteriological examination of milk.

Pasteurization is the process of applying heat, to milk, for a specified period for the purpose of killing pathogenic bacteria. There are two methods: holder method and flash method.

Option A: Methylene blue reduction test depends on the reduction of methylene blue by bacteria in milk when incubated at 37 °C in complete darkness.

Option B: Resazurin test is similar to methylene blue reduction test, but the dye resazurin on reduction passes through a series of colour changes from blue to pink to colourless. The shade of colour after incubation with milk for a particular period of time depends on the degree of contamination.

Option C: Phosphatase test is used to check whether milk has been pasteurised. Positive test after pasteurisation of milk shows contamination after pasteurisation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about hybridoma is false?
options: Specific antibody-producing cells are integrated with myeloma cells.
Myeloma cells using salvage pathway grow well in HAT medium.
Aminopterin, a folate antagonist, inhibits de novo pathway.
HGPRTase and thymidylate synthetase are required for salvage pathway.
questions.answer: B. Myeloma cells using salvage pathway grow well in HAT medium.
questions.explanation:
Aminopterin is a folate antagonist present in the HAT medium that inhibits the de novo pathway of nucleotide synthesis. Since myeloma cells cannot use the salvage pathway for nucleotide synthesis due to the lack of HGPRTase enzyme, they cannot survive in the HAT medium.

Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (monoclonal antibodies).

Hybridomas are somatic cell hybrids produced by fusing the antibody-forming spleen cells with myeloma cells. The resultant hybrid thus has both the antibody-producing ability of the B-cell and the ability to multiply indefinitely of the myeloma.

The following are the steps involved in hybridoma technology:

• Mice are immunized with an antigen. After several weeks of immunization, blood samples are obtained from mice for measurement of serum antibodies.

• When the antibody titer is high enough, mice are commonly boosted by injecting antigen without adjuvant intraperitoneally or intravenously. Then the mice are euthanized and their spleens removed for in vitro hybridoma cell production.

• Fusing antibody-producing spleen cells, which have a limited life span with myeloma cells (derived from an immortal tumor of lymphocytes) results in a hybridoma that is capable of unlimited growth.

• The cells are cultured in a medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine (HAT medium) which allows only the fused cells to survive in culture.

• Monoclonal antibodies are then harvested.

questions.question: Which of the following is both a diffusion and a dilution method of testing antibiotic sensitivity?
questions.explanation:
Epsilometer (E-test) is both a diffusion and a dilution method of testing antibiotic sensitivity.

It is a quantitative technique for determining the antimicrobial susceptibility (AST) and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) in µg/mL of gram-negative and gram-positive aerobic bacteria.

The antibiotic sensitivity tests are classified as follows:

• Diffusion methods: Kirby–Bauer method, Stokes method

• Dilution methods: Tube dilution method, Agar dilution method

• Diffusion and dilution method: E–test (Epsilometer)

questions.question: Which of the following methods of antibiotic susceptibility testing cannot be used to calculate the minimum inhibitory concentration of an antimicrobial drug?
questions.explanation:
Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) cannot be calculated using Kirby-Bauer's disk diffusion method and Stokes disk diffusion method as they are semi-quantitative methods.

MIC is the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial agent that will inhibit the visible growth of a microorganism.

Methods to determine MIC include:

• Tube dilution method

• Agar dilution method

• E-test method

questions.question: A microbiologist is about to run a polymerase chain reaction assay on the serum of a patient suspected to have Q fever. He wishes to quantify the PCR by monitoring the amplification process while the PCR is ongoing. Which of the following types of PCR should he perform?
questions.explanation:
Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can be used to quantify the PCR by monitoring the amplification process while the PCR is ongoing.

Types of PCR:

• Reverse transcriptase PCR- The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complementary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR.

• Real-time PCR- This helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It uses fluorescent dyes or specific DNA probes. It is also known as qPCR (Quantitative PCR)

• Multiplex PCR- Primers to more than one pathogen are used simultaneously and hence multiple products are obtained.

• Nested PCR- It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification. This ensures specificity.

questions.question: Which of the following investigations does not use antibody marking?
questions.explanation:
The hemagglutination test is not based on the principle of antibody marking.

When antibodies bind to antigens on the surface of red blood cells, the resultant clumping reaction is referred to as hemagglutination. It is routinely performed to type red blood cells in ABO blood-typing.

 The image below shows hemagglutination.

In ELISA, radioimmunoassay and immunofluorescence, the antigens or antibodies are labeled or marked with enzymes, fluorescent dyes, etc.

Note: If no hemagglutination occurs it means the patient’s serum has anti-haemagglutinin antibodies that bind to hemagglutinin and prevent the clumping reaction. This hemagglutination inhibition reaction is a method of detection of viruses and antiviral-antibodies and is used to make a diagnosis of influenza.

questions.question: Which of the following is not used as an immediate test in the screening of urinary tract infections?
questions.explanation:
Pour plate culture (quantitative test) is not used as an immediate test for screening of UTI. However, it is considered the best diagnostic test for confirmation of UTI due it’s high sensitivity and specificity.

The screening tests for UTI are as follows:

• Wet mount examination- It is done to demonstrate pus cells in urine.

• Leukocyte esterase test- It is a rapid and cheaper method and detects leukocyte esterases secreted by pus cells present in urine.

• Nitrate reduction test (Griess test)- Nitrate reducing bacteria like E. coli gives a positive result.

• Catalase test- E. coli and other bacteria that produce the enzyme catalase give a positive result.

Quantitative Culture:

• Standardized loop technique

• Pour plate method

questions.question: A patient who had been receiving ceftazidime and amikacin via central venous line for a week suddenly spiked a fever. Blood culture is positive for a vancomycin-resistant, catalase-negative organism whose Gram-stained image is given below. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
From the given case scenario and image we can deduce that the most likely organism involved is Enterococcus faecalis.

The image shows gram-positive cocci in chains, that are described as catalase negative. This helps rule out Staphylocococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococcus.

Streptococcus viridans is usually sensitive to penicillin and vancomycin hence it is ruled out.

The mechanism of vancomycin resistance seen in E. faecalis is the alteration of the D-alanyl–D-alanine chain in the cell wall.

questions.question: What type of immunity is being conferred to a neonate receiving the BCG vaccine?
questions.explanation:
The immunity conferred to a neonate receiving the BCG vaccine is artificial active immunity, as it involves administering a live attenuated vaccine form of Mycobacterium bovis to stimulate an adaptive immune response and develop antibodies, establishing long-term immunity.

Types of adaptive immunity:

• Natural active immunity: It results from either a clinical or an inapparent infection by a microbe.

• Artificial active immunity: It is the resistance induced by vaccines which are preparations of killed or attenuated microorganisms or their products.

• Natural passive immunity: It is the immunity passively transferred from mother to baby. In human infants, maternal antibodies are transmitted predominantly through the placenta, while in animals such as pigs, the transfer of antibodies occurs mainly through the colostrum.

• Artificial passive immunity: It is the resistance passively transferred to a recipient by the administration of antibodies. Hyperimmune sera of animal or human origin, convalescent sera, and pooled human immunoglobulin are used for this purpose.

• Combined immunization: A combination of the active and passive methods of immunization is used.

Examples of the above types of immunity:

Immunity
Description

Natural active
Clinical or subclinical infection

Artificial active
Vaccination

Natural passive
Transplacental transfer of antibody, colostrum

Artificial passive
Anti-tetanus serum, anti-diphtherial serum

Combined immunization
Antisera and vaccine are given at the same time, e.g- post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies

Note: Adoptive immunity is immunity in which immunologically competent lymphocytes are injected. The transfer factor is composed of these immunologically competent lymphocytes. It can passively transfer cell-mediated immunity against those antigens to which the donor is sensitive.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old with a large dirty wound on his knee and abrasions on his palms presents to the casualty. He does not remember the last time he received a TT injection and was thus given tetanus immunoglobulin. Which of the following is false about this type of immunity?

TT- Tetanus Toxoid
questions.explanation:
Giving pre-formed immunoglobulin (e.g. Tetanus immunoglobulin) directly is an example of passive immunity, which is not long-lasting.

The differentiating features between active and passive immunity:

Active Immunity

Passive Immunity

Actively produced by the host’s immune system

Passively received by the host

Induced by infection or immunogens

Readymade antibody is transferred

Immunological memory present

No memory

Immunity is effective after a lag period or latent period

Immediate immunity

Broad specificity

Narrow specificity

A negative phase may occur

No negative phase.

Booster effect on subsequent dose

The subsequent dose is less effective

Secondary type response seen

No secondary type of response

More effective

Less effective

Long-lasting (Years)

Short-lasting (Days to weeks)

Example: Vaccines

Example: Antisera

Negative phase: It is the time period during which the level of measurable immunity is lower than it was before the antigenic stimulus. This is because the antigen combines with any pre-existing antibody and lowers its level in circulation. It is seen at the beginning of the active immune response.

Secondary type response: If an individual who has been actively immunized against an antigen experiences the same antigen subsequently, the immune response occurs more quickly and abundantly than during the first encounter.

questions.question: A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis was administered transfer factor as treatment. What type of immunity does this result in?
questions.explanation:
Adoptive immunity occurs when transfer factor is given.

Transfer factor is composed of an extract of immunologically competent lymphocytes such as T lymphocytes, NK cells, macrophages, or B cells. It has the ability to passively transfer cell-mediated immunity against antigens to which the donor is sensitive.

It has been attempted in the treatment of lepromatous leprosy and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a pattern recognition receptor?
questions.explanation:
Bone morphogenetic protein-like receptors are not pattern-recognition receptors.

Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are essential for the innate immune system. They identify pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) common to classes of microbes and trigger immune responses. These receptors can be found on the cell surface, detecting extracellular pathogens, or within the endosomes and cellular matrix, detecting intracellular invading viruses.

PRRs activate pro-inflammatory pathways, promote phagocytosis in cells like macrophages, neutrophils and dendritic cells, and may act as secreted proteins binding directly to pathogens. Based on the localization and functional characteristics, PRRs are classified as:

• Membrane-bound PRRs:

• Toll-like receptors (TLR)- detect microbial carbohydrates and lipoproteins (Option B)

• C-type lectin receptors (CLR)- detect mannose residues

• Cytoplasmic (intracellular) PRRs:

• Nucleotide oligomerization (NOD)-like receptors (NLR) - NOD1 and NOD2 - Detects bacterial cell wall peptidoglycans (Option A)

• RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) - detect viral RNA (Option C)

• Secreted PRRs

On the contrary, BMP receptors are multifunctional transmembrane serine-threonine kinase receptors that belong to the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) superfamily, regulating cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis with no role in pattern recognition. Also, there are no receptors termed "BMP-like receptors".

Note: A mutation in the Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) gene enhances the proliferation and reduces the apoptosis of pulmonary vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, leading to hereditary pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

questions.question: A 23-year-old presents with diarrhea, fever, and vomiting. The given bacteria is implicated. Which toll-like receptor binds to the structure of the bacteria marked A?
questions.explanation:
The given image and clinical history suggest a typhoid infection. The structure marked A is the flagella of bacteria. Toll-like receptor (TLR) 5 binds to the flagella of bacteria.

Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are transmembrane receptors that have an extracellular domain, that detect infecting pathogens.

• TLR 1 - Mycobacteria and Gram-negative bacteria

• TLR 2 - Mycobacteria and Gram-positive bacteria

• TLR 3 - Viral RNA

• TLR 4 - Gram-negative bacteria

• TLR 5 - Flagella

• TLR 9 - Bacterial DNA, some herpes viruses, malarial parasite

TLRs act through the NF-KB pathway and initiate inflammation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about T cell dependent antigens?
options: Their response doesn't show immunological memory
They activate only mature B cells
questions.answer: B. They activate only mature B cells
questions.explanation:
T cell-dependent antigens activate only mature B cells.

Depending on their ability to induce the formation of antibodies, antigens are classified as T-cell dependent and T-cell independent antigens.

T cell-dependent antigens (TD)
T cell-independent antigens (TI)

Require helper T cell participation for the production of immune response
Directly stimulate antibody production by B cells

Structurally complex
Structurally simple

Activate only mature B cells monoclonally
Activate both mature and immature B cells polyclonally

B cells undergo affinity maturation and class switch over
B cells do not undergo affinity maturation and class switch over

All classes of antibodies are activated

Antibody response is restricted to IgM and IgG3

Rapidly metabolized
Slowly metabolized

Immunological memory present
No immunological memory

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a fever of 103°F, hypotension, confusion, and a diffuse rash as shown below. 3 days back, she had uncontrollable epistaxis for which a nasal pack was placed. What is the likely mechanism of action of the microbial toxin that has caused her current illness?
questions.answer: C. Polyclonal activation of T cells
questions.explanation:
This woman presented with fever, hypotension, and a diffuse erythematous rash, three days after a nasal packing was done. This is characteristic of toxic shock syndrome - commonly caused by staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), which is a superantigen.

Superantigens act by causing polyclonal activation of T cells. They activate a large number of T cells irrespective of their antigen specificity.

In contrast to regular antigens which bind to the binding groove on T cells, superantigens bind outside the groove directly to the lateral aspect of the TCR β chain. This leads to a massive release of cytokines and polyclonal activation of T cells.

Clinically, this manifests as fever, hypotension, and skin exfoliation.

Examples of organisms that produce superantigens:

1. Bacterial

• Staphylococcus aureus- Enterotoxins

• Group A streptococci - Pyrogenic exotoxin

• Mycoplasma arthritidis- mitogen 1

• Yersinia enterocolitica

• Yersinia pseudotuberculosis

2. Viral

• Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)

• Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

• Rabies nucleocapsid

• HIV-encoded negative regulatory factor.

3. Fungal- Malassezia furfur

questions.question: What are the changes in the variable regions of an immunoglobulin known as?
questions.explanation:
Changes in the variable regions of heavy and light chains of an immunoglobulin are called an idiotype.

Other options:

Option B: Isotypes are the changes in the constant regions of the heavy chain of the immunoglobulin.

Option C: Allotypes refer to multiple alleles that exist for some genes. This leads to subtle amino acid differences that occur in some but not all members of the same species.

Option D: An epitope is the smallest unit of antigenicity and it is an antigenic determinant.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about immunoglobulins is false?
options: IgG is used to diagnose fetal infection
questions.answer: A. IgG is used to diagnose fetal infection
questions.explanation:
IgG cannot detect fetal infections because it is not produced by the fetus in significant amounts.

IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn.

questions.question: Which of the following immunoglobulins acts as surface immunoglobulin on B cells?
questions.explanation:
Monomeric IgM is the major antibody receptor on the surface of B lymphocytes for antigen recognition.

IgD is the other class of antibodies which acts as the B cell receptors.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin is majorly responsible for the reaction demonstrated below?
questions.explanation:
The image shows blood typing, which works on the principle of agglutination. IgM is mainly responsible for agglutination.

It is the most efficient immunoglobulin in agglutination, complement fixation, and other antigen–antibody reactions and is important also in defense against bacteria and viruses.

It is a pentamer, and hence is more effective than IgG in opsonization (C3b mediated), bactericidal action and bacterial agglutination but less effective in neutralization of toxins and viruses.

questions.question: You are counseling a new mother about the importance of breastfeeding. What forms the secretory component of the antibody that is maximally present in breast milk?
options: Epithelial cells of lining mucosa only
questions.answer: B. Epithelial cells of lining mucosa only
questions.explanation:
The antibody maximally present in breast milk is IgA. The secretory component of IgA is formed by epithelial cells of lining mucosa.

IgA occurs in two forms- serum IgA (monomer) and secretory IgA.

Secretory IgA is a dimer formed by two monomer units joined together by a J-chain and a secretory component (secretory piece). Secretory IgA along with the J chain is synthesized by the plasma cells situated near the mucosal or glandular epithelium. The secretory component is synthesized by epithelial cells, not by plasma cells.

It is believed to protect IgA from denaturation by bacterial proteases.

questions.question: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, which of the following are the end products?
questions.explanation:
When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments.

Enzymatic digestion of antibody:

• Papain- 2 Fab fragments and one Fc fragment

• Pepsin- One F(ab’)2 fragment and many smaller fragments

• Mercaptoethanol- 2 H and 2 L chains

questions.question: An immunologist is conducting an experiment to understand precipitation reactions. He notes that on adding excessive amount of antigen to a serum sample containing small amount of antibodies, the amount of precipitate formed is less, compared to adding smaller amount of antigen to the same sample. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation:
This phenomenon is called post–zone phenomenon because it has excessive antigen in the test system, leading to weak or even absent precipitation.

Lattice hypothesis explains precipitation reactions. The amount of precipitate formed is greatly influenced by the relative proportions of antigens and antibodies.

• Prozone phenomenon is caused by excessive antibodies in the test system. (weak/absent precipitation- false-negative test)

• Zone of equivalence- antigen, and antibody are in optimum proportions and maximum precipitation occurs.

• Post–zone phenomenon is due to the presence of excessive antigen in the test system. (weaker/absent precipitation)

Flocculation: Instead of sedimenting, precipitate remains suspended as floculus.

questions.question: Double diffusion in two dimensions is called as ___________.
questions.explanation:
Double diffusion in two dimensions is called the Ouchterlony procedure. Ex: Elek’s test for testing toxigenicity in diphtheria bacilli.

The images below show the different types of immunodiffusion.

questions.question: A patient presented to the casualty with the following finding. A positive Nagler's reaction confirmed the presence of lecithinase-producing organisms. What is the principle behind this test?
questions.explanation:
Nagler’s reaction is an example of a neutralization test. It is done for the detection of lecithinase toxin produced by C. perfringens.

The alpha-toxin of C. perfringens has phospholipase activity. When grown on a medium containing egg yolk phospholipid, an area of opacity around the bacterial colonies is seen (Nagler's positive). The presence of antitoxin can inhibit this.

Other examples of neutralization tests are:

• Plaque inhibition test- neutralization of bacteriophages

• Schick test- neutralization of diphtheria toxin by antitoxin

• Anti-streptolysin O test- for beta-hemolytic Streptococci.

questions.question: A patient presents with a painless ulcer on his penis. A Wasserman test is done and is reactive. What is the principle of this test?
questions.explanation:
Wassermann's reaction is an example of a complement fixation test. It is a non-specific test for the diagnosis of syphilis.

An antigen combines with its (specific) antibody in the presence of complement, and the antigen-antibody complex adsorbs the complement. This reaction is not visible and requires the use of an indicator (sheep erythrocytes and the specific anti-erythrocyte antibody).

questions.question: Which of the following activates the classical complement pathway?
questions.explanation:
The classical pathway of complement is activated by immune complexes or antigen-antibody complexes. (antigen bound to IgM or IgG).

Lipopolysaccharide of gram-negative bacteria activates the alternative complement pathway.

The binding of mannose-binding lectin to mannose residues (on the surfaces of Salmonella, Neisseria, and Listeria) activates the lectin complement pathway.

questions.question: In the alternate complement pathway, which of the following functions as C3 convertase?
questions.explanation:
C3 convertase in the alternate pathway is C3bBb.

In the classical pathway and lectin pathway, the C3 convertase is C4b2a.

questions.question: A 23-year-old girl presents with the finding shown below. She has a history of multiple similar episodes in the past and reports that some of her family members have similar complaints. She has no itching. Which of the following is deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
This girl presents with features of hereditary angioneurotic edema, which is due to a deficiency of C1 inhibitor.

Hereditary angioneurotic edema is an autosomal dominant disorder that is more common than complement deficiency states. A deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein. This increases the production of vasoactive peptides such as bradykinin. It causes episodes of edema affecting the skin and mucosal surfaces such as the larynx and the gastrointestinal tract. This may result in life-threatening asphyxia or nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea after minor trauma or emotional stress.

Note -

• C1, C2, C4 deficiency - collagen vascular disorders.

• C5-C8 deficiency - recurrent bacteremia with Neisseria

chapters.chapter: Structure And Functions Of The Immune System & Immune Response

questions.question: In which of the following areas do B lymphocytes reside?
questions.explanation:
B lymphocytes reside in the splenic follicles.

Lymphocytes are part of the adaptive immune system. They include B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow and then migrate to secondary lymphoid organs - follicles of spleen and in follicles of lymph nodes. T lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus. They are also present in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) of spleen and paracortex of lymph node.

In a lymph node, follicles may contain a central region called germinal centre. This contains B cells that have been stimulated by an antigen.

questions.question: A mother brings her 1-year-old child to the hospital with complaints that he turns blue while breastfeeding. It resolves when he assumes a squatting position. On examination, a cleft palate is seen. Labs show hypocalcemia. Which of the following abnormalities is expected to be seen in the lymphoid organs?
options: Decreased size of germinal centres of lymph nodes
Decreased size of paracortical areas of lymph nodes
Increased size of the peri arteriolar lymphoid sheath of spleen
questions.answer: B. Decreased size of paracortical areas of lymph nodes
questions.explanation:
Turning blue on breastfeeding with resolution on squatting describes a tet-spell or a cyanotic spell, indicating a congenital cardiac defect. Cleft palate, cardiac defects and hypocalcemia (parathyroid hypoplasia/aplasia) suggest a diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome. In this disorder, a decreased size of paracortical areas of lymph nodes is noted.

DiGeorge syndrome is characterised by thymic aplasia, causing a deficiency of T cells and absent cell-mediated immunity. Thus, paracortical areas of lymph nodes and periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen, where T cells reside, are reduced in size. B cells are usually not affected.

questions.question:
Match the following specialized macrophages with the tissues they are found in.

Cell
Tissue

I. Hofbauer cells
A. Kidney

II. Histiocytes
B. Placenta

III. Kupffer cells
C. Connective tissue

IV. Microglia
D. Liver

V. Mesangial cells
E. Brain
questions.answer: D. I-B; II-C; III-D; IV-E; V-A
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is I-B; II-C; III-D; IV-E; V-A.

Cell
Tissue

I. Hofbauer cells
B. Placenta

II. Histiocytes
C. Connective tissue

III. Kupffer cells
D. Liver

IV. Microglia
