questions.question: A child presents to the OPD with an infective skin lesion over his leg. On microscopic examination of the pus from the lesion, gram-positive cocci in chains are visualized and pus culture shows β-haemolytic colonies on blood agar. Which of the following tests can be performed to identify the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
β hemolytic colonies on blood agar with gram-positive cocci in chains seen on microscopy suggest the organism is a β-hemolytic streptococcus. Bacitracin sensitivity is used to differentiate between group A and group B β-hemolytic streptococci.

Group A: Bacitracin-sensitive (S. pyogenes)

Group B: Bacitracin-resistant (S. agalactiae)

Options A & B: Bile solubility and optochin sensitivity are used to differentiate Streptococcus pneumoniae and viridans streptococci. They are both α hemolytic on blood agar but some species of viridans streptocci are non hemolytic.

Option D: Catalase test is used to differentiate streptococcus and staphylococcus. Staphylococcus appear as clusters of gram positive cocci on microscopy and not chains.

questions.question: Which of the following bacteria is associated with the causation of colorectal carcinoma, rectal polyp, endocarditis and septicaemia and is pyrrolidinyl arylamidase test negative?
questions.explanation:
Streptococcus gallolyticus is associated with the causation of colorectal CA, rectal polyp, endocarditis, and septicemia and is pyrrolidinyl arylamidase test (PYR test) negative.

Streptococcus gallolyticus, formerly called Streptococcus bovis, is a non-enterococcal Group D streptococci. It is bile insoluble, esculin hydrolysis positive, PYR negative and shows no growth in 6.5% NaCl.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms can survive up to 60°C, is PYR positive, and can grow on media with 6.5% NaCl?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, Enterococcus feacalis can survive up to 60°C, is PYR test positive, and can grow in the presence of 6.5% NaCl.

Enterococci have the following features:

• Formation of tiny deep pink colonies on MacConkey’s medium

• Survives at 600C for 30 minutes.

• Growth in the presence of 40 % bile, 6.5% sodium chloride at pH 9.6.

• PYR (Pyrrolidonyl Arylamidase) positive

• Esculin hydrolysis is positive.

• Usually nonhemolytic, but may show α or β hemolysis.

Option A: Streptococcus pyogenes is a delicate organism, easily destroyed by heat (54°C for 30 min), PYR positive.

Option B: Streptococcus agalactiae is PYR test negative.

Option D: Streptococcus pneumoniae are readily destroyed by heat (52°C for 15 min).

questions.question: A patient admitted to an ICU spiked a fever and his blood culture was positive for gram-positive cocci in chains, which are catalase-negative. He was being given ceftazidime and amikacin via a central venous line for the past week. Following this, you started him on vancomycin but his blood culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. Which of the following is the most likely organism causing the infection?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) infection.

Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative suggest that the organism belongs to Streptococcaceae family. Positive culture after 2 weeks of vancomycin therapy suggests resistance to vancomycin.

Option A: Streptococcus pyogenes are sensitive to vancomycin and are not commonly implicated in central venous line infections.

Option B: Viridans streptococci are usually mouth commensals and are sensitive to vancomycin.

Option D: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are gram-positive cocci in clusters which are catalase-positive. Hence, they can be ruled out.

questions.question: Oral examination of a young patient shows the following finding. Which bacteria belonging to viridans group is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows dental caries which are commonly caused by Streptococcus mutans. It belongs to the viridans group/α-hemolytic streptococci.

Streptococcus mutans breaks down the dietary sucrose producing acid and a tough adhesive dextran. The acid damages dentine while the dextrans bind together with food debris, epithelial cells, mucus, and bacteria to form dental plaques, leading to formation of dental caries.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man presented with high-grade fever, cough and shortness of breath. On examination, he was febrile, tachypneic and tachycardic. A chest X-ray was performed which is shown in the image. What is the single most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the X-ray showing right lower lobe consolidation is strongly suggestive of lobar pneumonia, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (>95 % of cases).

Lobar pneumonia is an acute exudative inflammation of an entire pulmonary lobe. The below image shows the histopathological picture of lobar pneumonia.

questions.question: A 70-year-old male presented with fever, chills and cough associated with chest pain. His sputum sample was sent for culture on blood agar which showed the presence of α-hemolytic colonies the following day. Which of the following best describes the organism likely implicated here?
options: Gram-positive cocci in short chains, catalase negative and bile resistant
Gram-positive cocci in pairs, catalase negative and bile soluble
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase positive and coagulase positive
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase positive and coagulase negative
questions.answer: B. Gram-positive cocci in pairs, catalase negative and bile soluble
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the growth of alpha-hemolytic colonies from the sputum of the patient are strongly suggestive of pneumococcal pneumonia. Pneumococci are gram-positive cocci in pairs, catalase negative, and bile soluble.

The image below shows Gram positive cocci in pairs. bile solubility, and catalase reaction.

The image below shows positive bile solubility test shown by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The below image shows catalse test.

questions.question: Quellung reaction is used to demonstrate_______.
questions.explanation:
Quellung reaction is used to demonstrate the capsule of streptococci.

Quellung reaction (Quellung = swelling):

• A suspension of pneumococci is mixed on a slide with a drop of type-specific antiserum and a loop full of methylene blue solution.

• In the presence of homologous antiserum, the capsule becomes apparently swollen, sharply delineated and refractile.

• The Quellung test can be done directly with sputum from acute pneumonia cases.

The below image shows the swollen capsule of pneumococci following the addition of homologous antiserum.

questions.question: Which of the following factors is responsible for the draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies?
questions.explanation:
The factor responsible for the draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies is autolysin.

When pneumococci are incubated on blood agar for a prolonged duration, the resultant colonies are surrounded with concentric rings and have a central umbonation. This appearance of pneumococcal colonies is known as carrom coin appearance or draughtsman appearance.

Autolysin is an amidase enzyme produced by pneumococci that cleaves peptidoglycan, leading to the autolysis of cells. It is also responsible for the bile solubility of pneumococci.

The below image shows the characteristic draughtsman appearance of pneumococcal colonies.

questions.question: In a splenectomized patient, there is an increased risk of infection by all capsulated organisms. Which of the following is least likely to cause an infection in such patients?
questions.explanation:
In splenectomized patients, there is an increased risk of infection by capsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Staphylococcus aureus does not have a capsule and so poses no increased risk to these individuals.

The phagocytosis of capsulated organisms is prevented by their capsule. Thus, the body's main defence against these organisms is the spleen.

Certain components called opsonins attach to these capsulated organisms, and then they are delivered to the spleen, where their uptake is facilitated by receptors present on the surface of splenic phagocytes. After splenectomy, this defence mechanism is lost leaving patients susceptible to infection from these bacteria.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the pneumococcal vaccine?
options: Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine PPSV23 is indicated in splenectomized patients.
Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine PCV13 is contraindicated in children less than 2 years.
Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine PPV 23 gives protection for 10 years.
Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine is contraindicated if age > 65 years.
questions.answer: A. Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine PPSV23 is indicated in splenectomized patients.
questions.explanation:
Pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine PPSV23 is indicated in splenectomised patients.

There are two kinds of polyvalent pneumococcal vaccines:

1. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine - PPSV23

• It is indicated in splenectomized patients, sickle cell disease, immunocompromised patients, and patients above 65 years of age.

• CDC currently recommends the administration of one additional dose of PPSV23 at least 5 years after the last dose.

• Children younger than 2 years old should not get this vaccine since they fail to mount an adequate response.

2. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine-

• It includes PCV10 and PCV13.

• It is indicated in children less than 2 years.

questions.question: A child injures his knee while playing. A few days later, the wound on his knee shows signs of inflammation. The wound is cultured and its Gram-stained smear is given below. Further testing shows that the cultured organism is coagulase-positive. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
An infected wound culture showing Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters which are coagulase-positive suggest that the cultured organism is Staphylococcus aureus.

Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci that are catalase-positive. They grow in clusters because the cells divide successively in three perpendicular planes, with the daughter cells remaining attached to one another following each successive division. Among the 45 different species of Staphylococcus, Staphylococcus aureus is the only one which is coagulase positive.

Other options:

Option A: Streptococci are catalase negative. They are Gram-positive cocci arranged in chains.

Options C & D: S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are both coagulase negative.

Different bacteria with their typical arrangements are given below:

1. Staphylococcus: Clusters

2. Streptococcus: Chains

3. Pneumococcus: Pairs/lanceolate shaped

4. Micrococcus: Tetrads

questions.question: The specimen obtained by performing incision and drainage of a breast abscess was sent for culture on nutrient agar. An image of the culture plate is given below. Microscopy of the isolated organism revealed gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters. Which of the following is a false statement regarding this organism?
options: Golden yellow pigmentation is due to β-carotene
Pigment production is enhanced by adding milk to culture media
Confluent growth presents a characteristic 'oil-paint appearance'
questions.answer: A. Pigment production occurs optimally at 35°C.
questions.explanation:
Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters that produce golden-yellow pigment on nutrient agar is suggestive of Staphylococcus aureus. The pigment production occurs optimally at 22°C.

Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive coccus. On nutrient agar, its colonies are large (2-4 mm in diameter), convex, smooth, shiny, opaque and easily emulsifiable. The colonies appear golden yellow due to the presence of staphyloxanthin (carotenoid). Pigment production occurs optimally at 22°C and in aerobic conditions. It is enhanced when 1% glycerol or milk is incorporated in the medium.

On a nutrient agar slope, there is confluent growth of Staphylococcus, which appears as a characteristic oil-paint appearance.

questions.question: Which factor forms the basis of co-agglutination reaction shown by Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.explanation:
Protein A forms the basis of the co-agglutination reaction shown by Staphylococcus aureus.

Protein A bearing staphylococci are coated with IgG antiserum. Protein A binds to the Fc terminal of IgG, leaving the Fab terminal free to combine with its specific antigen. The corresponding antigen is then added to this mixture which causes agglutination of the bacteria. This is known as the co-agglutination reaction. It is used for streptococcal, gonococcal or hemophilus typing.

questions.question: Which of the following toxins exhibits hot-cold phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
β-hemolysin exhibits a hot-cold phenomenon.

β-hemolysin is a sphingomyelinase that is hemolytic only for sheep cells but not human cells. It initiates hemolysis at 370C but the hemolysis is evident only after chilling. This is called the hot-cold phenomenon.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus are called synergohymenotropic toxins?
questions.explanation:
γ-toxin and Panton-Valentine-toxin (leucocidin) of Staphylococcus aureus are called synergohymenotropic toxins.

Synergohymenotropic (synergo - working together, hymenotropic - form pores) toxins are a family of bicomponent toxins that act through the synergistic activity of 2 non-associated secretory proteins - class F and class S proteins. Gamma hemolysin has two components necessary for its hemolytic action. It is encoded by three genes HlgA and HlgC (belonging to class S) and HlgB (belonging to class F), resulting in 2 pairs of class S and F components - HlgA and HlgB, or HlgC and HlgB.

Panton-Valentine Leucocidin is composed of two components- S and F - encoded by two contiguous and cotranscribed genes, lukS-PV and lukF-PV. It is associated with the majority of community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA).

questions.question: A college student with a history of intravenous drug abuse presents with a fever for the last 3 weeks. Echocardiography is performed which reveals large friable vegetations on the cusps of the tricuspid valve. Which of the following organisms is the most common cause for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Fever with vegetations on the tricuspid valve points to a diagnosis of right-sided infective endocarditis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of right-sided infective endocarditis among intravenous drug abusers.

Infective endocarditis is the microbial infection of heart valves or endocardium, leading to the formation of vegetations (thrombotic debris and microbial organisms).The following image shows a graphical illustration of vegetations seen in infective endocarditis.

questions.question: By which of the following mechanisms is penicillin resistance commonly transferred to Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.explanation:
Penicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus is determined by plasmids that are most commonly transferred by transduction.

Penicillin resistance in Staphylococci most commonly occurs due to bacterial production of beta-lactamase, which inactivates penicillins by splitting their beta-lactam ring. These enzymes are inducible and are plasmid-mediated. They confer resistance to penicillin G, ampicillin, piperacillin etc.

The genetic transfer of antibiotic resistance can occur in the following ways:

• Transformation: After death or cell lysis, some bacteria release their DNA into the environment. Other bacteria, generally of the same species, can come into contact with these free DNA fragments, take them up and incorporate them into their DNA by recombination.

• Transduction: This method involves the transfer of DNA, episome or plasmid from one bacterium to another with the use of a bacteriophage.

• Conjugation: This mechanism requires the presence of a special plasmid called the F plasmid that codes for the sex pilus. It is the most common method of transfer of antibiotic resistance in most other bacteria.

Note: Change in penicillin binding proteins (PBPs) and production of β-lactamases are modes of penicillin resistance seen in S. aureus but the question asks for methods of transfer of drug resistance.

questions.question: An outbreak of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection was reported in the surgical ward of a hospital. Which of the following precautionary measures would you recommend to best curb its spread?
options: Administration of vancomycin empirically to all the patients
Wearing masks before performing invasive procedures
Washing of hands before & after treating the patients
questions.answer: D. Washing of hands before & after treating the patients
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, washing hands before and after treating the patients is the most effective way to curb the spread of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections.

In addition to this, personnel with active S. aureus lesions and carriers should be excluded from areas having patients at highest risk for severe staphylococcal infections like newborn nurseries, intensive care units, operating rooms, and cancer chemotherapy wards. In such individuals, the application of topical antiseptics such as mupirocin to nasal or perineal carriage sites may diminish the shedding of MRSA.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presented with multiple tender, erythematous fluctuant skin lesions as shown in the image. You suspect it to be a case of botryomycosis. Which of the following is the most likely organism implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of botryomycosis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Botryomycosis is a rare chronic bacterial granulomatous disease that usually involves the skin and rarely viscera. It is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus but can also be caused by Pseudomonas, Escherichia coli, Proteus, and Streptococci. Patients present with chronic, suppurative, granulomatous skin lesions like nodules, abscesses and sinuses.

Actinomycetoma, eumycetoma and botryomycosis are difficult to distinguish clinically but are readily distinguished with microbiologic testing or biopsy. Granules of botryomycosis consist of loose masses of cocci. Organisms can also be seen in wound discharge or histologic specimens.

questions.question: An 18-year-old girl presented with burning micturition and fever with chills for three days. Urine culture grew bacteria which were coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant. Which of the following is the most likely organism implicated here?
questions.explanation:
Burning micturition and fever with chills in a young woman points to a diagnosis of urinary tract infection (UTI). The most likely organism implicated here is Staphylococcus saprophyticus as it is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a part of the normal flora of human skin and periurethral area and thus is a common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in young women.

Option A: Staphylococcus aureus is a coagulase-positive bacterium. It is an uncommon cause of UTI.

Options B and C: Staphylococcus hominis and Staphylococcus epidermidis are coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive. They are usually considered contaminants if found on urine culture but they may also cause UTIs in children with underlying urinary tract abnormalities.

questions.question: Choose the incorrect statement regarding Micrococci.
options: It is rarely associated with disease.
questions.answer: D. It is arranged in chains.
questions.explanation:
Micrococci are arranged in pairs, tetrads or clusters of eight.

Micrococci are Gram-positive cocci that are often mistaken for S. aureus. However, they are larger in size and mostly occur in pairs, tetrads or clusters of eight. They form smaller colonies in culture in comparison to S. aureus. Hugh-Leifson oxidation-fermentation test can be used to differentiate between micrococci (oxidative pattern) and staphylococci (fermentative pattern).

Micrococci are catalase-positive and modified oxidase-positive. They are ordinarily non-pathogenic but can rarely cause infections in an immunocompromised host. They are part of normal bacterial flora in the body.

The following image shows the tetrad arrangement of micrococci:

Different bacteria with their typical arrangements are given below:

1. Staphylococcus: Clusters
2. Streptococcus: Chains
3. Pneumococcus: Pairs/lanceolate shaped
4. Micrococcus: Tetrads

questions.question: Which of the following organisms is capsulated?
questions.explanation:
Clostridium perfringens is the capsulated organism among the given options.

Most of the clostridial species are non-capsulated except C.perfringens and C.butyricum.

All clostridia are motile, with a peritrichate flagella, with the exception of:

• C. perfringens

• C. tetani type VI.

questions.question: A young man presented with complaints of severe abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea eight hours after consuming meat at a restaurant. A stool sample was sent for culture and the isolated organism showed this appearance on litmus milk fermentation. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the image showing stormy fermentation of lactose in litmus milk is suggestive of gastroenteritis caused by Clostridium perfingens type A.

The fermentation of lactose by this organism leads to the formation of acid which coagulates the casein in litmus milk. The clotted milk is disrupted due to vigorous gas production and this characteristic finding is obtained that is called stormy fermentation.

questions.question: Which of the following reactions are positive for Clostridium perfringens?
questions.answer: C. Target hemolysis, Reverse CAMP test
questions.explanation:
Target hemolysis and reverse CAMP test are positive for Clostridium perfringens.

A narrow zone of complete hemolysis due to θ-toxin and a wider zone of incomplete hemolysis due to α-toxin results in development of target hemolysis on blood agar by C. perfringens.

In the reverse CAMP test, C.perfringens is streaked over the centre of the plate and Streptococcus agalactiae is streaked at right angles to it. A positive reverse CAMP test shows the presence of an arrow-shaped zone of enhanced hemolysis pointing towards C.perfringens. α-toxin produced by C.perfringens interacts with the CAMP factor and produce synergistic hemolysis.

M'fadyean reaction is positive Bacillus anthracis.

The CAMP test is positive for Streptococcus agalactiae where it is inoculated on a plate streaked with Staphylococcus aureus.

Elek's test is positive for Corynebacterium diptheriae.

questions.question: A middle-aged diabetic man presented to the ER with severe abdominal pain, diarrhea and vomiting following consumption of pork and sweet potato curry. Following admission, the patient developed intra-abdominal sepsis and was taken into emergency surgery. Histopathology of the resected intestine showed mucosal necrosis. Which of the following toxins is likely implicated in his condition?
questions.explanation:
The condition described here is necrotising enteritis(pigbel) that is caused by β-toxin of Clostridium perfringens type-C.

This is a severe and often fatal enteritis caused by C.perfringens type C strains with heat-resistant spores that germinate in the intestine producing beta toxin, causing mucosal necrosis. The evocative name 'pigbel' is New Guinea pidgin for abdominal pain and diarrhea following unaccustomed feasting on pig meat along with trypsin inhibitors like sweet potatoes.

Immunisation with the type C toxoid has been shown to protect against this condition.

questions.question: Which of the toxins produced by clostridium species is the basis of Nagler's reaction?
questions.explanation:
α-toxin produced by Clostridium perfringens forms the basis of Nagler's reaction.

The α-toxin of C.perfringens has lecithinase activity. When C.perfringens is grown on a media containing egg yolk with the α-antitoxin spread on one half of the plate, colonies on the other half without the antitoxin will be surrounded by a zone of opacity. There will be no opacity around the colonies on the half of the plate with the antitoxin due to the specific neutralization of α-toxin. This is known as Nagler's reaction.

questions.question: A patient presents with a laceration over his leg following trauma with an unclean sharp metal rod 3 days ago. He also complains of difficulty in opening his mouth and abdominal cramps. Microscopy of the wound discharge revealed rod-shaped bacilli with terminal spherical spores. Which of the following is the organism most likely implicated here?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of tetanus caused by Clostridium tetani. It is a gram-positive, slender bacillus that has a spherical and terminal spore, giving it a characteristic drumstick appearance.

The genus clostridium consists of gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacilli.

Classification of Clostridium based on shape and position of spores:

• Central or equatorial: Clostridium bifermentans

• Subterminal: Clostridium perfringens, Clostridium novyi, and Clostridium botulinum

• Oval and terminal (tennis racket shaped ): Clostridium tertium and Clostridium difficile

• Spherical and terminal (drumstick appearance): Clostridium tetani

The below image shows the characteristic drumstick appearance of C. tetani.

questions.question: Which of the following is the first sign of generalized tetanus?
questions.explanation:
The first sign of generalized tetanus is increased tone of the masseter muscle, which results in trismus or lock-jaw.

Tetanus:

• Route of entry of organism- injury, unhygienic surgery, abortion/delivery, otitis media

• The incubation period is 6-10 days.

• First clinical sign- increased masseter tone (trismus/lock-jaw) followed by descending tetanus

• Deep tendon reflex is exaggerated.

• In neonates, difficulty in feeding is the usual presentation.

• Diagnosis is always clinical, microscopy is unreliable.

• Treatment includes cleaning the entry wound first in order to remove anaerobic foci of infection and prevent further toxin production. Metronidazole is preferred for antibiotic therapy. Antitoxin should be given early in an attempt to deactivate any circulating tetanus toxin. Spasms are controlled by heavy sedation with benzodiazepines. Symptomatic treatment is given for respiratory and cardiovascular derangements.

questions.question: Strychnine toxin acts by blocking the action of glycine at the post-synaptic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. Which of the following has a similar mechanism of action but acts presynaptically?
questions.explanation:
Tetanus toxin has similar mechanisms of action as strychnine but acts pre-synaptically.

Strychnine prevents the uptake of glycine at inhibitory synapses post-synaptically, while tetanospasmin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters like glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) pre-synaptically. This leads to increased release of acetylcholine, thereby leading to the development of spastic paralysis.

The image below depicts the mechanism of action of tetanus toxin.

questions.question: An 18-year-old girl presents with a contaminated wound sustained 4 hours ago. She had received complete immunization against tetanus 7 years ago. Which of the following injections should be given to her?
options: Human tetanus immunoglobulin and single dose of toxoid
questions.explanation: As she has received complete immunization against tetanus 7 years back, she should be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid for her contaminated wound.

questions.question: An elderly diabetic man presented to the ER with a contaminated wound with necrotic material. As a first-year surgical resident, which of the following would be your first step in treating the conditon?
questions.explanation:
Initial treatment for contaminated wounds with necrotic material is debridement.

A contaminated wound with necrotic material is suggestive of a higher risk of clostridial infection that may lead to gas gangrene. Emergent surgical exploration and thorough debridement are extremely important in the management of gas gangrene. Antibiotics (penicillin G plus clindamycin) and anti-gas gangrene serum have to be initiated after debridement. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may also be considered.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presented with sudden onset descending paralysis and blurred vision 3 days after the intake of canned food. On examination, the patient has quadriparesis with areflexia. Both the pupils are nonreactive. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette of acute onset descending flaccid paralysis with a history of consumption of canned food is suggestive of botulism.

The incubation period from ingestion of contaminated food to the onset of symptoms in food-borne botulism is usually 8–36 h but can be as long as 10 days and is dose-dependent. The clinical syndrome of botulism consists of bilateral cranial-nerve palsies that may progress to respiratory compromise, a bilateral descending flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles, and even death.

Cranial nerve deficits may manifest as some of the following:

• diplopia

• dysarthria

• dysphonia

• ptosis

• ophthalmoplegia

• facial paralysis and impaired gag reflex

The absence of cranial nerve palsies makes botulism highly unlikely, as does a lack of cranial nerve deficits at the onset of illness. Pupillary reflexes may be depressed and fixed or dilated pupils are sometimes noted.

The cornerstones of treatment for botulism are meticulous intensive care and administration of botulinum antitoxin.

Option A: In poliomyelitis, weakness is generally asymmetric, more proximal than distal, and may involve the legs (most commonly), the arms, or the abdominal, thoracic, or bulbar muscles.

Option C: Guillain–Barre syndrome is usually associated with ascending flaccid paralysis.

Option D: Tetanus causes spastic paralysis.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms is predominantly proteolytic in Robertson cooked meat medium?
questions.explanation:
Clostridium botulinum A is predominantly proteolytic in Robertson cooked meat medium.

In Robertson cooked meat media, the saccharolytic species like C.perfringens, C.difficile, and C.septicum turn the meat pink, while the proteolytic species such as C.botulinum A turn the meat black.

Examples of predominantly proteolytic clostridia:

• C.bifermentans

• C.botulinum A, B, F

• C.histolyticum

C. tetani is slightly proteolytic but not saccharolytic.

Examples of predominantly saccharolytic clostridia:

• C.perfringens

• C.septicum

• C.novyi

• C.difficile

C.botulinum C, D and E are saccharolytic but not proteolytic.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms form the citron bodies?
questions.explanation:
Citron bodies are boat or leaf-shaped pleomorphic bacteria, usually associated with Clostridium septicum.

It is a gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacterium.

Gram stain morphology of Clostridium septicum from CSF (a) and blood culture (b) in 1000× magnification with spore formation(arrow) is shown below.

questions.question:
An elderly diabetic lady was brought to the hospital with complaints of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. She had recently been treated with intravenous clindamycin for cellulitis. She was febrile at the time of examination and the blood reports revealed a Hb level of 12g/dl; WBC count of 18000/mm3; and C-reactive protein 160mg/l. What is the most sensitive test to detect the causative organism?

Hemoglobin: 12g/dl
WBC count: 18000/mm3
C-reactive protein: 160mg/l
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette of a patient having diarrhea following antibiotic administration is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile. Toxigenic culture is the most sensitive method for the detection of Clostridium difficle infection.

The methods for diagnosis of Clostridium difficle infection are:

• Toxigenic culture- Anaerobic incubation of the sample in cycloserine-cefoxitin-fructose agar (CCFA) or its variant for several days. This is followed by identification of the organism in the growth and tests to confirm toxin production. This method has a sensitivity of 100%.

• Cell cytotoxicity neutralization assay (CCNA)- A stool filtrate is prepared and applied onto a monolayer of an appropriate cell line. The cells are observed for toxin-induced cytopathic effect (CPE). This is followed by a neutralization assay to confirm that the CPE is attributable to C.difficile toxins. Sensitivity is around 75-85% when compared to toxigenic culture (reference standard)

• Nucleic acid amplification tests (e.g.PCR)- More sensitive (93.3%) for C.difficile detection than toxin immunoassays but less sensitive than toxigenic culture.

• Toxin immunoassays- Enzyme immunoassays using monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies against C.difficile toxins. Sensitivity is lower than other tests.

• Glutamate dehydrogenase immunoassays- Detects glutamate dehydrogenase, a metabolic enzyme produced by all isolates of C.difficile (toxigenic and nontoxigenic). The test is highly sensitive but has low specificity.

questions.question: Which of the following bacilli characteristically shows the M’Fadyean’s reaction?
questions.explanation:
M'Fadyean’s reaction is shown by Bacillus anthracis.

When a blood film containing anthrax bacilli is stained with polychrome methylene blue for a few seconds and examined under the microscope, amorphous purplish material is noticed around the bacilli. This represents the capsular material and is called M'Fadyean’s reaction.

The following micrograph shows M'Fadyean's reaction:

questions.question: A dairy farmer presented to the dermatology OPD with an ulcer with central black eschar over the forearm. Which of the following media can be used as a selective medium for the growth of the likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Based on his profession and clinical description of the lesion, the diagnosis is most likely to be cutaneous anthrax (most common form of anthrax) caused by Bacillus anthracis. The selective medium for this organism is PLET (polymyxin-lysozyme-EDTA-thallous acetate) medium.

Other options:

Option B: Buffered charcoal yeast extract medium is used for Legionella.

Option C: Cetrimide agar is a selective medium for Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Option D: Mannitol, Egg Yolk, Phenol red, Polymyxin Agar (MYPA) medium is a selective medium for Bacillus cereus.

questions.question: A swab was taken from an ulcer and sent to the laboratory for culture. The following image depicts a blood agar culture plate on which gamma phage suspension has been applied. Which of the following is the most likely organism implicated?
questions.explanation:
The given image with a circular spot of diminished growth in the culture plate from a swab from an ulcer depicts the gamma phage lysis assay. The most likely organism implicated is Bacillus Anthracis.

This test is performed by inoculating Bacillus Anthracis in sheep blood agar followed by the application of gamma phage suspension over one area of the culture plate. The gamma phage suspension inhibits the growth of Bacillus anthracis colonies resulting in an an area of diminished growth called a plaque.

questions.question: Which of the following tests is used for the diagnosis of anthrax?
questions.explanation:
Ascoli's thermoprecipitation test is used for the diagnosis of anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. It is an example of a ring precipitation test.

Option A: Paul-Bunnell test is used to diagnose infectious mononucleosis.

Option B: Kahn test is used to diagnose syphilis.

Option D: Rose-Waaler test is used to diagnose rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: A young patient presented to the medicine OPD with complaints of nausea and vomiting. He gave a history of having fried rice from a local Chinese restaurant a few hours ago. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Based on the symptoms and a history of consuming fried rice 6 hours ago, we can diagnose this to be a case of food poisoning due to Bacillus cereus.

Food poisoning cause by B. cereus is of two types:

Bacillus cereus
Diarrheal type
Emetic type

1-5 hours

Preformed

Heat stable

Food items
Meat
Rice

Clinical feature
Diarrhea, abdominal cramps
Vomiting, abdominal cramps

questions.question: Which of the following is the component of mycobacteria which makes it acid fast?
questions.explanation:
Mycobacteria are acid-fast due to the presence of mycolic acid in their cell walls.

On being stained with carbol fuchsin or fluorescent dyes such as auramine-O or rhodamine, they resist decolourization by 20% sulphuric acid and absolute alcohol for 10 minutes. This property is referred to as acid and alcohol fastness and is routinely used to identify mycobacteria.

questions.question: A patient presents early in the morning to the DOTS center to provide sputum samples. Which of the following reagents are used in the digestion and decontamination of his samples before smear preparation?
questions.explanation:
NaOH and N-acetylcysteine are used for the digestion and decontamination of sputum used in smear preparation for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Sputum and specimens from non-sterile sites need prior treatment for digestion (to liquefy the thick pus), decontamination (to inhibit the normal flora), and concentration (to increase the yield) before they can be used for testing.

Methods used for digestion and decontamination of sputum:

• Petroff’s method- Uses 4% NaOH and HCl.

• N-acetyl cysteine (NALC) + 2% NaOH - NALC liquefies the sputum and NaOH kills the normal flora. This method is better suited for automated culture systems and is superior to Petroff’s method.

Note: Formalin or hypochlorite can be used only if smear microscopy is being done. They are not useful for culture or animal pathogenicity testing.

questions.question: A patient with suspected tuberculosis gives a sputum sample for microscopic examination. What is the minimum number of acid-fast bacilli that should be present in 1 mL of sputum for them to be detected by this method?
questions.explanation:
At least 10,000 acid-fast bacilli should be present per milliliter of sputum for them to be readily demonstrable in direct smears.

questions.question: A patient has chronic cough with occasional blood in the sputum. He has a history of significant weight loss and night sweats. Which of the following media cannot be used to culture the organism causing his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
This patient with chronic cough and hemoptysis with a concurrent history of significant weight loss and night sweats most likely has tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. McLeod's medium is not used to culture M. tuberculosis. It is a selective medium for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Culture media used to cultivate Mycobacterium tuberculosis include:

• Solid- Loeffler's medium is a serum-containing solid medium used for the culture of M. tuberculosis. Other solid media used include Lowenstein- Jensen medium, Dorset medium, Tarshis medium, and Pawlowsky's medium.

• Liquid- Middlebrook’s media are used for the preparation of antigens and vaccines and in sensitivity testing. Other examples of liquid mycobacterial culture media include Dubos' medium, Sula's medium and Sauton's medium.

• Automated culture methods:

•

• BACTEC 460- uses radioisotopes for detection

• BacT alert- colorimetric method of detection

• BACTEC MGIT- fluorometric detection method.

questions.question: A microbiology resident is performing liquid automated culture on the sputum sample of a TB suspect patient. Which of the following culture media would he not use for the same?
questions.explanation:
Tarshis medium is a solid growth medium used for culturing mycobacterium species. Versatrek, BactiAlert, and BACTEC MGIT 960 are liquid automated cultures used for tuberculosis.

The diagnostic tools for TB are as follows:

1. Sputum microscopy for AFB

• Ziehl Neelson staining

• Fluorescence staining

2. Culture

• Solid media– Lowenstein-Jensen (most common), Petragnini and Dorset, Tarshis, Loeffler, Pawlowsky.

• Liquid automated culture – Versatrek, BactiAlert, BACTEC MGIT 960 (MGIT stands for Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube)

• Drug Sensitivity Testing / Proportionate Sensitivity Testing:

• Using MGIT, LJ medium

3. Rapid molecular diagnostic testing

• Line probe assay

• CB-NAAT- Nucleic acid amplification test using GeneXpert system

4. Other diagnostic tools are as follows:

• Chest X-ray

• Tuberculin sensitivity testing

questions.question: Which of the following tests can simultaneously detect TB and rifampicin resistance in <2 hours?
questions.explanation:
Xpert MTB/RIF detects tuberculosis (TB) and rifampicin resistance simultaneously within 2 hours. It is a fully automated, real-time nucleic acid amplification technology, with high specificity and sensitivity.

The WHO recommends its use worldwide as the initial diagnostic test in adults and children who are presumed to have multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) or HIV-associated TB. Xpert MTB/RIF should also be the first test applied to the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients in whom tubercular meningitis is suspected as well as a replacement test (over conventional microscopy, culture, and histopathology) for gastric lavage, pleural and other biopsies, and fine-needle aspiration specimens.

The image below shows the Xpert MTB/RIF system.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a method of testing drug susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Disc diffusion method is used for drug susceptibility testing for most bacteria; however, it is not used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The disc diffusion technique is not suitable for testing Mycobacterium tuberculosis because the organism grows so slowly that the drug has time to diffuse throughout the medium, and sharp zones of inhibition are not seen.

Methods used in the drug susceptibility testing of M.tb include:

Conventional drug-sensitivity testing
Radiometric Techniques

Molecular methods

1. Proportion method

2. Absolute concentration method

3. Resistance ratio method

1. BACTEC 460

2. MB/BacT

3. Mycobacteria growth indicator tube (MGIT)

4. VersaTREK

1. PCR-based assays

2. DNA probe-based

3. DNA microarray

4. GeneXpert

For agar-based methods, 7H10 or 7H11 Middlebrook media are used and only the proportion method can be applied.

Radiometric techniques measure the metabolic activity of the bacteria. Based on changes in these values, drug susceptibility can be estimated.

questions.question: A urine LAM (Lipoarabinomannan) assay was performed in an HIV +ve patient with a CD4+ count of 40/μL. Infection with which of the following organisms can be diagnosed using this test?
questions.explanation:
Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis.

Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in the mycobacterial cell wall, released from metabolically active cells or degenerating cells of patients having tuberculosis. Urine LAM is a useful tool in diagnosing tuberculosis, especially in patients with HIV and low CD4+ T cell count.

Most diagnostic tests for tuberculosis rely on sputum samples, which are difficult to obtain and have low sensitivity in immunocompromised patients, patients with disseminated TB, and children, delaying treatment initiation. Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) is the only WHO-endorsed TB biomarker that can be detected in urine, an easily collected sample.

questions.question: A middle-aged man came with a history of fever and night sweats for the past 2 weeks. He has had noticeable weight loss. Bronchoalveolar lavage was done, but Mycobacterium tuberculosis was not detected. Extra-pulmonary TB is suspected. Which site is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Lymph nodes are the most common site of extrapulmonary TB.

The diagnosis is established by fine needle aspiration biopsy.

In descending order of frequency, the extrapulmonary sites most commonly involved in TB are:

• lymph nodes

• pleura

• genitourinary tract

• bones and joints

• meninges, peritoneum and pericardium.

In less than 50% of these cases, there is associated pulmonary disease.

questions.question: Your neighbour is worried about a scar on her 5-month-old daughter's arm that is shown below. She tells you the child has received all vaccines on time. Which of the following statements is true about the vaccine that caused this finding?
options: Distilled water is used as diluent for this vaccine
The route of administration is subcutaneous
WHO recommends Danish 1331 strain for vaccine
questions.answer: D. WHO recommends Danish 1331 strain for vaccine
questions.explanation:
The scar shown in the image results from the BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) vaccine. The WHO recommends Danish 1331 strain for BCG vaccine production.

Normal saline is recommended as the diluent for the BCG vaccine as distilled water is an irritant.

The dose administered is 0.1ml containing 0.1mg.

It is administered intradermally by using 26 gauge tuberculin syringe on the left deltoid.

questions.question: You are performing the pre-employment check up of a young man. You need to perform a tuberculin skin test as a part of this process. Which of the following tests would you not use for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
QuantiFERON-TB gold is not a type of tuberculin skin test. It is a type of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), a whole-blood test that can aid in diagnosing Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

There are 3 described methods for tuberculin skin testing (TST):

• Mantoux test, also known as the Pirquet test (preferred method)

• Heaf test

• Tine test

In contrast, IGRAs that have been approved by the FDA are:

• QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QFT-GIT)

• T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot)

• QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus)

IGRA is not used in India due to a higher probability of a false positive due to universal BCG vaccination. It can also lead to a diagnosis of active TB in a patient with latent TB and may lead to overtreatment. This test is banned in India after the WHO advised against it in low and middle-income countries.

questions.question: Which of the following is a pigment-producing species of mycobacteria?
questions.explanation:
Mycobacterium scrofulaceum is a pigment-producing species of mycobacteria.

M. scrofulaceum is a scotochromogen which produces yellow or orange colored pigments, even in the dark. It belongs to group II of Runyon's classification. It can cause scrofula or cervical adenitis in children.

M.ulcerans, M.avium intracellulare complex (MAC), and M. xenopi belong to group III-non photochromogens as they do not form pigment even on exposure to light.

questions.question: A microbiologist working with mycobacteria notes moist, smooth, flat, white colonies growing on Lowenstein-Jensen media. Which species of mycobacteria is she likely studying?
questions.explanation:
The species of mycobacteria being studied here is Mycobacterium bovis. It forms moist, smooth, flat, white colonies on Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) media that break-up easily when touched.

Mycobacterium bovis belongs to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. It causes tuberculosis-like disease in humans.

Lowenstein–Jensen medium is a commonly used, egg-based, selective media for mycobacteria. It contains:

1. Egg- Provides fatty acids and protein required for metabolism

2. Malachite green- Prevents the growth of contaminants. Makes it a selective medium.

3. Mineral salt solution- Buffer

4. Glycerol- Source of carbon, favors growth of M. tuberculosis, but not M. bovis. LJ medium without glycerol, which contains pyruvate, is used for culture of M. bovis.

5. L-asparagine- Nitrogen source

The image below shows M.bovis colonies on LJ media.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis colonies on LJ medium are dry, rough, raised and irregular with a wrinkled surface. They are creamy white or buff-colored, tenacious and difficult to emulsify(rough, tough, buff).

questions.question:
The following findings are obtained during biochemical testing of a mycobacterial species. Identify the organism.

• Catalase - Strongly positive

• Peroxidase - Negative

• Niacin - Positive

• Arylsulfatase - Positive
questions.explanation:
The given biochemical findings are characteristic of Mycobacterium simiae. Eventhough atypical mycobacteria or non-tuberculous mycobacteria(NTM) are usually niacin test negative, some NTM like M. simiae and M. chelonae give a positive niacin test positive.

questions.question: A 54-year-old male presents with an ulcer on his hand. On swab culture, growth of M. ulcerans is seen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Mycobacterium ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer.

M. ulcerans produces a toxin called mycolactone which leads to formation of Buruli ulcer. This is a chronic, debilitating, necrotizing disease of the skin and soft tissue which is characterized by the formation of ulcers that progressively enlarge over time if left untreated. The ulcers heal with disfiguring scars.

The image below shows a Buruli ulcer.

Option A: Hunner's ulcers are seen in a subset of patients with interstitial cystitis. These are areas of inflammation on the bladder wall.

The image below shows a cystoscopic image of a Hunner's ulcer.

Option B: Meleney's ulcer or post-operative synergistic bacterial gangrene occurs in immuno-compromised individuals following abdominal surgery. It is caused by a synergistic interaction between microaerophilic nonhemolytic Streptococcus and hemolytic aerobic Staphylococcus aureus.

Option D: Marjolin ulcer is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds.

The image below shows a Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man who works at an aquarium and handles the fish without protective equipment presents to the OPD with the following finding. Infection with which of the following bacteria led to his condition?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a fish tank granuloma that is caused by M. marinum.

The typical clinical presentation is as a single, small violet papule or nodule confined to one extremity, developing 2-3 weeks after trauma. The nodule may break down to form an indolent ulcer. M. marinarum is a natural pathogen of fish and amphibians, which spreads to humans who come in contact with contaminated swimming pools or fish tanks.

Other non-tuberculous mycobacteria causing disease in humans include:

• M. kansasii: Disease resembles pulmonary TB

• M. scrofulaceum: Cervical lymphadenitis

• M. avium complex: Pulmonary, disseminated TB, especially in AIDS patients

• M. fortuitum: Nail salon furunculosis

M. paratuberculosis (aka Johne’s bacillus) causes Johne’s disease in cattle. It is associated with Crohn’s disease in humans.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the microbiological diagnosis of the disease afflicting the patient shown below?
options: Acid fast staining is done by Ziehl-Neelsen technique, using 25% sulphuric acid
Sample should be collected from the centre of the lesion
The number of samples to be collected is 3-4
It is cultivated in nine banded armadillos and foot pads of mice
questions.answer: D. It is cultivated in nine banded armadillos and foot pads of mice
questions.explanation:
The image depicts leonine facies in a patient suffering from leprosy or Hansen's disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It is cultivated in nine-banded armadillos and footpads of mice.

M. leprae is a Gram-positive, weakly acid fast bacillus. Thus, 5% sulphuric acid (option A) is used for decolourisation to demonstrate M.leprae's acid-fastness. On microscopy, the bacilli appear bound together in masses called globi, within which they are arranged in a 'cigar bundle' appearance.

For leprosy diagnosis, specimens are collected from the nasal mucosa, skin lesions and earlobes. Nasal smears are collected from the internal septum of the nose. Skin smears are collected from the edges of the lesions (option B) rather than from the centre. Slit skin smears are taken as well. The skin is pinched up tight to minimise bleeding and a cut is made with a scalpel, deep enough to get into the infiltrated layers. This is done over the buttocks, forehead, chin, cheek, and ears (at least 5-6 different areas) (option C).

questions.question: What is the generation time of lepra bacilli?
questions.explanation:
The generation time of lepra bacilli is 12-13 days.

Generation time, also known as doubling time, is the time it takes for the bacterial population to double. It can also be measured as the time between two cell divisions under optimum conditions. The generation time of different bacilli are given below:

• Lepra bacilli- 12-13 days average (may vary from 8-42 days)

• Tubercle bacilli- 15-20 hours

• Coliform bacilli- 20 minutes

questions.question: What are the bacteria present in Virchow's cells?
questions.explanation:
The bacteria present in Virchow’s cells is M. leprae.

Lepromatous leprosy lesions contain large aggregates of lipid laden macrophages (lepra cells/Virchow cells) which are often filled with globi (masses) of acid fast bacilli.

The image below shows a high-power Fite-Faraco stain of a skin lesion showing globi of M.leprae.

questions.question:
You counsel a patient with leprosy about lepra reactions before starting her on multidrug therapy. Which among these is correct regarding these reactions?

1. Type 1 reactions are unrelated to drug therapy, whereas as type 2 may occur within a year of starting treatment.

2. Type 1 reaction is seen in the borderline spectrum and type 2 is seen in lepromatous leprosy.

3. New lesions appear in type 1 and they are tender and erythematous

4. Fever, keratitis, iritis, and nephritis can occur with a type 2 reaction.

5. Steroids are the drug of choice for severe type 1 reactions.
questions.explanation:
Statements 2, 4, and 5 regarding lepra reactions are correct.

Type 2 lepra reactions are unrelated to drug therapy, whereas type 1 reactions may occur within a year of starting treatment.

New lesions typically appear in type 2 lepra reactions. They are tender and erythematous subcutaneous and dermal nodules. Existing lesions show no changes.

questions.question: A patient diagnosed with leprosy was undergoing further evaluation for classification of type and immune response. Which of the following statements is false regarding the intradermal test used in such evaluation?
options: It has no value in prognostication of leprosy
BCG vaccine may convert a negative test to positive
questions.answer: B. It has no value in prognostication of leprosy
questions.explanation:
The lepromin test has value as a prognostic test for leprosy.

The lepromin, or Mitsuda test, is a method to measure cellular immunity in leprosy. It is a skin test for delayed hypersensitivity to lepra antigens. A bacillary suspension of inactivated M. leprae is injected just under the skin and the induration reaction is measured 3–4 weeks after.

It is used to classify leprosy. A negative lepromin test is seen in lepromatous and borderline leprosy. It is negative in children <6 months of age, it may be positive at the end of 1st year. BCG vaccine is capable of converting a negative lepromin test to a positive.

questions.question: You are performing the test shown in the image on a patient. How many days later do you ask the patient to return so that you get an accurate read on the Mitsuda reaction?
questions.explanation:
Mitsuda's reaction is read in the 3rd week, i.e., on the 21st day or 20 days after the day of injection.

Lepromin test is a skin test for delayed hypersensitivity to lepra antigens. It is the only method for studying immunity in leprosy. A bacillary suspension of inactivated M. leprae is injected just under the skin.

The first reaction to occur is the early reaction of Fernandez, which consists of erythema and induration developing in 24-48 hours. It usually remains for 3-5 days; it is usually poorly defined and carries less significance. The second and more meaningful result is the late reaction of Mitsuda, starting at 1-2 weeks (7-10 days), reaching a peak in three or four weeks, and gradually subsiding over the next few weeks. On the 21st day, if there is a nodule more than 5 mm in diameter, the reaction is said to be positive.

Note: The 21st day is 20 days after the day of injection which is counted as the 1st day.

questions.question: A leprosy vaccine is being introduced on a pilot basis in India. Which of the following mycobacterial species is the basis for its development?
questions.explanation:
Mycobacterium indicus pranii is the basis for the development of a leprosy vaccine.

The leprosy vaccine species was originally called Mycobacterium W (M.w) but was later renamed Mycobacterium indicus pranii. The vaccine is administered via intradermal route. The dose is 0.1 ml. It is divided into two equal doses and given on both arms.

Booster doses will be given to maintain the immunity level. These are given only in one arm.

questions.question: An old woman presented to the OPD with dysuria and frequent micturition. Urinalysis showed pus cells, and culture on MacConkey agar showed the following. Which organism is involved here?
questions.explanation:
This patient who presented with dysuria and frequent micturition with urinalysis showing pus cells, and growth of lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar suggests a diagnosis of urinary tract infection by Escherichia coli.

Enterobacteriaceae family is classified based on their action on lactose present in MacConkey's medium as:

• Lactose fermenters - Escherichia, Klebsiella

• Late lactose fermenters - Shigella sonnei

• Non-lactose fermenters- Salmonella species, Shigella species

The image below shows lactose fermenting and non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar.

Mnemonic to remember non-lactose fermenters: (SPY PSM)

• Salmonella

• Proteus

• Yersinia

• Providencia- late fermenter

• Shigella (except S.sonnei which is a late lactose fermenter)

• Morganella

questions.question:
The stool culture of a patient with suspected food poisoning produced hemolytic colonies on blood agar. The isolated organism gave a positive indole test and a positive MUG test. You observe the following colonies on eosin methylene blue agar. Identify the organism.

MUG - 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-glucuronide
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of a patient with suspected food poisoning with stool culture growing hemolytic colony on blood agar with a positive indole test and MUG test with a iridescent green colony growth on eosin methylene blue agar is characteristic of Escherichia coli.

E. coli produces the enzyme β-glucuronidase which is tested using the MUG test. In it, the substrate MUG (4-methylumbelliferyl-β-glucuronide) is reduced by the enzyme to produce a fluorescent color which indicates a positive MUG test.

questions.question: What is the cut-off for bacteriuria beyond which a diagnosis of catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) can be made?
questions.explanation:
The cut-off value for bacteriuria to diagnose catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) is >103 CFU/mL.

The minimum criterion for catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (CA-ASB) is >102 CFU/mL.

questions.question: A tourist came to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and watery diarrhea. Which of the following strains of E. coli is most commonly implicated in this case?
questions.explanation:
This patient with watery diarrhea most likely has traveller’s diarrhea caused by Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).

Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common organism that causes diarrhea in travelers. It produces the following toxins:

• LT (heat-labile toxin) - acts by ↑cAMP

• ST (heat-stable toxin) - two types of ST are known, ST-A (ST-I) and ST-B (ST-II)

• ST-A is soluble in methanol and acts by ↑ cGMP in the intestine.

• ST-B is insoluble in methanol, and the mode of action is not known.

Other options:

Option A: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes infantile diarrhea in developing countries. It adheres to the mucosal surface of the small intestine using E. coli adherent factor (EAF) and locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) and causes effacement of microvilli.

Option B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) produces verocytotoxin, which targets vascular endothelium. It causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome.

Option D: Enteroinvasive E.coli (EIEC) invades interstitial epithelial cells in the intestine and causes a condition resembling shigellosis. This ability is determined by a plasmid, which can be detected as a diagnostic test.

questions.question: You are investigating an outbreak of diarrhea. You find out that the etiological agent causes stacked-brick formation on hep-2 cells as shown below. What is the likely organism?
questions.explanation:
The stacked-brick pattern of adherence on hep-2 cells is caused by enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC).

Enteroaggregative E. coli has been associated with persistent diarrhea. Intestinal colonization of EAEC is mediated by aggregative adherence fimbriae (AAF). EAST-1 toxin (enteroaggregative heat-stable toxin) is considered to be a major virulence factor for EAEC.

The given image shows the stacked-brick pattern of adherence on microscopy at 600x magnification.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman presented with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. She was diagnosed with hemolytic uremic syndrome and treated with plasmapheresis and dialysis. What is false about the infectious causative agent?
options: It does not produce a Shiga like toxin
There is person to person transmission.
questions.answer: B. It does not produce a Shiga like toxin
questions.explanation:
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) is caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) serotype O157:H7. It produces a Shiga like toxin, therefore EHEC is also known as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC).

Other options:

Option A - Strains of E. coli producing verocytotoxin or Shiga toxin (stx2a-g) can cause diarrheal disease ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal hemorrhagic colitis and HUS. The most common EHEC belongs to serotype O157:H7.

Option C - In EHEC diarrhea, fecal leukocytes are commonly seen (70%) but although it is an infectious condition, fever is not seen. The absence of fever can lead to its misdiagnosis as a non-infectious condition such as intussusception or ischemic bowel disease.

Option D - The disease is transmitted through contaminated feces. Person-to-person transmission can occur if infected persons do not wash their hands after using the toilet or after changing diapers.

Note: Shiga toxin produced by S. dysenteriae is referred to as Stx.

questions.question: Sereny test was employed for laboratory diagnosis of which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
The Sereny test is an animal pathogenicity test that used to be employed for laboratory diagnosis of enteroinvasive E. coli and Shigella.

Freshly isolated suspension of bacteria is instilled into the eyes of guinea pigs which leads to mucopurulent conjunctivitis and severe keratitis.

It is not in use anymore as we have better methods of detecting toxigenicity now like molecular methods.

questions.question: What is the culture media used to differentiate E. coli O157:H7 from other E. coli?
options: Thiosulphate citrate Bile salt sucrose medium
questions.explanation:
Sorbitol-MacConkey agar is used to differentiate E. coli O157:H7 from other E. coli.

E. coli O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol and produces pale colonies on Sorbitol-MacConkey agar. All other strains of E. coli ferment sorbitol. Thus they produce pink colonies on Sorbitol-MacConkey agar.

O157:H7 strains do not contain β-glucuronidase and so are unable to use the substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-glucuronide(MUG). Thus, they give a negative MUG test.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false?
options: E.coli is an aerobe and facultative anaerobe.
Proteus infection increases risk of uric acid stones.
E.coli is motile by peritrichous flagella.
Proteus can metabolise phenylalanine to phenylpyruvic acid.
questions.answer: B. Proteus infection increases risk of uric acid stones.
questions.explanation:
Proteus increases the risk of struvite stones in the bladder as it leads to the alkalinisation of urine. Struvite stones are magnesium-ammonium phosphate stones that appear as rectangular/coffin-lid crystals shaped on urine microscopy. Uric acid stones are precipitated in acidic urine.

Proteus produces enzyme phenylalanine deaminase which converts phenylalanine to phenyl pyruvic acid. This property is the basis for the phenylalanine deaminase test.

The test is performed by inoculating the organism in phenylalanine agar. After incubation, 10% ferric chloride is added to the media. If phenyl pyruvic acid was produced, it will react with the ferric chloride and turn dark green. If the medium remains a straw colour, the organism is negative for phenylalanine deaminase production.

E. coli is an aerobe and facultative anaerobe. Its motility is due to the presence of peritrichous flagella. It is the most common cause of urinary tract infections.

questions.question: Which of the following shows Dienes phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Dienes phenomenon is exhibited by Proteus mirabilis.

When two identical strains of Proteus are inoculated at different places of the same culture plate, the resulting swarms of growth coalesce and no line is formed between swarming cultures of the same strain. However, if they are from two different strains, the spreading films of growth fail to coalesce and remain separated by a narrow but easily visible furrow (known as Dienes line). This is known as Dienes phenomenon.

The image below shows Dienes phenomenon.

questions.question: Blood culture of the sputum sample taken from a patient diagnosed with hospital-acquired pneumonia, showed a characteristic phenomenon as shown in the image. Identify the bacteria that exhibit this phenomenon.
questions.explanation:
The given image of the blood culture finding shows the characteristic bull's eye swarming pattern exhibited by Proteus.

Proteus species move very actively with the help of peritrichous flagella, resulting in swarming on solid media. It can be suppressed by the addition of:

• phenyl ethyl alcohol

• chloral hydrate

• sulphonamides

• sodium azide

• boric acid

• increasing the concentration of agar to 6%.

Swarming does not occur on MacConkey medium and cystine-lactose-electrolyte-deficient (CLED) medium.

Proteus is a gram-negative bacillus seen as a normal gastrointestinal flora. The two most common species causing infection in humans are P. mirabilis and P. vulgaris, which can be differentiated by spot indole test. P. mirabilis is indole negative while P. vulgaris is indole positive. Production of urease enzyme by Proteus, which hydrolyses urea to ammonia causes alkalinization of urine. Alkalinization of urine leads to the precipitation of organic and inorganic compounds which contributes to the formation of Struvite stones. P. mirabilis is associated with urinary tract infections while P. vulgaris is usually associated with wound and soft tissue infections.

Other organisms that show swarming include:

• Clostridium tetani

• Vibrio parahaemolyticus

• Serratia

questions.question: A middle-aged man from north India presents with a deformity as shown in the image below. He gives a history of foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge before this nodule appeared. Which of the following organisms is responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
The above image and clinical scenario are suggestive of rhinoscleroma and it is caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.

K. rhinoscleromatis is a gram-negative bacillus also known as Frisch bacillus. It is endemic in north India. Rhinoscleroma is characterized by chronic granulomatous hypertrophy of the nose. Biopsy of the lesion shows:

• Mikulicz cells- large foamy cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated, cytoplasm containing causative bacilli.

• Russell bodies- eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in the plasma cells. These are also observed in multiple myeloma.

Other options:

Option A: Rhinosporidium seeberi causes rhinosporidiosis.

Option C: K. ozaenae causes atrophic rhinitis.

Option D: K. oxytoca is associated with hemorrhagic colitis.

questions.question: You notice a sputum sample of a patient suspected of having ventilator-associated pneumonia turns progressively redder over time. Microscopic examination of the sample reveals an absence of red blood cells. Which of the following organisms could have caused this?
questions.explanation:
The given condition of sputum sample turning redder over time can be caused by Serratia marcescens.

Serratia marcescens are pleomorphic coccobacilli that can grow in sputum after collection and can mimic hemoptysis because they produce a red pigment called prodigiosin.

S. macescens mainly cause healthcare-associated infections such as ventilator-associated pneumonia, meningitis, endocarditis, septicemia and peritonitis. They can contaminate IV fluids, surgical instruments, and antiseptic solutions.

questions.question: A 19-year-old boy presented with a single painless papule on his penis with no enlarged lymph nodes. A smear was made from the lesion and stained with Wright- Giemsa stain which showed the finding as shown in the following picture. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette and the image showing Donovan bodies in Wright/Giemsa-stained impression smears indicate a diagnosis of donovanosis caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. They appear as rounded coccobacilli within cystic spaces in large mononuclear cells (called Pund cells).

Klebsiella granulomatis shows bipolar condensation of chromatin giving a safety pin appearance.

Bipolar staining (safety pin appearance) is shown by:

• H. ducreyi

• Vibrio parahaemolyticus

• Klebsiella granulomatis

• Yersinia pestis

• Burkholderia pseudomallei

• Burkholderia mallei

questions.question: A child presents with a high fever, acute abdominal pain, and malaise. The child passes small amounts of bloody mucopurulent stools with increasing tenesmus and cramps. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Acute onset of symptoms (fever, abdominal cramps) with dysentery (bloody mucopurulent stools) and tenesmus is most likely due to Shigella dysenteriae.

Shigella dysenteriae is a Gram-negative bacillus causing bacillary dysentery in humans. It is spread through faeco-oral transmission.

Other options:

Option A: Vibrio cholerae results in watery diarrhea with characteristic rice watery stools.

Option B: Viruses such as rotavirus and norovirus causes watery diarrhea through mucosal irritation.

Option D: Entamoeba histolytica results in gradual onset of symptoms usually 1-3 weeks with dysentery.

questions.question:
Which of the following toxins acts by inhibiting protein synthesis?

(ETEC - Enterotoxigenic E. coli)
questions.explanation:
Shiga toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis.

Shiga toxin or verotoxin is an exotoxin produced by Shigella species. It consists of two subunits A and B. The B subunit binds to globotriaosylceramide receptors on the target cell, and then, the A subunit gets internalized. The A subunit leads to inhibition of 60S ribosome, leading to shut down of protein synthesis. Its site of action is in the endothelial cells of small blood vessels of GIT.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy developed bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen did not ferment lactose or mannitol. Which of the following organisms is implicated here?
questions.explanation:
Shigella dysenteriae does not ferment mannitol and lactose.

Shigella species cause bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps). They do not ferment lactose, except S.sonnei which is a late lactose fermenter. To differentiate between the various Shigella species, mannitol fermentation is noted.
