questions.question: Which of the following differentiates meningococcus from gonococcus?
questions.explanation:
Only meningococcus can ferment maltose, whereas both gonococcus and meningococcus can ferment glucose.

Both species are catalase and oxidase positive and neither of them can reduce nitrate. The only Neisseria species that can reduce nitrate is N. mucosa.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man has treatment-resistant gonorrhea. You plan to send a sample of his urethral discharge to the lab for culture and sensitivity testing. What transport media would you use for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Stuart’s medium is the transport media used for Neisseria gonorrheae and Neisseria meningitidis.

Stuart’s medium is a semisolid, non-nutrient medium, which prevents microbial proliferation. It ensures that microorganisms present are able to survive for a sufficiently long period of time.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common manifestation of gonorrhoea in males?
questions.explanation:
Gonorrhea in males most commonly manifests as acute urethritis.

In males, the disease starts as acute urethritis. This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis. Chronic urethritis may lead to stricture formation. The infection may also spread to the periurethral tissues causing abscesses and multiple discharging sinuses (watercan perineum).

In females, the initial infection involves the cervix, uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. The vaginal mucosa is not usually affected in adults because the stratified squamous epithelium is resistant to infection by the cocci, and also because of the acidic pH of vaginal secretions.

Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) which may also occur following Chlamydia trachomatis infection.

questions.question: A patient with a history of sexual intercourse with a commercial sex worker 3 days back has developed genital discharge resembling 'flow of seed' as shown below. What medium should be used for the culture of the discharge?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of gonococcal urethritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Thayer-Martin and modified Thayer-Martin media are used for the culture of this organism. Gonorrhoea may manifest as mucopurulent genital discharge which can be described as resembling 'flow of seed' (semen).

Thayer-Martin medium contains vancomycin, colistin and nystatin.

Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by N. gonorrhea. The major symptoms include urethritis, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria. In the laboratory diagnosis of N. gonorrhea, the discharge on Gram's stain reveals gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. It acidifies glucose but not maltose in serum sugars. Stuart's medium is used for transport while Thayer-Martin agar is used as a selective medium used to isolate N. gonorrhoeae. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar.

Stuart’s medium is the transport media used for Neisseria gonorrhea and Neisseria meningitides. It is a semisolid, non-nutrient medium. Charcoal present in the medium neutralizes certain bacterial inhibitors while a reducing agent prevents oxidation.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a content of modified Thayer-Martin medium?
questions.explanation:
Modified Thayer-Martin medium does not include polymyxin B. It includes polymyxin E, which is also known as colistin.

Modified Thayer–Martin medium is a selective media for Neisseria species. It includes:

• Vancomycin - to inhibit most gram-positive bacteria.

• Colistin (Polymyxin E) - to inhibit most gram-negative bacteria other than Neisseria.

• Nystatin or anisomycin - to inhibit yeast.

• Trimethoprim - to inhibit proteus.

The contents of the Thayer-Martin medium are the same as that of the modified Thayer-Martin medium except for the presence of trimethoprim in the modified version. The image below depicts Thayer-Martin medium.

questions.question: An unresponsive middle-aged man with fever and petechial rashes was rushed into the ER. You successfully resuscitate him. Abdominal ultrasound shows bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Which of the following statements is false regarding his condition?
options: Patients who recover may suffer from sloughing of the skin
The implicated organism can be isolated from the petechial rashes
The causative organism is Neisseria gonorrheae
Hypoplastic spleen is a risk factor for this condition
questions.answer: C. The causative organism is Neisseria gonorrheae
questions.explanation:
The above scenario depicts Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome which is a complication seen in infection with meningococci. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is also known as hemorrhagic adrenalitis or fulminant meningococcemia and is characterized by bilateral adrenal gland hemorrhage.

Though Waterhouse-Freiderichsen syndrome is most often associated with meningococcal septicemia, it may complicate sepsis caused by other organisms like certain streptococcal species also. Hypoplastic spleen may also be associated with this condition and the implicated organism can be isolated from the petechial rashes.

Complications :

• Shock, extensive hemorrhage within the skin

• May fall into a coma

• Death, usually after a few hours, due to adrenal insufficiency

• Patients who recover may suffer from extensive sloughing of the skin and loss of digits due to gangrene.

Fulminant meningococcemia is a medical emergency and needs to be treated with adequate antibiotics as fast as possible. Ceftriaxone is an antibiotic commonly used nowadays.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of recurrent pelvic inflammatory disease presents to the OPD with fever and right upper abdominal pain. A diagnostic laparoscopy was done and the findings are as given below. Which of the following organisms could be the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The scenario depicted is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome which is a rare complication of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) following infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

It causes liver capsule inflammation leading to the creation of violin-string adhesions which can be seen on laparoscopy. On CT imaging it appears as perihepatic inflammatory stranding and hepatic capsular enhancement.

The major symptom and signs include right upper quadrant pain. It is also associated with minimal pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, or cervical motion tenderness.

questions.question: Which is the true statement regarding gonococcal urethritis?
options: Symptoms are more severe in females than in males
Infection does not involve rectum and prostate
Dysuria is the most common presentation
Single dose of cefixime is the first line of treatment
questions.answer: C. Dysuria is the most common presentation
questions.explanation:
Acute urethritis is the most common clinical manifestation of gonorrhea in males and major symptoms include urethral discharge and dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency.

Other options:

Option A: The stratified squamous epithelium of the vagina is resistant to gonococcus, so infection is less severe in females.

Option B: In males, it can involve rectum, prostate, and epididymitis, but it never involves testes.

Option D: Rising minimum inhibitory concentration of cefixime worldwide has led the CDC to discontinue its recommendation of this agent as first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea.

Third-generation cephalosporins have remained highly effective as single-dose therapy for gonorrhoea. Ceftriaxone (250mg, IM) single dose + azithromycin 1 g PO, single dose or doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 7 days is given. This also covers treatment for chlamydia (if chlamydial infection is not ruled out).

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
options: It is exclusively a human pathogen
Some strains may cause disseminated disease
Vaccination has no role in prevention
Drug resistance is only due to acquisition of plasmids
questions.answer: D. Drug resistance is only due to acquisition of plasmids
questions.explanation:
Neisseria gonorrheae acquires resistance to antibiotics either by chromosomal mutations or by the acquisition of plasmids (R factors). These resistant strains are also known as:

• PPNG - penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae (plasmid-borne resistance)

• TRNG - tetracycline-resistant N. gonorrhoeae (plasmid-borne resistance)

• CMRNG - chromosomally mediated resistance in N. gonorrhoeae (resistance to both penicillin and tetracycline)

• QRNG - quinolone resistant N. gonorrhoeae (due to alterations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV)

Other options:

Option A: N. gonorrhea is a fastidious organism and is exclusively a human pathogen.

Option B: Some strains of N. gonorrhea can ascend up the genital tract and can lead to many disseminated diseases such as septic arthritis and pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option C: Vaccines are not effective against N. gonorrhea due to its antigenic variation and ability to invade neurophils.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Moraxella catarrhalis?
options: An uncommon cause of COPD exacerbation
questions.explanation:
Moraxella catarrhalis is a DNAse positive gram-negative diplococcus. It is the second most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations (after H. influenzae). It can also cause otitis media, sinusitis, tracheobronchitis, and pneumonia.

It differs from pathogenic Neisseria as:

• It does not ferment any carbohydrates - Asaccharolytic

• Gives a positive tributyrin hydrolysis test.

• Shows positive DNAse test.

Angular conjunctivitis is caused by Moraxella lacunata, which is a gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria.

Treatment is with oral amoxicillin and clauvulanic acid.

questions.question: Transovarial transmission is a feature of which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Transovarial transmission is a feature of Orientia tsutsugamushi which causes scrub typhus.

Transovarial transmission refers to passing on the disease-causing bacteria from parent arthropod to offspring arthropod. Orientia tsutsugamushi is maintained by transovarial transmission in trombiculid mites. It is also seen in Rickettsia rickettsii, Rickettsia conorii, and Rickettsia akari.

The image below shows a trombiculid mite.

Trench fever (option D) is caused by Bartonella quintana.

questions.question: A 36-year-old trekker presented with fever, headache, and rashes following a tick bite. He was later diagnosed to have Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Which of the following statements is false about the microbe implicated?
questions.explanation:
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. A cell wall is present in rickettsial organisms.

Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular, gram-negative pleomorphic coccobacilli. They are unable to grow in cell-free media and are thus cultured in yolk sacs of embryonated eggs. They are non-motile, non-capsulated organisms that contain both DNA and RNA. They reproduce by binary fission and are transmitted by arthropods like ticks and lice (except Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella henselae).

The rickettsiae are localized in endothelial cells of small blood vessels (except Ehrlichia and Anaplasma) in humans. They cause endothelial cell enlargement and degeneration, predisposing to thrombus formation. Tetracyclines, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones are effective against this group but, beta-lactams are ineffective.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding endemic murine typhus?
questions.explanation:
The vector for endemic murine typhus is the rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis.

Endemic murine typhus is cuased by Rickettsia typhi (option B) while epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. The zoonotic reservoir for R. typhi is the rat. Humans are infected when flea feces contaminate pruritic bite lesions. Transmission can also occur via inhalation of aerosols of dried feces of rickettsemic rat flea. No man-to-man transmission occurs. Patients present with fever, chills, vomiting and a maculopapular rash that is more prominent on the trunk. Diagnosis is by serology and treatment is with doxycycline.

When male guinea pigs are inoculated intraperitoneally with blood from a case of endemic typhus, they develop fever and a characteristic scrotal inflammation. The scrotum becomes enlarged and the testes cannot be pushed into the abdomen. This is known as the Neil-Mooser reaction. It is positive with Rickettsia typhi (option D) and negative with Rickettsia prowazekii.

The image below shows the rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis.

questions.question: Multiple inmates at a prison are suspected to have epidemic typhus following an arthropod infestation. Which of the following vectors is implicated in the spread of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Louse (image B), Pediculus humanus corporis, transmits epidemic typhus.

Gaol fever/ Jail fever/ epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man from Kashmir presents with fever, chills and rash for 1 week. The rash appeared on the 5th day of the fever starting from the trunk and progressing to the limbs. Epidemic typhus is suspected. Which of the following statements is incorrect about the disease?
options: Brill-Zinsser disease is a recrudescent form
Rash is present on palms and soles
questions.answer: C. Rash is present on palms and soles
questions.explanation:
Epidemic typhus rash spares the palms and soles.

Epidemic typhus, caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, is transmitted by the louse Pediculus humanus corporis. There is no transovarial transmission of R. prowazekii. The disease spreads through infected louse feces deposited when the louse feeds on the human host. It is commonly seen in poor unhygienic or cold conditions.

Epidemic typhus starts with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, starting on the trunk and spreading over the limbs but sparing the face, palms, and soles. In some patients who recover from epidemic typhus, the rickettsiae may remain latent in the lymphoid tissues or organs for years. Such latent infection may, at times, be reactivated leading to recrudescent typhus (Brill-Zinsser disease).

Transovarial transmission refers to passing on the disease-causing bacteria from parent arthropod to offspring arthropod. It occurs with Orientia tsutsugamushi, Rickettsia rickettsii, R. conorii and R. akari.

Note: Rash on palms and soles is typically described in Rocky Mountain spotted fever, secondary syphilis and hand, foot, and mouth disease

The image below shows the rash of epidemic typhus.

questions.question: What is the drug of choice for scrub typhus?
questions.explanation:
The drug of choice for scrub typhus is doxycycline.

To treat scrub typhus, oral doxycycline 100 mg is given twice daily for 7–15 days. In the case of pregnant women, oral azithromycin 500 mg for 3 days may be used as doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Scrub typhus is a rickettsial infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is a trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, myalgia, meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK alone is agglutinated in scrub typhus.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man came with complaints of fever and a skin lesion as shown below. He gives a history of hiking in scrub forests a week prior, where he suffered an insect bite. On examination, there is regional lymphadenopathy and a maculopapular rash. Which of the following arthropods is involved in the spread of this disease?
questions.explanation:
A history of contact with scrub vegetation with fever, regional lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, and eschar at the bite site is suggestive of scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by trombiculid mite. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 7-14 days is the drug of choice for treatment of scrub typhus in adults. In case of pregnant women and children, azithromycin or chloramphenicol may be preferred where doxycycline is relatively contraindicated.

questions.question: A wildlife photographer presents with a blackish lesion at the site of an insect bite from a few days back. He also gives a history of fever. A positive Weil-Felix test with OX K agglutinins was observed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
In the above clinical scenario, a history of insect bite followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the site of the bite and a positive Weil-Felix test with OX K agglutinins suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus.

Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX 19, OX 2, and OX K. The basis of the test is sharing an alkali stable carbohydrate antigen by some Rickettsiae and by some strains of Proteus.

questions.question: A veterinarian presents with new-onset mitral regurgitation and fever. An echo reveals valve vegetations and blood cultures show no growth. Q fever is suspected. Which of the following statements is false regarding the organism implicated?
questions.explanation:
Coxiella burnetii is the causative organism of Q fever. It is transmitted by ixodid ticks in animals; however, it is not transmitted to humans via ticks.

Coxiella burnetii is a filterable, obligate intracellular pathogen. They are gram-negative but are better stained with Gimenez, Giemsa stains. They are heat resistant and hence survive Holder's method of pasteurization.

Q fever is a zoonosis and the primary source of human infection are infected cattle, sheep, and goats. It spreads through the inhalational route. Veterinarians are at higher risk due to increased exposure. Acute disease resembles influenza, nonbacterial (atypical) pneumonia, and hepatitis. Chronic disease presents as culture-negative bacterial endocarditis in patients with valvular heart disease.

questions.question: A patient presents with redness of the eye and foreign body sensation. On examination, there is follicular hypertrophy in the lower lids and moderately abundant exudates. Chlamydial infection is suspected. Which strains could have caused this condition?
options: Serotypes A, B, Ba and C
questions.explanation:
Redness, foreign body sensation with follicular hypertrophy in the lower lids and moderately abundant exudates suggests inclusion conjunctivitis which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D to K.

Inclusion conjunctivitis is a type of acute follicular conjunctivitis caused by C. trachomatis serotypes D to K. The infection is transmitted to the eye from genitals, or contaminated swimming pools. Patients present with foreign body sensation, redness and mucopurulent discharge. On examination, there is acute follicular hypertrophy of the lower palpebral conjunctiva and fornix, non-tender pre-auricularlymphadenopathy and superficial keratitis in upper half of cornea.

C. trachomatis is a Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria. It cannot produce ATP. It causes a variety of human diseases (ocular and genitourinary) and has two main biological variants:

• TRIC biovar which causes trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC biovar). This is further divided into 12 serological variants:

• A, B, Ba, C serovars which cause blinding or endemic trachoma

• D to K servovars which cause inclusion conjunctivitis

• LGV biovar (L1, L2, L3 serotypes) which causes lymphogranuloma venereum

questions.question: A thick, yellowish discharge is noted from the eyes of a five-day-old neonate in the step-down ward during rounds. An iodine-stained smear of the exudates is positive for large cytoplasmic inclusions as shown in the image. Which of the following is false about the organism responsible for the above condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a thick yellowish discharge from the eye showing iodine-stained inclusion bodies is suggestive of inclusion conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. As chlamydia is a bacteria, it possesses both DNA and RNA.

Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular organisms that produce basophilic inclusion bodies. They are filterable like viruses. They are called energy parasites as they lack enzymes for ATP synthesis. They cannot grow on artificial media but can grow on cell lines like McCoy, HeLa, or the yolk sac of the chick embryo.

Chlamydiae occur in two forms, the elementary body and the reticulate body. The extracellular, infective form is called the elementary body. The intracellular, non-infective, growing, and replicative form is called the reticulate body. These are found inside a membrane-bound compartment called the inclusion body which can be visualized within infected epithelial cells by iodine or Giemsa stain. The cell wall of the reticulate body is fragile and pliable, leading to pleomorphism.

questions.question: A poultry worker was admitted to ICU with severe pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage was done; it showed Levinthal Cole Lillie bodies. Which of the following is the causative organism for the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Pneumonia in a poultry worker with Levinthal-Cole-Lillie bodies on bronchoalveolar lavage specimens is suggestive of psittacosis.

Levinthal-Cole-Lillie bodies are inclusion bodies of Chlamydia psittaci seen in infected cells including alveolar macrophages from patients suffering from psittacosis. C. psittaci can be transmitted to humans by direct contact with infected birds or by inhalation of aerosols from avian feather dust. Psittacosis presents with fever, chills, muscular aches and pains, severe headache, hepatosplenomegaly and gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe pneumonia may develop. It is treated with tetracycline.

questions.question: A patient presented with painful swellings on both sides of the groin as shown in the image. The clinician suspects lymphogranuloma venereum. Which is the most common serovar causing the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused most commonly by Chlamydia trachomatis LGV serovar L2.

LGV is a sexually transmitted disease, characterized by suppurative inguinal adenitis.

questions.question: Lesion scrapings from a genital ulcer show numerous polymorphs, but no bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate culture medium for organisms responsible for the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Clinical scrapings from a genital ulcer showing polymorphs in the absence of bacteria is suggestive of chlamydial infection and the most appropriate culture medium is McCoy cells (human synovial carcinoma cell line).

C. trachomatis is a small gram-negative bacte­rium and an obligate intracellular parasite that appears as an intracytoplasmic inclusion body. The gram stain of the cervical smear would show leucocytes but no organisms. Hence, selective culture media like the McCoy cells culture is used to isolate the organism.

Option B: Thayer–Martin agar is used for isolation of Neisseria spp.

Option C: Robertson’s cooked meat is used for the culture of anaerobes, especially Clostridia

Option D: Pleuropneumonia-like organisms (PPLO) broth is used to culture Mycoplasma spp. and Ureaplasma spp.

Note: Abnormal urethral gram stain showing >10 PMNs/1000Å~ field in women with dysuria but without coliform bacteriuria supports the diagnosis of chlamydial urethritis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of mucopurulent cervical discharge. Gram staining of the discharge revealed numerous pus cells, but no organisms. What is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of this infection?
questions.explanation:
Mucopurulent cervical discharge for 3 days is suggestive of acute cervicitis. As gram stain does not show any organism, gonococcal infection is less likely. In this case, Chlamydia trachomatis is the most likely organism. For C. trachomatis, the investigation of choice is the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT).

NAATs are the most sensitive tests to detect chlamydia. These tests also have a high specificity comparable to culture, and in contrast to culture, do not depend on viable pathogens. Therefore, NAATs are generally considered the test of choice for chlamydia and have replaced culture as the diagnostic gold standard.

Mucopurulent cervicitis is the inflammation of the columnar epithelium and subepithelium of the endocervix in women. Its commonly caused by Neiserria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

questions.question: Which of the following microbes is also referred to as Eaton's agent ?
questions.explanation:
Eaton's agent refers to Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Eaton was the first to isolate Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Because it was filterable, it was considered to be a virus previously.

It was formerly known as PPLO– Pleuro pneumonia-like organism.

questions.question: A 20-year-old military recruit presented with fever, sore throat, and non-productive cough which showed no improvement with beta-lactam antibiotics. X-ray showed peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings. Primary atypical pneumonia is suspected. Which of the following statements is false regarding the organism responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario of fever, non-productive cough, no improvement with beta-lactam antibiotics along with X-ray features showing peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings is suggestive of Mycoplasma pneumonia, also known as primary atypical pneumonia or walking pneumonia.

Mycoplasmas are not obligate intracellular parasites. They are free-living bacteria devoid of cell walls. They are highly pleomorphic, with no fixed shape or size.

Because of their plasticity, they can pass through bacterial filters and have often been mistaken for viruses.

Mycoplasmas do not possess spores, flagella, or fimbria. Some species exhibit gliding motility. Mycoplasmas are gram-negative, but are better stained by Giemsa stain.

questions.question: Diene’s method of staining is used for which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Diene's method is used for mycoplasma.

Mycoplasma shows a ‘fried-egg’ colony on Diene’s method of staining. The central dark bluish area represents the area of mycoplasmal down growth whereas the pale blue periphery indicates superficial growth of mycoplasma on the agar.

questions.question: Mycoplasma is inherently resistant to which of the following antibiotics?
questions.explanation:
Mycoplasma is inherently resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.

Mycoplasma lack cell wall, and therefore, are inherently resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics as these drugs act on the cell wall.

questions.question: Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
.The given image shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy.

Treponemes are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals.

Option A: Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends as shown in the image below

Option C: Borrelia are large with irregular and wide open coils.

Option D: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral rod (bacilli) that is not classified as a spirochete.

questions.question: A 30-year-old truck driver presented with a painless ulcer in the genital area. On examination, a single ulcer with an indurated base was found. An image of the tissue section is shown below. Identify the staining method.
questions.explanation:
The given image shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by Levaditi's method. Single painless ulcer with indurated base points towards the diagnosis of syphilis.

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacillus. It is a sexually transmitted infection. Intrauterine transmission can lead to congenital syphilis.

It shows corkscrew motility which can be demonstrated by darkfield microscopy.

Treponema can be stained by silver impregnation methods.

• Fontana's method is used on smear

• Levaditi's method is used for tissue sections

The clinical manifestations of syphilis include:

Primary syphilis: The typical primary chancre usually begins as a single painless papule that rapidly becomes eroded and usually becomes indurated, with a characteristic cartilaginous consistency on palpation of the edge and base of the ulcer.

Inguinal lymphadenopathy is bilateral and may occur with anal as well as with genital chancres. The chancre generally heals within 4–6 weeks (range, 2–12 weeks), but lymphadenopathy may persist for months.

Secondary syphilis: The various features include mucocutaneous or cutaneous lesions and generalized nontender lymphadenopathy. macular, papular, papulosquamous, and occasionally pustular syphilides. Other features of secondary syphilis include sore throat, fever, weight loss, malaise, anorexia, headache, and meningismus. Ocular findings associated with secondary (or later/ unknown-stage) syphilis include pupillary abnormalities and optic neuritis as well as the classic iritis or uveitis.

Latent syphilis: Early latent syphilis is limited to the first year after infection, whereas late latent syphilis is defined as that of 1 year’s duration (or of unknown duration). T. pallidum may still seed the bloodstream intermittently during the latent stage, and latent syphilis in a pregnant woman may infect the fetus in utero.

Neurosyphilis: The major clinical categories of symptomatic neurosyphilis include meningeal, meningovascular, and parenchymatous syphilis.

Cardiovascular syphilis: Cardiovascular involvement results in uncomplicated aortitis, aortic regurgitation, saccular aneurysm (usually of the ascending aorta), or coronary ostial stenosis.

Congenital syphilis: The earliest manifestations of congenital syphilis include rhinitis, or “snuffles”; mucocutaneous lesions, bone changes, including periostitis detectable by x-ray examination of long bones; hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis.

Serologic tests for syphilis recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):

1. Screening or diagnosis (RPR or VDRL),

2. Quantitative measurement of antibody to assess clinical syphilis activity or to monitor response to therapy (RPR or VDRL)

3. Confirmation of a syphilis diagnosis in a patient with a reactive RPR or VDRL test (FTA-ABS, TPHA, EIA/CIA)

Treatment of syphilis is with 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.

questions.question: What type of motility is shown by Treponema pallidum?
questions.explanation:
Treponema pallidum show corkscrew motility, i.e movement by rotation around the long axis.

The characteristic feature of spirochetes is the presence of endoflagella, situated between the outer membrane and cell wall, that facilitates this movement.

questions.question: A 32-year-old pregnant lady tests VDRL positive at her 1st-trimester antenatal check-up. An FTA-ABS confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following is a false statement about the organism causing this disease?
options: It cannot be cultured in vitro
Endoflagella is in the periplasmic space.
Humans are the only known natural hosts
questions.explanation:
VDRL positive status is suggestive of syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum. Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) is a confirmatory test.

Reiter’s strain is a cultivable, non-pathogenic treponeme, showing morphological and antigenic similarities with T.pallidum. It is widely used as the antigen in group-specific treponemal tests for the diagnosis of syphilis.

Nichol's strain is virulent and non-cultivable in artificial media. However, it can be grown in cell culture through serial passage in live rabbit testes.

questions.question: A patient had a solitary, painless penile ulcer 2 months back. Now, he presents with a generalized maculopapular rash over the body. What is the sensitivity of VDRL at this stage of the disease?
questions.explanation:
The sensitivity of VDRL is 100% in secondary syphilis. History of solitary painless ulcer with a generalized maculopapular rash is consistent with secondary syphilis.

The VDRL test becomes positive 4–5 weeks after exposure to T. pallidum and 1–2 weeks after the appearance of the chancre.

The VDRL test is a highly sensitive test. The sensitivity of the test depends on the stage of the disease:

• Primary syphilis- 60–75%

• Secondary syphilis- 100%

• High antibody titers may be found in patients developing gummatous lesions and neurovascular or cardiovascular complications.

• Tertiary syphilis- usually negative

• Negative test:

• Early primary syphilis

• Latent acquired syphilis

• Late congenital syphilis

Secondary syphilis is the most infective stage in the course of the illness. The patient may present with a roseolar or papular skin rash, condyloma lata, and mucous patches.

The image below shows lesions of secondary syphilis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding the serological tests of syphilis?
options: Rapid plasma reagin test is a group specific treponemal test
VDRL test is the test of choice for response to therapy
VDRL is the test of choice for examining CSF
Treponemal tests are likely to remain reactive even after adequate therapy
questions.answer: A. Rapid plasma reagin test is a group specific treponemal test
questions.explanation:
RPR is a non-specific test. It uses the VDRL antigen (cardiolipin) containing carbon particles. Hence, results can be seen by the naked eye, whereas VDRL requires a microscope for visualization of flocculation.

The test of choice for monitoring response to treatment and for examining CSF is VDRL

The test of choice for syphilis screening is RPR.

After treatment, in early syphilis,

• Non-treponemal tests- titers decline or become non-reactive

• Treponemal tests- remain reactive

For diagnosis of syphilis, a 2 test approach is used i.e., screening with an NTT (non-treponemal test) which includes either VDRL or RPR. Confirmation of syphilis is done by a treponemal test, most commonly by TPHA (Treponema pallidum hemagglutination test).

Follow-up is done using NTT (as treponemal tests remains positive for years after treatment).

questions.question: A 55-year old man was brought to the OPD with complaints of rapid decline in cognition, impaired position, and vibratory sense. There is a history of sporadic short-term relationships with many promiscuous sexual partners. Romberg’s sign is positive and bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils are seen on checking for pupillary reflex. Which of the following is the investigation of choice?
questions.answer: B. Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario given above with a positive sexual history, Romberg test, and Argyll Robertson pupils is suggestive of neurosyphilis. The investigation of choice for neurosyphilis is VDRL.

The CSF VDRL test is highly specific and, when reactive, is considered diagnostic of neurosyphilis.

Involvement of the CNS in syphilis is detected by examination of CSF for:

• Mononuclear pleocytosis (>5 white blood cells/μL).

• Increased protein concentration (>45 mg/dL).

• CSF VDRL reactivity.

questions.question: You treated a case of secondary syphilis with a single dose of benzathine penicillin-G 2.4 million IU IM. What follow-up advice would you give for the assessment of the patient's response to treatment?
options: Follow up with VDRL after 6 months and 12 months
Follow up with VDRL after 3 months and 6 months
Follow up with TPHA after 6 months and 12 months
Follow up with TPHA after 3 months and 6 months
questions.answer: A. Follow up with VDRL after 6 months and 12 months
questions.explanation:
The investigation used to assess response to treatment in syphilis is VDRL. In the case of secondary syphilis, follow-up VDRL should be done at 6 months and 12 months.

VDRL and RPR become negative after adequate treatment whereas specific treponemal tests remain positive indefinitely despite treatment.

Guidelines for follow up:

• Patients with primary or secondary syphilis should be examined 6 and 12 months after treatment.

• Patients with latent or late syphilis should be examined at 6, 12, and 24 months after treatment.

questions.question: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks of gestational age tested VDRL positive but negative for specific treponemal tests. What is your interpretation?
questions.explanation:
Pregnancy can give rise to false-positive VDRL.

Biological false-positive (BFP) reactions are defined as positive reactions obtained in non-specific treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) with negative results in specific treponemal tests, in the absence of past or present treponemal infections and not caused by technical faults.

questions.question: A 2-month-old infant presented with a runny nose and bullous lesions on the skin and legs. Her X-ray (given below) showed features suggestive of periostitis. Which of the following is the initial investigation of choice?
questions.answer: A. Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test
questions.explanation:
The newborn baby has characteristic signs and symptoms of congenital syphilis. Periostitis is a hallmark of skeletal manifestation. VDRL or RPR is the initial investigation of choice in congenital syphilis.

The earliest manifestations of congenital syphilis include rhinitis, or “snuffles”; mucocutaneous lesions, bone changes, including periostitis detectable by x-ray examination of long bones; hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis.

All neonates born to mothers who have reactive nontreponemal and treponemal test results should be evaluated with a quantitative nontreponemal serologic test (RPR or VDRL) performed on the neonate’s serum, because umbilical cord blood can become contaminated with maternal blood and yield a false-positive result.

FTA-ABS or TPHA is used for confirmation of syphilis in a patient with reactive RPR or VDRL test.
T. pallidum cannot be detected by culture.

questions.question: What is the causative agent of yaws ?
questions.explanation:
Causative agent of yaws is Treponema pertenue.

It is one of the endemic treponematoses that spreads by direct contact.

The image shows ulcerative skin lesions seen in yaws.

Causative agent

T. pallidum
Venereal syphilis

T. carateum

questions.question: What is the causative organism and the corresponding vector for epidemic relapsing fever?
questions.explanation:
Epidemic relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia recurrentis and is transmitted by louse.

Endemic relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia duttoni, Borrelia hermsii, Borrelia parkeri, etc, and is transmitted by ticks.

questions.question: During a louse outbreak among jail inmates, a few of them developed fevers that subsided after 3-5 days. The fever relapsed after a week and subsided again. Many patients had tender splenomegaly on examination. Which culture medium is used to isolate the organism implicated here?
options: Mannitol, egg-yolk, phenol red, polymyxin agar
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of louse-born relapsing fever (LBRF) caused by Borrelia recurrentis. Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly broth medium is used to isolate all Borrelia species except for B.miyaotoi.

Tender splenomegaly and relapsing fever in the background of a louse outbreak point towards the diagnosis of LBRF.

It was very common during wars and in the jails of former days but with improvements in hygiene and the discovery of insecticides, it has now become rare.

questions.question: Which one of the following micro-organisms uses antigenic variation as a major means of evading the host immune system?
questions.explanation:
Borrelia recurrentis uses antigenic variation as a major means of evading the host immune system. It causes relapsing fever.

Borrelia readily undergoes antigenic variations in vivo and this is believed to be the reason for the occurrence of relapses in the disease. Antigenic variations occur because of DNA rearrangements in linear plasmids present in borrelia.

questions.question: A 23 year old presented with fever, myalgia, and skin lesion as shown in the image. What is the causative organism for the above condition?
questions.explanation:
The image shows erythema migrans, seen in Lyme disease. It is caused by Borrelia Burgdoferi.

The lesion has a target center with partial central clearing and a bright red outer border. It usually begins as a red macule or papule at the site of the tick bite.

The tick implicated is the black-legged tick, Ixodes scapularis, shown in the image below.

The most severe manifestation of Lyme disease is Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), reported in 10–15% of individuals with localized erythema migrans. The activation of the inflammatory response in LNB contributes to the pathogenesis of a broad spectrum of neurologic disorders.

questions.question: Following a flood, there is an outbreak of fever. Water samples from various sources are being studied for pathogens. The bacteria shown in the given image was isolated as a potential cause of disease. Which of the following animals is the most important reservoir of these organisms?
questions.explanation:
The electron micrograph shows the spirochete, Leptospira interrogans, which causes the water-borne disease, leptospirosis. Rats are the most important reservoir.

Transmission of leptospires may follow direct contact with urine, blood, or tissue from an infected animal or exposure to environmental contamination.

questions.question: A farmer who works in paddy fields presented with fever, intense myalgia, and hematochezia. Lab investigations showed sharply elevated creatinine levels and high liver enzymes. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of Weil's disease which is caused by leptospira.

Long hours of working in a field with water (paddy field), is a high-risk factor for the development of leptospirosis.

Weil’s syndrome is the severe form of leptospirosis that encompasses the triad of hemorrhage, jaundice, and acute kidney injury.

The treatment of choice is IV penicillin or IV ceftriaxone.

questions.question: At a relief camp in Karnataka, a few people developed fever, myalgia, and conjunctival suffusion. Rapid diagnostic IgM ELISA tests performed in the field showed leptospirosis. Which of the following culture media can be used to confirm this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Ellinghausen, McCullough, Johnson, Harris (EMJH) media is the culture medium used for leptospira.

Other culture media that can be used are Korthof's, Stuart's, and Fletcher's media.

The image below shows EMJH medium, with Dinger's ring/zone. The growth of the leptospires is at a maximum density at this zone. It is identified as an area of increased turbidity, beneath the surface of the semi-solid medium. It is the zone of optimum oxygen tension for the growth of the bacteria.

questions.question: What is the protein coat covering the nucleic acid in a virion known as?
questions.explanation:
The protein coat covering the nucleic acid in a virion is called capsid.

The parts of a virus include:

• Nucleocapsid- capsid with enclosed nucleic acid

• Tegument- proteinaceous structure present between the envelope and capsid.

• Envelope- lipid-containing membrane that surrounds some virus particles. It is acquired during viral maturation by a budding process through a cellular membrane.

• Peplomers- virus-encoded glycoproteins, on the outer surface of the envelope as projections.

Characteristics of viruses:

• Do not have a cellular organization

• Have either DNA or RNA but never both

• Obligate intracellular parasites

• Lack enzymes necessary for protein and nucleic acid synthesis

• Filterable

• Cannot be grown on artificial media

• Unaffected by antibiotics.

Note : Martinus beijerinck proposed the theory of contagium vivum fluidum (living infectious fluid) while studying the cause of mosaic disease of tobacco plant. He is known as the father of virology.

questions.question: Which of the following viruses has a single-stranded DNA?
questions.explanation:
Parvovirus has single-stranded DNA.

All DNA viruses are double-stranded, except parvovirus. (only single-stranded DNA virus)

All RNA viruses have only one copy of single-stranded RNA except:

• Reovirus- double-stranded RNA virus.

• Retroviruses- Two copies of single-stranded RNA.

Parvovirus is the smallest DNA virus that infect human beings.

DNA
 RNA

Largest virus
Poxvirus
Filovirus

Parvovirus
Picornavirus

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding enveloped viruses?
questions.explanation:
The lipid of enveloped viruses is largely of host-cell origin, whereas protein is virus coded.

The following are the differences between enveloped and non-enveloped viruses.

Enveloped viruses
Non-enveloped viruses

Ether sensitive
Ether resistant

Heat labile
Heat stable

Pleomorphic
Non-pleomorphic

Susceptible to bile salts
Resistant to bile salts

questions.question: Which of the following is an enveloped virus?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis C virus is an enveloped virus.

It has a linear, single-stranded RNA genome, enclosed within a core and surrounded by an envelope.

questions.question: A patient in the ICU requires fresh frozen plasma (FFP). The FFP that arrives from the blood bank is labeled as Solvent/Detergent plasma, which destroys lipid-enveloped viruses. Which of the following viral infections is the patient still susceptible to?
questions.explanation:
The patient is still susceptible to hepatitis A infection. It is a non-enveloped virus, and hence it’s not affected by SD plasma.

Solvent/Detergent plasma (SD plasma) is a form of blood plasma made from plasma collected from many people which is then processed with solvents in an attempt to remove viruses.

Only the viruses with an envelope are susceptible to SD plasma destruction. Hepatitis B, C, and Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are enveloped.

questions.question: In which of the following viruses is a segmented genome found?
questions.explanation:
Segmented genome is found in orthomyxovirus.

Segmentation of viral genomes allows for the exchange of intact genes between related viruses during coinfection. This recombination is known as reassortment. There is a rearrangement and joining of nucleic acid sequences to form a unique chimeric genome. The new genome is usually less fit than the parent viruses, but occasionally, it results in an evolved virus with increased fitness.

Examples of segmented viruses (ARBO):

• Arenavirus (2 segments)

• Rotavirus (11 segments)

• Bunyavirus (3 segments)

• Orthomyxovirus (8 segments)

The image below shows the segmented genome seen in the influenza virus (Orthomyxoviridae)

questions.question: A 6-year-old with HIV is brought with complaints of the rash shown below. Where does DNA replication occur in the viruses falling in the same family as the microbe causing this rash?
questions.explanation:
The image shows pink, fleshy umbilicated papules suggesting molluscum contagiosum. It is caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus belonging to Poxviridae. DNA replication in these viruses occurs in the host cytoplasm.

DNA viruses
RNA viruses

Replication
Nucleus
Cytoplasm

Exception
Poxvirus- cytoplasm
Orthomyxovirus, retrovirus- nucleus

questions.question: An epidemic involving an ss-RNA virus with 3'-5' RNA has broken out in West Africa. Which of the following enzymes do such viruses use in genome replication?
questions.explanation:
An ss-RNA with a 3'-5' strand is a negative-stranded RNA. These viruses use RNA replicase or RNA-dependent RNA polymerase during genome replication.

In positive-stranded RNA viruses, the viral RNA itself acts as mRNA.

In negative-stranded RNA viruses, the polarity is opposite that of mRNA. So the genome requires RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to synthesize their mRNA.

Examples of negative-stranded RNA viruses (Mnemonic: Always bring da polymerase or fail to replicate):

• Arenaviruses

• Bunyaviruses

• Deltaviruses

• Paramyxoviruses

• Orthomyxoviruses

• Filoviruses

• Rhabdoviruses

questions.question: The virus shown below was suspected to be the cause of a deadly hemorrhagic fever outbreak in Guinea in March 2021. How is it transmitted?
options: Direct contact with infected body fluids
questions.answer: A. Direct contact with infected body fluids
questions.explanation:
The image shown above is the Ebola virus. It is spread by direct contact with infected body fluids.

Ebola is a filamentous virus with a single-stranded RNA genome.

The shapes of some viruses are shown below.

Rotavirus: Wheel-shaped virus

questions.question: An elderly diabetic man presents with a complaints of fever, cough and difficulty in breathing for the past 3 days. He gives a history of international travel 10 days back. Laboratory reports show positive for COVID-19. What is the symmetry of the causative virus?
questions.explanation:
The patient is suffering from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). The coronavirus implicated shows an enveloped helical symmetry.

Properties of Coronaviridae family:

• They are enveloped RNA viruses.

• They contain a genome of unsegmented single-stranded and positive-sense RNA

• They have helical nucleocapsid

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding symmetry of viruses ?
options: Viral symmetry is studied by heavy metals stains.
The most efficient closed shell sub-unit arrangement is icosahedral.
Icosahedral symmetry involves 12 faces and 20 vertices .
It is not possible for 'empty' helical particles to form
questions.answer: C. Icosahedral symmetry involves 12 faces and 20 vertices .
questions.explanation:
Icosahedron has 20 faces (each an equilateral triangle) and 12 vertices.

Option A: Study of viral symmetry by standard electron microscopy requires the use of heavy metal stains (e.g., potassium phosphotungstate) to emphasize surface structure. It is a form of negative staining.

Option B: Symmetry observed with animal viruses is of the icosahedral pattern. It is the most efficient arrangement for subunits in a closed shell.

Option D: A regular, periodic interaction between capsid protein and nucleic acid is required to maintain a stable helical symmetry. Therefore, it is not possible for empty helical particles to form.

Given below is Icosahedron:

questions.question: Which of the following viruses shows an enveloped icosahedral symmetry?
questions.explanation: Enveloped icosahedral symmetry is seen in the rubella virus.

questions.question: An immunologist is working on growing the influenza virus for vaccine production at the National Institute of Virology, Pune. Which of the following sites is used for the given purpose in a fertilized egg?
questions.explanation:
Allantoic cavity inoculation (1) is used for the growth and replication of the influenza virus for vaccine production.

Embryonated eggs are used for the cultivation of viruses.

Note: Both allantoic and amniotic cavity inoculation are recommended for initial isolation of the influenza virus. However, it is simpler to inoculate the virus into the allantoic cavity, as compared to the amniotic cavity, thus allantoic inoculation is the best answer.

questions.question: Quantitative infectivity assay of viruses is done by _______.
questions.explanation:
Quantitative infectivity assay of viruses is done by plaque assay.

Assay of infectivity of viruses

Physical methods
Biological methods

Can estimate total viral count

Can detect infectious virus

questions.question: Which virus causes the cytopathic effect of syncytium formation?
questions.explanation: The cytopathic effect of syncytium formation is caused by the measles virus.

questions.question: A 23-year-old lady presents with the lesions shown below. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The lesions shown are cold sores, also known as herpes labialis caused by Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). Herpes labialis primarily affects the lip and typically present as thin-walled, umbilicated vesicles, the roof of which breaks down with superficial ulcers. They generally heal without scarring.

HSV-1 can be isolated from lesions in and around the mouth and is transmitted by direct contact or droplet spread from cases or carriers. HSV-2 is responsible for the majority of genital herpes infections and is commonly transmitted venereally.

The images below show lesions of herpes labialis.

questions.question: Cowdry Type A inclusions are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in the vesicles of Herpes Simplex infection

The classic Cowdry type A inclusion appears as a light purple, homogeneous intranuclear structure surrounded by a clear halo. The inclusions stain with antibodies to HSV, permitting a rapid, specific diagnosis of HSV infection.

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl has had 4 episodes of meningitis over the last 4 years, with the disease lasting a few days at a time, leaving slowly resolving neurological symptoms such as visual and memory loss. A CSF cytology shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and a diagnosis of Mollaret’s meningitis is made. Which organism is implicated here?
questions.explanation: Mollaret’s meningitis or benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis is most commonly caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). Demonstration of HSV antibodies in CSF or persistence of HSV DNA in CSF can establish the diagnosis.

questions.question: A dentist presents to the surgery OPD with the findings shown below. He is febrile. Microscopic examination of the tissue reveals Tzanck cells. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The image suggests herpetic whitlow, confirmed by the presence of Tzanck cells on microscopy. It is caused by HSV-1.

It is often contracted by health care workers that come in contact with the virus when exposed to oral secretions.

On Tzanck smear, which is a rapid, diagnostic method, Tzanck cells are seen. These are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Tzanck smear is also used in the diagnosis of Hailey-Hailey disease, Darier’s disease, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, etc.

Diagnosis of herpes simplex virus:

• Most sensitive test- HSV DNA- PCR (can differentiate between HSV 1 and 2)

• Most definitive test- virus isolation using human diploid fibroblast in which cytopathic changes can be observed as early as 24 - 48 hours.

• Microscopy - Tzanck smear is prepared by Wright or Giemsa stain. Intranuclear type A inclusion bodies may be seen in Giemsa-stained smears.

questions.question: Your neighbor’s child complains of fever and develops a rash. On examination, the rashes are present all over the body, and look like ‘dewdrops lying on the skin’. The child says that his friend in school had similar complaints a few days ago. Which of the given statements is true about this rash?
options: The rash usually starts on the distal parts of limbs
All the lesions are of same age
Scabs are also infectious in chicken pox
questions.answer: A. It is centripetal in distribution
questions.explanation:
The condition described here is chickenpox. It is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. The following are the characteristics of rash seen in chicken pox :

• The rash is centripetal in distribution.

• It evolves rapidly, progressing through macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, and finally scab.

• It is a pleomorphic rash and appears in crops, hence varying stages of lesions can be noticed at a given time.

• The lesions resemble a dewdrop lying on the skin, as they are superficial and do not involve the deeper layers of the skin.

questions.question: While on rounds in the NICU, you notice a newborn baby with a zig-zag dermatomal cicatrix on the forehead and left side of the face. The limbs are small and atrophied. Microcephaly is noted. Which maternal infection are these findings characteristically associated with?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital varicella syndrome. Hence, an antenatal history of varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection would be significant in the mother of this baby.

Fetal varicella infection occurs if the mother gets infected during the first half of pregnancy.

Clinical features include:

• Cicatrix, a zigzag scarring in a dermatomal distribution

• Microphthalmia

• Cataracts

• Optic atrophy

• Chorioretinitis

• Microcephaly

• Limb hypoplasia

• Motor and sensory deficits

questions.question: An infant is brought by his worried parents with a rash and yellowish discoloration of the skin. On examination, the baby has petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and microcephaly. The developmental assessment shows global developmental delay. An axial cut of the non-contrast CT of the brain is given below. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and imaging suggest a diagnosis of congenital CMV infection. The non-contrast CT head shows periventricular calcifications and ventriculomegaly.

Features of congenital CMV infection:

• Petechial rash

• Jaundice

• Hepatosplenomegaly

• Microcephaly

• Deafness

• Chorioretinitis

• IUGR

• Periventricular calcification and ventriculomegaly

Option A: Congenital rubella syndrome is a triad of cardiac defects, cataracts, and congenital hearing loss.

Option B: Neonatal herpes presents as skin lesions with eye involvement, encephalitis, and disseminated disease.

Option D: Fetal varicella syndrome is manifested as cicatrizing/scarring skin lesions, chorioretinitis, hypoplastic limbs, low birth weight, and CNS defects due to cerebral atrophy.

Note: In 15-20% of infants with congenital CMV infection, microcephaly is not detected at birth. It may develop as the child grows and is detected at follow-up visits for other complaints.

questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding CMV.
options: Ganciclovir resistance is due to mutation in UL97 phosphotransferase gene
CMV can be cultured in vitro in any mammalian cell
Commonest manifestation of CMV associated disease is watery diarrhea
UL54 mutated CMV strains do not show cross resistance to Foscarnet
questions.answer: A. Ganciclovir resistance is due to mutation in UL97 phosphotransferase gene
questions.explanation:
Resistance to ganciclovir most commonly occurs due to mutations in the UL97 phosphotransferase gene.

Option B: Human CMV replicates in vitro only in human fibroblasts, although the virus is often isolated from epithelial cells of the host.

Option C: CMV infection is mostly subclinical.

Option D: UL54 mutations can confer resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir, and foscarnet.

questions.question: Where are owl's eye inclusion bodies seen?
questions.explanation: Owl’s eye inclusion bodies are intranuclear basophilic inclusion bodies seen in CMV infection.

questions.question: What does the Paul-Bunnell test diagnose?
questions.explanation:
Paul-Bunnell test is used to diagnose kissing disease (infectious mononucleosis) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

It is a heterophile agglutination test used to identify the heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep erythrocytes. Patients suffering from infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) will produce antibodies that will react and agglutinate sheep erythrocytes.

questions.question:
You are studying the association of human herpesvirus-4 with other diseases. Which of the following patients have diseases associated with this virus?

1. A college student with infectious mononucleosis

2. An African child with Burkitt’s lymphoma

3. A 60-year-old tobacco chewer with oral submucous fibrosis

4. A middle-aged man with adult T-cell leukemia

5. An HIV-positive man with hairy leukoplakia
questions.explanation:
Human herpesvirus-4 or Epstein-Barr virus causes infectious mononucleosis, Burkitt’s lymphoma, and is associated with oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV patients.

EBV may cause the following malignancies:

• Burkitt’s lymphoma

• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (in people of Chinese origin),

• Lymphomas in immunodeficient persons such as AIDS or transplant recipients.

Endemic or African Burkitt's lymphoma has got nearly 100% association with EBV, as compared to non-endemic and HIV-associated Burkitt's lymphoma.

Oral hairy leukoplakia is triggered by EBV in patients with poor immune status, most commonly with HIV.

Oral submucous fibrosis is associated with the human papillomavirus (HPV).

Adult T cell leukemia is associated with the human T-cell leukemia virus.

questions.question: Which of the following viruses is known to cause hemorrhagic cystitis, diarrhea, and conjunctivitis?
questions.explanation:
Adenovirus is known to cause hemorrhagic cystitis, diarrhea, and conjunctivitis.

Acute hemorrhagic cystitis in children is caused by adenoviruses types 11 and 21.

The following table shows various syndromes caused by adenoviruses and associated serotypes:

questions.question: Which organism causes the disease shown below?
questions.explanation:
The image showed a rash on the cheeks and face, with a slapped cheek appearance, characteristic of erythema infectiosum/ fifth disease. It is caused by Parvovirus B19.

Parvovirus B19 usually presents as a respiratory infection, with an erythematous maculopapular rash and arthralgia. The rash starts as prominent erythema of the cheek, popularly known as slapped-cheek appearance. The rash further spreads to the trunk and limbs followed by lymphadenopathy and arthralgia.

It induces aplastic crisis in sickle cell anemia patients.

Infection during pregnancy leads to non-immune fetal hydrops (highest risk in the first half of gestational period).

questions.question: An 8-year-old child presents with skin lesions, suspected to be molluscum contagiosum. How is the diagnosis of this condition typically made?
questions.explanation:
Diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum is based on clinical appearance.

Molluscum contagiosum manifests as pink pearly wart-like lesions with a characteristic dimple at the center (umbilicated), not associated with inflammation and necrosis.

Option B: Skin biopsy or smear of expressed material shows characteristic inclusion bodies but is necessary only when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Options A and C: Viral culture and PCR for viral DNA are not used for diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the causative organism of the condition shown below?
questions.explanation:
The image shows condyloma acuminata. It is most commonly caused by Human papillomavirus (HPV) 6 and 11.

Condyloma acuminata is a benign, genital wart which is a moist, soft, pedunculated wart found on the external genitalia.

Microscopically, the characteristic features include:

• A branching villous structure with connective tissue stroma

• Epidermis showing hyperkeratosis and acanthosis (thickening)

• Cytoplasmic vacuolization of the squamous cells (koilocytosis) is characteristic of HPV infection.

• No evident dysplasia

Option A: Treponema pallidum can cause condylomata lata in secondary syphilis. It is smoother and flatter and may be associated with induration and ulceration. (image below)

Option C: Human papillomavirus 16 and 18 are associated with carcinoma of the cervix and anogenital region.

Option D: Hemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid. Given below is the image of chancroid.

questions.question: A patient presents with plantar warts as shown below. Which type of human papillomavirus is responsible for causing these?
questions.explanation:
HPV types 1a, 57, and 27 accounts for most plantar warts.

HPV 7 causes hand warts in butchers (butcher's warts).

HPV 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminata, sinonasal papilloma, and squamous papilloma of the larynx.

questions.question: As a CHC medical officer, you organize an outreach program for HPV vaccination and the prevention of cervical cancer. Which protein is used for antigenic response in this vaccine?
questions.explanation:
The HPV vaccines use virus-like particles (VLPs) that consist of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells.

These VLPs contain the same epitopes as the HPV virion. But they do not contain genetic material and cannot transmit infection. The immunogenicity of the HPV vaccines relies on the development of conformational neutralizing antibodies to epitopes displayed on viral capsids.

The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil-9. It has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers.

HPV Vaccine

16, 18

questions.question: Nonavalent HPV vaccine works against which of the following strains of the virus?
questions.explanation:
The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil-9. It has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers.
