questions.question: An HIV-positive patient presents with the following skin lesions. Which of the following diseases is associated with the virus implicated here?
questions.explanation:
The above image showing red-purple macules and plaques in an HIV-positive patient is suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma, caused by human herpesvirus 8. It also causes primary effusion lymphoma. It is one of seven currently known human cancer viruses or oncoviruses.

 HHV-8 or Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is known to cause Kaposi’s sarcoma, in immunocompromised persons. Cancer patients receiving chemotherapy, AIDS patients, and organ transplant recipients are all at a high risk of showing signs of infection.

KSHV is a known causative agent of four diseases:

1. Kaposi's sarcoma

2. KSHV-associated multicentric Castleman's disease (MCD)

3. Primary effusion lymphoma

4. KSHV inflammatory cytokine syndrome

questions.question: Which of the following viruses is implicated in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?
questions.explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by the JC virus. JC virus-induced progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is one of the neurologic diseases associated with HIV infection.

Option B: BK virus is associated with nephropathy in transplant recipients.

Option C: The long-term sequelae associated with measles infection is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

Option D: Herpes simplex virus causes temporal lobe encephalitis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-enveloped virus that causes hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A and E are non-enveloped viruses, while Hepatitis B, C, and D are enveloped viruses.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man hailing from Mumbai presents to you with complaints of abdominal pain and malaise. On examination, he is icteric and the liver is palpable 6 cm below the costal margin. On further questioning, he informs you that a few weeks back the drains surrounding his house were overflowing due to the monsoon flooding. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario with icterus, hepatomegaly, and environmental history is suggestive of acute viral hepatitis, likely to be caused by hepatitis A or E viruses.

Hepatitis A and E are transmitted by feco-oral route. Overcrowding, poor hygiene, and fecal contamination of water supplies such as after monsoon flooding can lead to spreading of the disease.

Hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted by parenteral routes, e.g. blood transfusions.

questions.question: A 18-year-old man presents with fever, diarrhea, and jaundice. He gives a history of consuming food at a roadside stall. Which of the following statements is incorrect about the etiological agent?
options: It is transmitted by feco-oral route
A formalin inactivated vaccine is used for prevention
questions.answer: A. It belongs to family Hepatoviridae
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of viral hepatitis which is most likely to be Hepatitis A. Hepatitis A virus belongs to the family Picornaviridae. It is transmitted by feco-oral route and most of the infections are symptomatic.

There is no definitive treatment, thus, only supportive therapy is given.

questions.question: What is the average incubation period for Hepatitis A virus?
questions.explanation: The average incubation period of the Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is around 30 days. It ranges from 15-50 days. The clinical disease has a prodromal stage and an icteric stage.

questions.question: Which of the following is also referred to as Dane particle?
questions.explanation:
Dane particle refers to Hepatitis B.

Sera from hepatitis B patients when observed under an electron microscope show three types of particles:

• Spherical particle: 22nm, most abundant, contains only HBsAg.

• Filamentous or tubular particle: 22nm, contains only HBsAg.

• A double-walled spherical structure: 42nm diameter, is the complete Hepatitis B virus. It was described by Dane and is called Dane particle.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male patient with chronic hepatitis B has high levels of serum HBeAg. Which of the following viral genes is involved in coding the same?
questions.explanation:
HBeAg is coded by the C gene. The presence of high levels of HBeAg (and HBV DNA) suggests high infectivity.

HBV Genome has four overlapping genes. They code for:

• S gene-It codes for surface antigen.

• C gene-

• When the C region alone is translated: HBcAg is formed.

• When translation begins from Pre C region, HBeAg is formed.

• P gene- Codes for DNA polymerase.

• X gene- Codes for a non-particulate protein HBxAg.

questions.question: While drawing blood from a patient with hepatitis B, it splashes into the eyes of a nurse. Which of the following markers will appear first in her blood if she gets infected?
questions.explanation:
HBsAg is the first marker to appear in the blood after infection.

It can be detected even before the elevation of serum transaminases and onset of clinical illness. Usually, it disappears within 2 months of onset of clinical disease but may last for even 6 months and beyond. If it persists beyond 6 months, it indicates chronic hepatitis.

Anti-HBs is the protective antibody, which appears soon after HBsAg, disappears and remains in serum for a long time.

questions.question: A patient with hepatitis B presents to OPD for follow-up. Which of the following serological markers will not be detected in his blood?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) is not present in blood because it is enclosed within the HBsAg coat. However, antibodies against HBc (Anti-HBc) are the earliest antibody markers to be seen in the blood after 1-2 weeks.

Note:

• HBsAg: Earliest marker to be detected in the serum of Hepatitis B-infected persons.

• Anti HBc: Earliest antibody to be detected in the serum of Hepatitis B-infected persons.

The given image shows hepatitis B virus and its antigens

questions.question: Which of the following is not synthesized by pre-core mutants of hepatitis B virus?
questions.explanation:
Pre-core mutants of hepatitis B virus are unable to synthesize HBeAg.

In the HBV genome, the C gene consists of 2 regions:

• Pre-C region- When translation begins from the Pre-C region, HBeAg is synthesized.

• C-region- When it begins from the C-region, HBcAg is synthesized.

In the HBeAg sequence of pre-core mutants, there is a G to A switch at the 28th amino acid, causing a stop codon. Hence, pre-core mutants are unable to synthesize HBeAg.

The image below shows the HBV genome :

questions.question:
The serological profile of a patient is given below. What is your diagnosis?

HBsAg: + ve
HBeAg: + ve
Anti HBc: IgM: + ve
Anti HBs: - ve
Anti HBe: - ve
options: Acute HBV infection with high infectivity
Chronic HBV infection with high infectivity
Acute HBV infection with low infectivity
questions.answer: A. Acute HBV infection with high infectivity
questions.explanation: HBsAg and IgM Anti-HBc are positive, indicating an acute hepatitis B infection. HBeAg positive indicates that the patient is highly infectious.

questions.question: An HBsAg positive primigravida presents to you for routine antenatal care. She asks you about the risk of transmission of HBV to her baby. Which of the following is not related to the same?
questions.explanation:
Breastfeeding is not related to the vertical transmission of hepatitis B virus. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in HBsAg-positive mothers.

Mother-to-child transmission of HBV can occur via three modalities:

• Intrauterine transmission- Transplacental transmission is uncommon. Another route is via a breach in the placental barrier exposing maternal blood to fetal blood e.g. - threatened preterm labor.

• Transmission during delivery- It is the most frequent method of vertical transmission. It is mostly due to newborn contact with the mother’s infected secretions or blood at the time of delivery (normal/instrumental).

• Postpartum transmission- Though HBV DNA is present in breast milk, it is not transmitted to the fetus. However, cracked nipples expose the infant to maternal blood, and can transmit the virus to the infant.

Immunoprophylaxis with HBIg is indicated for babies born to HBsAg-positive mothers followed by a three-dose hepatitis B recombinant vaccine.

questions.question: An intern takes a hepatitis B vaccine booster dose before his ward postings begin. Which of the following serological markers will indicate immunity against HBV in this case?
questions.explanation: Presence of anti-HBs with the absence of all other serological virus markers indicates immunity following HBV vaccination.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding HBV vaccination?
options: The current vaccine is prepared by cloning 'S gene' of HBV in Baker’s yeast
A single dose of HBV vaccine is recommended for high-risk groups for pre-exposure prophylaxis
For high-risk mothers who are seronegative, hepatitis B vaccine can be given during pregnancy.
Hepatitis B vaccine should be administered intramuscularly in the deltoid muscle.
questions.answer: B. A single dose of HBV vaccine is recommended for high-risk groups for pre-exposure prophylaxis
questions.explanation:
Pre-exposure prophylaxis consists of administration of a 3–4 dose series of hepatitis B vaccine given over a 6-month period.

The pre-exposure prophylaxis of Hepatitis B vaccine schedule is as follows:

Group

 Vaccine dose in mL (Active ingredient in µg/mL)

 Schedule

Newborn

 0.5 mL (10µg)

 <24 hours, 6 weeks, 14 weeks (if administration of the first dose within 24 hours of birth is not possible, then 6, 10, and 14 weeks)

Healthy persons aged ≤19 years

 0.5 mL (10 µg)

 0, 1, 2 / 6 months

Healthy persons aged ≥20 years

 1.0 mL (20 µg)

 0, 1, 2 / 6 months

Persons on hemodialysis or immunocompromised persons

 2.0 mL (40 µg)

 0, 1, 2, 6 months

The vaccine is genetically engineered by cloning 'S gene' in baker’s yeast. It has non-glycosylated HBsAg particles given along with an alum adjuvant.

Pregnancy is not a contraindication for hepatitis B vaccination. The efficacy has been shown to be similar to that for non-pregnant adults, with overall seroconversion rates approaching 95 percent after three doses which can be taken during routine prenatal care.

The vaccine is given intramuscularly, in the deltoid muscle and can be co-administered with other vaccines.

questions.question: A known case of hepatitis B going into hepatic failure is found to have a high viral load. Which of the following serological markers will not contribute to the viral load?
questions.explanation:
Anti-HBs will not contribute to the high viral load, as it is not a marker of active viral replication.

HBeAg, HBV DNA, and HBV DNA polymerase are markers of active viral replication and will contribute to the high viral load.

HBeAg is a qualitative marker while HBV DNA is a quantitative marker of the replicative phase.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man with heroin addiction presents with fatigue, palpable purpura, joint pains, and abdominal pain. Urine analysis shows massive proteinuria. Which of the following viruses should be tested for in this patient?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mixed cryoglobulinemia, which is strongly associated with hepatitis C. Hence, the patient should be tested for hepatitis C.

questions.question: Which hepatitis virus shows maximum chronicity in adults?
questions.explanation:
Maximum chronicity is seen in HCV infection, followed by HBV infection.

5-10% of adults infected with HBV develop chronic infection. The majority of neonates affected with hepatitis B develop chronic hepatitis.

HEV is associated with chronic infection only in immunocompromised individuals. HAV is not associated with chronicity.

Note: The most common cause of post-transfusion hepatitis in developed countries is hepatitis C

questions.question: A patient with fulminant hepatitis is found to have coinfection with hepatitis B and hepatitis D viruses. Which of the following structures of HBV aid in the survival of HDV?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is an incomplete/defective virus. It requires HBV, to provide the envelope protein (HbsAg) to aid in its survival. Hepatitis D is called the delta virus.

Two types of infection may occur:

• Co-infection - acute HDV and HBV infections occur simultaneously

• Super-infection - Delta viral infection occurs in a person already harboring HBV. This most often leads to chronic hepatitis

Coinfection and superinfection can cause fulminant hepatitis. HBV vaccination is protective against HDV.

questions.question: In the year 1955, following sewage contamination of drinking water in New Delhi, an outbreak of jaundice ensued. Electron microscopy of fecal samples from the affected population revealed a virus resembling caliciviruses. Which of the following was the etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) resembles caliciviruses in morphology and physical characteristics. Hepatitis E is a non-enveloped virus with ssRNA genome

Note: The largest HEV epidemic occurred in New Delhi in 1955-1956.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about viral hepatitis?
options: Anti LKM-3 antibody is associated with hepatitis B infection
Anti-LKM1 antibodies are associated with hepatitis C infection
IgM anti-HAV antibody appears during the late incubation period
Enterically transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis is caused by hepatitis E virus
questions.answer: A. Anti LKM-3 antibody is associated with hepatitis B infection
questions.explanation:
The anti-LKM-3 antibody is associated with hepatitis D infection, not hepatitis B.

Anti–liver-kidney microsomal antibodies (anti-LKM) are many of several autoantibodies that are detected in the serum of patients with different types of acute or chronic liver disease. These antibodies are targeted against antigens of the cytochrome P450 system.

They are also associated with chronic hepatitis C and autoimmune hepatitis.

Option C: IgM anti-HAV antibody indicates current/recent infection. It appears during the late incubation period, peaks in 2-3 weeks, and disappears after 3-4 months. IgG denotes remote infection or immunity. It appears around the same time, peaks at 3-4 months, and persists for a long time.

Option D: Hepatitis E infection was previously known as an epidemic or enterically transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis. It is transmitted by feco-oral route.

questions.question: Which of the following subtypes of HIV is most common in India?
questions.explanation:
Subtype C of HIV is the most common in India. It causes more than 95% of HIV infections.

Subtypes A and C are more readily transmitted by heterosexual contact than subtype B, which is mainly transmitted by homosexual contact and injections.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about HIV?
questions.explanation:
HIV is a thermolabile virus. It is readily inactivated by heating to 60 °C for 10 minutes and at 100 °C in seconds. At room temperature (20–25 °C) in the dried blood, it may survive for 1 week.

Option A: HIV crosses the blood-brain barrier. It may cause encephalopathy leading to loss of higher functions, progressing to dementia.

Option B: HIV is a spherical, enveloped virus. Its genome is composed of two copies of identical single-stranded positive-sense RNA.

Option C: HIV is inactivated by treatment with 0.3% hydrogen peroxide, 50% ethanol, 35% isopropanol or 10% household bleach. A 2% solution of glutaraldehyde is effective for the disinfection of medical instruments.

questions.question: Which of the following is a nonstructural gene of HIV?
questions.explanation:
The tat gene (trans-activating gene) is a non-structural gene.

HIV has structural and non-structural genes:

• Structural genes- Genes coding for structural protiens:

• gag- Codes for core and shell protein p55, which is cleaved to p15, p18 and p24

• env- Codes for envelope glycoprotein gp160 which is cleaved to gp120 and gp41

• pol- Codes for enzymes: Polymerase, reverse transcriptase, protease and endonuclease

• Non-structural and regulatory genes:

• tat- Trans-activating gene

• nef- Negative factor gene

• rev- Regulator of virus gene

• vif- Viral infectivity factor gene

• vpu- (only in HIV-1) and vpx (only in HIV-2)

• vpr- Stimulates only the promoter region of the virus

• LTR- Long terminal repeat sequences

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of HIV replication?
questions.explanation:
HIV replicates by the sequence RNA-DNA-RNA. The provirus initiates viral replication by directing the synthesis of viral RNA and other components. Hence, the sequence is RNA–ssDNA–dsDNA–RNA.

HIV genome is composed of 2 single-stranded positive-sense RNA. When a virus infects a cell, the viral RNA is transcribed by the enzyme reverse transcriptase, first into single-stranded DNA and then to double-stranded DNA which is integrated into the host chromosome.

Note: If the options include RNA-DNA-RNA and RNA-DNA-DNA-RNA then the latter would be the choice.

The given image represents HIV replication

questions.question: As part of developing the public health policy on HIV in India, which of the following modes of transmission would you focus on the most?
questions.explanation:
Heterosexual transmission is the most common mode of transmission of HIV infection in developing countries such as India and African countries. In many Western countries, male-to-male sexual transmission is the dominant mode of transmission.

Blood transfusion carries the highest risk per 10000 exposures of getting HIV from an infected person. However, it is not the most common mode of transmission.

questions.question: A 35-year-old bisexual man goes to an ICTC centre for counselling about HIV. Which of the following is false about HIV transmission?
options: Male-to-female HIV transmission has more risk of causing infection than female-to-male transmission
The risk of acquiring HIV with unprotected receptive anal intercourse is lower than that with penile-vaginal intercourse
The quantity of HIV-1 in plasma is a primary determinant of the risk of HIV-1 transmission
Male circumcision is associated with a lower risk of HIV acquisition for heterosexual men
questions.answer: B. The risk of acquiring HIV with unprotected receptive anal intercourse is lower than that with penile-vaginal intercourse
questions.explanation:
The risk of HIV acquisition associated with unprotected receptive anal intercourse is relatively higher than that seen in penile-vaginal intercourse. This is because the rectal mucosal membrane is thin and fragile and anal intercourse is associated with microtrauma (rectal tears).

The differences in transmission rates between men and women are because the vagina and cervix are exposed to semen for a longer duration, increasing the risk of transmission. However, the penis and urethral orifice are exposed relatively briefly to infected vaginal fluid, lowering the risk.

questions.question: Specific binding of the HIV to the CD4 receptor occurs via which of these?
questions.explanation:
The specific binding of the HIV to the CD4 receptor is by the envelope glycoprotein gp120.

Option B - Cell fusion occurs via binding to gp41. Cell fusion is essential for infection to take place.

Option C, D - Binding to CD4 receptor requires the participation of a co-receptor CXCR 4 for T cell tropic HIV strains and CCR 5 for macrophage-tropic strains.

questions.question: A patient presents to you with a history of sharing needles during IV drug abuse with an HIV-positive partner. HIV-antibody spot test was negative, however p24 antigen assay was positive. You explain to him that he is currently in the window period for HIV. Which of the following statements would you use to explain the concept to him?
options: It is the time period between infection and onset of first symptoms
It is the time period between infection and detection of antibodies
It is the time period between exposure and onset of viral multiplication
It is the time period between exposure and appearance of symptoms
questions.answer: B. It is the time period between infection and detection of antibodies
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the patient has experienced a high-risk exposure to HIV due to sharing needles during IV drug abuse with an HIV-positive partner.

The period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV is known as the window period.

The window period may last anywhere between 2–8 weeks to a few months. During this period, the individual may be highly infectious. HIV infection can be detected during this period by p24 antigen assay and PCR.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man was admitted for hernioplasty and initial investigations revealed that he is HIV-positive. He gives no history of contact and has no HIV-associated symptoms. Which of the following statements is incorrect about this phase of HIV infection?
options: Rapid decline of CD4 count is common
questions.answer: D. Rapid decline of CD4 count is common
questions.explanation:
The given patient is in the latent period of HIV infection. During the latent phase of HIV infection, the CD4+ T cell count declines steadily and not rapidly.

All patients infected with HIV pass through a phase of clinical latency during which they are asymptomatic. This can last for years. During the latent phase, patients show positive HIV antibody tests and they are infectious. There will be varying degrees of viral multiplication.

Throughout the course of untreated infection and even during the stage of clinical latency, HIV is actively replicating or is sequestered in lymphoid tissues.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the clinic requesting an HIV test. He had unprotected sexual contact with another man 3 weeks ago. Antibodies against which of the following will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot?
questions.explanation:
Antibodies against gp41 will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot.

Antibodies to HIV usually appear within 3–6 weeks of primary infection. The appearance of HIV-binding antibodies occurs prior to the appearance of neutralizing antibodies. The only viral proteins that elicit neutralizing antibodies are the envelope proteins gp120 and gp41.

The order of appearance of antibodies is as follows:

Antibody to envelope gp41 > Antibodies to gag protein (p24 and p55) > Antibodies to envelope gp120 > Antibodies to gag protein p17 > Antibodies to pol gene products (p31 and p66).

Note: The earliest antigen to appear in the blood following HIV infection is p24.

questions.question: You are an officer with the Center for Disease Control and are screening a high-risk population for HIV. Which of the following methods will you use as a screening tool?
questions.explanation:
ELISA is most commonly used as a screening test for HIV.

Screening tests possess high sensitivity but are not highly specific. ELISA is a simple, relatively inexpensive screening test.

The most commonly used confirmatory test is Western blot. Western blot demonstrating antibodies to products of all three of the major genes of HIV (gag, pol, and env) is conclusive evidence of infection with HIV. It is considered positive if it shows antibodies against at least two of the following gene products: p24, gp41, gp120/160.

questions.question: Which of the following RNA viruses has an 8 segmented genome with its site of replication being the nucleus?
questions.explanation:
Influenza virus has an 8 segmented genome. Its site of replication is the nucleus, unlike other RNA viruses. Influenza virus belongs to the Orthomyxoviridae family.

Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except pox. Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, except retroviruses and orthomyxoviruses.

Examples of segmented viruses (ARBO):

• Arenavirus (2 segments)

• Rotavirus (11 segments)

• Bunyavirus (3 segments)

• Orthomyxovirus (8 segments)

The image below shows the segmented genome seen in the influenza virus (Orthomyxoviridae)

questions.question: A microbiologist working on influenza virus in a lab, observes reversal of hemagglutination. What is this phenomenon known as?
questions.explanation:
Elution is the process of reversal of hemagglutination and the release of the virus from the red cell surface.

Influenza virus contains two surface antigens:

• Hemagglutinin (HA) - causes RBC agglutination; facilitates viral entry into cells

• Neuraminidase (NA) - an enzyme that destroys the receptor HA uses to bind to RBCs causing elution/reversal of hemagglutination. Hence, it is also called a receptor destroying enzyme (RDE).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding antigenic drift?
options: There is a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure
It doesn’t account for the periodic epidemics of influenza
The new antigens thus formed are totally unrelated to the previous antigens
Antibodies to the predecessor viruses do not neutralise the new variants
questions.answer: A. There is a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure
questions.explanation:
Antigenic drift causes a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure.

It accounts for periodic epidemics. This property forms the basis for the development of annual influenza vaccines.

Antigenic variation is a property of influenza viruses by which it alters the antigenic structure on its surface and thus avoids a host immune response. It is of two types - Antigenic shift and antigenic drift.

Antigenic shift
Antigenic drift

Antigenic structure
Abrupt, drastic change
Gradual, sequential change

Periodicity
 10 - 20 years
2 - 3 years

Epidemiological effect
Pandemics and major epidemics
Periodic epidemic and sporadic cases

Genetic cause
Large genetic re-assortment
Point mutation

Antibodies to predecessor strains
Do not neutralize the new variant
Neutralizes the new variant to varying degrees

Clinical relevance
Animal-origin viruses infecting humans e.g. Swine flu, COVID-19

Annual influenza vaccine development

Common cold - People can get flu more than once

questions.question: You receive multiple patients from a poultry farm presenting with fever, dyspnea, cold, and cough. You suspect an outbreak of Avian flu. Which of the following virus strains causes the same?
questions.explanation:
H5N1 is a strain of avian influenza.

Transmission occurs only from birds (e.g. poultry). Recombination occurs in pigs. Human-to-human transmission is very rare.

It causes flu-like symptoms and can cause severe respiratory illness.

Option A: H1N1 causes swine flu

Option C: H3N2 causes Hong Kong flu

Option D: H2N2 caused a pandemic in 1957

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl with a history of fever, rhinorrhea, sore throat, and myalgia presented with multiple episodes of vomiting and seizures. She was diagnosed with Reye's syndrome. Which of the following is incorrect about the most likely etiological agent?
options: Virus shedding is present before symptoms begins
5-12 years is a high risk group
questions.answer: B. 5-12 years is a high risk group
questions.explanation:
The most likely etiological agent in the given case of Reye's syndrome is the influenza virus. Children <5-years, especially those <2-years of age are at the highest risk of serious complications related to influenza infection. Other high-risk groups for influenza include adults ≥60 years of age, persons with chronic diseases, persons who are immunocompromised.

Option A: The virus is shed in respiratory secretions a day before the onset of illness and for 3-4 days thereafter.

Option C: Birds, especially aquatic birds act as reservoirs of influenza viruses.

Option D: Secondary attack rate is 5-15%.

Note: Reye's syndrome is precipitated by the interaction of a viral infection (such as influenza) with salicylates. Therefore, aspirin is not given to pediatric patients with influenza and influenza-like illness.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of headache and drowsiness since 2 days. He had a history of fever, ear pain, and difficulty in swallowing for 1 week. On examination, you see the following. Brudzinki's sign is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with fever, parotitis, headache, drowsiness, and positive Brudzinki's sign is suggestive of meningitis secondary to mumps.

Mumps is caused by the mumps virus and is characterized by fever, bilateral or unilateral parotid swelling which may be tender. Parotitis can present with ear pain and difficulty in swallowing. It usually resolves in a week.

Meningoencephalitis/aseptic meningitis can occur before, along with, or after parotitis. Most commonly, it manifests 5 days after parotitis. It can present with headache, neck stiffness, and drowsiness.

Complications of mumps:

• Aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis

• Epididymo-orchitis- Usually unilateral. Seen in post-pubertal males

• Oophoritis

• Other complications include pancreatitis and myocarditis

Note: Non-mumps parotitis can be caused by:

• Epstein-Barr virus - causes infectious mononucleosis

• Coxsackievirus - causes herpangina

• Parainfluenza virus - causes croup

questions.question: A 9-month-old child is brought to the OPD for MMR vaccine. Which strain of mumps virus is used in the same?
questions.explanation:
The strain of mumps virus used in the MMR vaccine (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) is the Jeryl-Lynn strain.

The virus is attenuated by serial passage in embryonated eggs and grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture.

Note: The schedule of MMR vaccine as per the National Immunisation Schedule is from 9 completed months to 12 months. (can be given till 5 years of age).

questions.question: A mother brings her 5-month-old baby to the casualty with complaints of fast breathing and poor feeding. She also gives a history of fever, cold, and cough for 3 days. On examination, nasal flaring and expiratory wheeze are present. Which of the following statements is false about the viral etiology of the same?
options: The cytopathic effect is syncytium formation
Ribavirin is the drug of choice
It is the most important cause of bronchiolitis
questions.answer: C. Omalizumab is given for prophylaxis
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiolitis caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Palivizumab is given for RSV prophylaxis in high-risk infants such as premature babies, immunocompromised infants, etc.

Option A - The characteristic cytopathic effect is syncytium formation (multinucleated giant cell).

Option B - Inhaled ribavirin is the drug of choice.

Option D - RSV causes upper and lower respiratory tract infections in infants, and is the most common cause of bronchiolitis from ages 6 weeks to 6 months. It can cause pneumonia and tracheobronchitis and is common during winters and monsoon.

questions.question: An unimmunized man presents with fever, malaise, and an erythematous rash starting from behind the ears and progressing to the face and trunk. Given below is an image of lymphoid tissue taken from this patient. What pathological finding do you see here?
questions.explanation:
Warthin-Finkeldey cells are seen here. These are multinucleate giant cells, which are found in the lymphoid tissues of patients with measles.

The cytopathic effect of measles consists of multinucleate syncytium formation with numerous acidophilic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions, as shown in the image below.

Option B: Warthin-Starry stain is used to detect spirochetes and to stain H. pylori and B. henselae

Option C: Langhans giant cells are seen in tuberculosis

Option D: Aschoff giant cells are seen in rheumatic fever

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy with no prior immunization history presents with fever, cough, and coryza. On examination of the buccal mucosa, you see the following. Which stage of the disease is this finding seen in?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows Koplik’s spots present in measles. They are seen during the prodromal phase of the illness.

Koplik's spots are small bluish-white ulcerations on the buccal mucosa opposite to the first and second lower molars and are pathognomonic of measles. They contain giant cells, cytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions, and virion components. They can involve the entire buccal mucosa and fade as the maculopapular rash develops.

Stages of measles:

The natural history of measles has 3 stages as follows:

1. Prodromal stage - It begins 10 days after infection and lasts until day 14. It consists of cough, coryza, redness of eyes, lacrimation, photophobia, vomiting, and diarrhea. Koplik's spots appear in this stage.

2. Eruptive stage - A dusky, red maculopapular rash appears. It starts behind the ears spreads downwards to the trunk and lower extremities. Antibodies appear in this stage and are detectable by IgM ELISA. The symptoms such as fever and rash usually resolve spontaneously or go on to develop complications.

3. Post-measles stage - Weakness and weight loss may persist. The infection may become chronic and cause secondary infections such as cancrum oris, candidiasis etc.

The image below shows Koplik's spots

The image below shows the characteristic maculopapular rash in measles

questions.question: A 26-year-old pet-groomer was brought to the casualty with a history of breathlessness, excessive agitation, and restlessness. His bystanders give a history of progressive behavioral change and he had a fever, sore throat, and generalized weakness 1 month back. On examination, pulse was 100 bpm, SpO2 was 98% on room air. Which of the following samples will not be preferred to detect the etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario is highly suggestive of rabies. Corneal impression smears are not performed, as they are of low diagnostic yield.

Laboratory diagnosis of rabies is performed by the following methods:

• Antigen detection - Direct immunofluorescence (IF) from specimens of :

• Skin biopsy from the nape of the neck including hair follicles. Rabies antigen is present in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles. It is the most sensitive and specific test.

• Corneal smears were previously used. They are not used anymore as they are of low diagnostic yield.

• Viral isolation- Intracerebral inoculation in mice can be attempted from the brain, CSF, and saliva.

• Antibody demonstration from serum and CSF.

• Viral RNA detection by RT-PCR .

• Postmortem examination of brain tissue samples- demonstration of Negri bodies.

questions.question: An officer of the Indian Forest Services is bitten by a rabid fox while on duty. Which of the following statements is true about the etiological agent?
options: The incubation period is 4 to 5 days
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of infection with the street form of rabies virus. Street rabies causes disease.

All mammals are susceptible to rabies. Cattle, cats and foxes are highly susceptible, whereas dogs and humans have intermediate susceptibility.

Differences between street rabies and fixed rabies:

Street rabies
Fixed rabies (produced by repeated passages)

Causes disease
Doesn't cause disease

Produces Negri body
Doesn't produce Negri body

Affects salivary glands
Doesn't affect salivary glands

Incubation period- 3 months
Incubation period- 4-5 days

questions.question: A 23-year-old man was brought to you with a history of fever, behavioral changes, and seizures. He is foaming at the mouth and is unable to ingest liquids. The patient was admitted to the ICU, however he died soon after. Post mortem brain samples showed the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image showing Negri bodies and the case scenario of fever, neurological symptoms like seizures and altered sensorium, hydrophobia (due to painful muscle contractions during swallowing liquids), and hypersalivation are suggestive of encephalitic rabies.

Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons that are composed of rabies virus proteins and viral RNA. These are commonly observed in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and in pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus. Their presence is a characteristic pathologic finding in rabies.

The image below shows Negri bodies:

questions.question: Babes nodules are seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Babes nodules are seen in rabies. Mononuclear inflammatory infiltration in the leptomeninges, including microglial nodules are called Babes nodules.

The most characteristic pathologic finding in rabies is the Negri body. These are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in brain neurons that are composed of rabies virus proteins and viral RNA. The image given below shows Negri bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding rabies vaccination?
options: Bitten dog should be observed for a minimum of 10 days.
Four-dose regimen is given as 0.1ml intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 28.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis regimen consists of 3 doses.
The dose of human anti rabies immunoglobulin is 20 IU/kg.
questions.answer: B. Four-dose regimen is given as 0.1ml intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 28.
questions.explanation:
According to the Updated Thai Red Cross Regimen (2-2-2-0-2) for post exposure prophylaxis, reconstituted rabies vaccine is given as follows:

• 0.1 ml intradermally

• Sites - two sites at the same visit. It is given in both the deltoids

• Schedule - Days 0, 3, 7, and 28

Healthy dogs, cats, or ferrets may be confined and observed for 10 days.

The dosage of equine rabies immunoglobulin (eRIG) is 40 IU/kg while that of human anti-rabies immunoglobulin (hRIG) is 20 IU/kg body weight.

PrEP regimens for individuals of all ages are as follows:

• Three intramuscular or intradermal vaccine doses on days 0, 7, and 21 or 28.

questions.question: Which family does yellow fever virus belong to?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever virus belongs to the family flaviviridae, which contains the genus Flavivirus.

The important species under genus Flavivirus include:

• Yellow fever virus

• Dengue virus

• Japanese encephalitis virus

• Kyasanur forest disease virus

• West Nile encephalitis

• Zikavirus

Note: Arbovirus is a term used to refer to any viruses that are transmitted by arthropod vectors. There is no family or order by the name arbovirus. The word arbovirus stands for ARthropod-BOrne virus.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy from Uttar Pradesh was rushed to the emergency department with a headache, fever, and blurred vision followed shortly by unresponsiveness to verbal commands. He is suspected to have viral encephalitis. Which of the following transmits this endemic disease?
questions.explanation:
Endemic viral encephalitis is suggestive of Japanese encephalitis. It is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnuii.

It is the leading cause of childhood neurological viral infection in India. In endemic areas such as North India, it typically affects children <15 years of age as by early adulthood, the majority of the population has protective immunity following natural exposure to the virus.

Ardeid birds like herons and egrets are reservoir hosts, while the amplifier hosts are pigs. It is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, and human infection is a tangential dead end.

questions.question: A mother brings her 9-month-old child for vaccination against Japanese encephalitis. Which of the following statements is false regarding this vaccine?
options: Two doses are recommended at age 9 months and 18 months
Inactivated vero cell culture is given 4 weeks apart
Live vaccine SA 14-14-2 is administered intramuscularly
The live attenuated vaccine can be given to adolescents
questions.answer: C. Live vaccine SA 14-14-2 is administered intramuscularly
questions.explanation:
Live SA 14-14-2 strain of Japanese encephalitis (JE) vaccine is administered subcutaneously.

Types of JE Vaccines:

SA 14-14-2 cell culture derived vaccine
Inactivated vero cell culture derived Kolar (Jenvac 82156XY)

Live attenuated
Inactivated

Route of administration
Subcutaneous
Intramuscular
Intramuscular

 Dosage
2 doses
2 doses
2 doses

 Duration between doses
At ages 9months and 16-18 months
4 weeks apart
4 weeks apart

 Ages
9 months, 16-18 months, adolescents and non-immune adults
up to 15 years
