questions.question: A patient presents with fever, arthralgia, and pain behind the eyes for 3 days. On examination, she has the following rash. Lab reports show thrombocytopenia and leucopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the symptoms and the rash suggests dengue fever.

It presents with sudden-onset fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, and a rash. The rash in dengue appears as white islands on a red sea due to erythema with petechiae. The alternative name for dengue, breakbone fever, comes from the associated muscle and joint pains.

Suspected cases of dengue are confirmed by the presence of NS1 antigen or IgM antibodies.

The treatment of dengue is supportive with hydration taking top priority.

questions.question: A 35-year-old wildlife photographer presents with sudden onset of fever, headache, and myalgia. On examination, you notice gingival bleeds and conjunctival hemorrhages. He recently visited a forest in Karnataka that has a large population of monkeys. Which of these is the vector for the suspected disease?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario with exposure to monkeys, fever, myalgia, headache, conjunctival hemorrhage and gingival bleeds is suggestive of Kyasanur forest disease (KFD), which is transmitted by ticks (Haemophysalis spinigera). It is endemic to the forests of Karnataka and Kerala.

The clinical features include:

• Fever

• Headache

• Conjunctivitis

• Myalgia

• Meningoencephalitis

• Hemorrhagic symptoms- hemorrhages in skin, mucosa and gastrointestinal bleeds.

The case fatality rate is about 5 percent.

Monkeys are amplifier hosts, rodents are reservoirs and humans are incidental hosts.

A killed KFD virus vaccine was used in a small field trial and appeared to provide some degree of protection.

questions.question: A middle-aged man presents with delirium, fever, jaundice, and a hemorrhagic diathesis. The patient is agitated and has had no urine output in the last 6 hours. On investigation, there is azotemia and elevated liver enzymes. A viral disease with the vector shown below is suspected. Which of the following inclusion bodies may be seen?
questions.explanation:
The image shows the Aedes aegypti mosquito and the clinical scenario with hepatic and renal dysfunction with delirium points towards a diagnosis of yellow fever. Torres bodies are amorphous eosinophilic nuclear inclusions associated with yellow fever, a disease caused by the Flavivirus.

Inclusion bodies are structures with distinct sizes and shapes that are seen in virus-infected cells under light microscopy.

Note: Dengue hemorrhagic fever can be a differential diagnosis, but there are no inclusion bodies seen in dengue.

questions.question: What is the duration of validity of 17D vaccination?
questions.explanation:
17D vaccine (yellow fever vaccine) is valid for a lifetime, beginning 10 days after vaccination. According to the amendment in 2016 to International Health Regulations 2005, the validity of the related international certificate of vaccination against yellow fever has been changed from ten (10) years to the lifespan of the person (traveler) vaccinated.

It is a live-attenuated vaccine derived from the 'Asibi strain', administered subcutaneously. Immunity after a single dose is long-lasting and provides lifetime protection. It is thermolabile.

Vaccination is compulsory for travel to and from endemic areas.

In India, 17D is manufactured at the Central Research Institute, Kasauli.

questions.question: A pest control technician with a history of fever, vomiting, hematuria, and decreased urine output was diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. Which of the following statements is false about the causative virus?
options: Hantaviruses are the natural pathogens of rodents
Transmission primarily occurs by Culex mosquitoes
Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome presents with pulmonary edema
questions.answer: B. Transmission primarily occurs by Culex mosquitoes
questions.explanation:
Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is caused by Hantaviruses. They are rodent-borne viruses that are transmitted by inhalation of the virus contained in dried excreta of rodents. They are the natural pathogens of rodents like mice, rats, and voles.

HFRS presents with acute kidney injury, hemorrhages, fever, and circulatory collapse. Hantaviruses can also cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.

Note: In Aug 2016, The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), has renamed and moved the genus Hantavirus to Orthohantavirus.

questions.question: An epidemic of paralytic poliomyelitis occurs in a non-immune population. Which among the following strains of poliovirus is the most common cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Type 1 poliovirus is the most common cause of epidemics in populations.

Poliovirus strains have been classified into 3 types:

• Type 1- most common and causes most of the epidemics.

• Type 2- endemic infections.

• Type 3- epidemics but rarer than type 1.

Immunity is type-specific.

Note :- Type 2 is declared eradicated in September, 2015 and Type 3 is declared eradicated in October, 2019

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrics OPD with a history of lower-limb paralysis and the following deformity. Which of the following will be the most common form of presentation of this illness?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario with a history of lower limb paralysis and deformity is suggestive of poliomyelitis. The given image shows deformity of the right lower limb, namely hyperextension at the knee joint and muscle wasting.

Inapparent infection is the most common (90-95%) presentation of polio. Only seroconversion occurs without any clinical manifestations.

Option B: Abortive poliomyelitis is associated with primary viremia and presents as fever, headache, sore throat, and malaise lasting for 1-5 days.

Option C: Paralytic poliomyelitis occurs following minor illness, characterized by biphasic fever with headache, stiff neck, and flaccid paralysis.

Option D: In non-paralytic poliomyelitis, the disease does not progress beyond the stage of aseptic meningitis.

questions.question: A 20-year-old unimmunized patient presents to you with complaints of weakness of lower limbs, inability to pass urine, and fever, for 3 days. His stool samples were sent to the district lab to confirm the diagnosis. Which region of the spinal cord will primarily be affected in these cases?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario of fever, lower limb paralysis, urinary retention, and stool samples being sent for diagnosis, is suggestive of paralytic polio. The anterior horn cells of the spinal cord are primarily affected, causing acute flaccid paralysis. Posterior horns and intermediate columns/lateral horns may also be involved to some extent.

In the central nervous system, the virus multiplies selectively in the neurons and destroys them. The earliest change is the degeneration of Nissl bodies (chromatolysis). Nuclear changes follow.

Note: Fecal samples of all cases of acute flaccid paralysis are obtained (2 samples) and transported to the laboratory within 72 hours of collection at 4–8°C or frozen at -20°C. This is known as the reverse cold chain and is done as a part of gold standard polio surveillance/acute flaccid paralysis surveillance (AFP surveillance).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding vaccination against polio?
options: Sabin type has the live attenuated virus
OPV should not be administered to immunocompromised persons
Salk vaccine is associated with mutations that lead to reversal of virulence
Both OPV and IPV induce humoral IgG
questions.answer: C. Salk vaccine is associated with mutations that lead to reversal of virulence
questions.explanation:
Salk type is the killed vaccine, hence there is no risk of mutation that can lead to a reversal of virulence.

There are two types of vaccines for polio - IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine) and OPV (oral poliovirus vaccine).

questions.question: Which of the following strains of poliovirus have been eradicated worldwide?
questions.explanation:
Type 2 and 3 have been eradicated worldwide.

Type 2: In September 2015, WHO declared the eradication of the wild type 2 poliovirus strain. In India, the last type 2 infection was detected in 1999.

Type 3: It has not been detected anywhere in the world since November 2012. On World Polio Day in October 2019, the type 3 virus was declared to be eradicated worldwide.

The only circulating strain is type 1.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presented with acute chest pain which was stabbing type in nature. The pain is spasmodic and associated with fever spikes. There's an outbreak of coxsackievirus B in her community. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario with stabbing type chest pain which is spasmodic in nature, associated with fever spikes, and history of an outbreak of coxsackievirus B is suggestive of Bornholm disease or epidemic pleurodynia.

Symptoms include paroxysms of acute pleuritic chest pain associated with fever spikes. Involved muscles are tender. Chest X-ray is usually normal. Most cases occur during epidemics of coxsackievirus B. The disease is named after the Danish island of Bornholm where early cases occurred.

The treatment is non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents or hot fomentation of the involved muscles.

Other diseases associated with coxsackievirus B:

• Neonatal myocarditis and pericarditis

• Juvenile diabetes mellitus

• Orchitis

• Severe disseminated congenital infection- hepatitis, meningoencephalitis, adrenocortical involvement

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with headache, fever, and vomiting. On examination, you observe the following. He is diagnosed with herpangina. Which group of viruses causes the same?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows palatal ulcers in herpangina. It is caused by the coxsackievirus A, a large subgroup of the enteroviruses.

Herpangina or vesicular pharyngitis is characterized by grayish- white papulovesicular lesions on an erythematous base that ulcerate. These are present on:

• Soft palate

• Anterior pillars of tonsils

• Uvula

• Posterior oropharynx

It is a common clinical manifestation of coxsackievirus A infection in children, but it can also be caused by coxsackievirus B, echoviruses, or enterovirus 71.

Treatment is usually only supportive, as the disease is self-limiting and usually runs its course in less than a week.

questions.question: A 60-year-old presented with eye pain, watering of eyes, and increased sensitivity to light. On examination, you see the following. Which of the following viruses can cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario is suggestive of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC) caused mainly by Enterovirus 70 and Coxsackievirus A24 variant (CA24v).

It is characterized by sudden swelling, congestion, and watering of the eyes. Subconjunctival hemorrhages are a characteristic feature and corneal involvement may occur transiently.

There is no treatment currently available. The disease is self limiting, and resolves within a five to seven-day period.

Note: Acute follicular conjunctivitis is caused by Adenovirus serotypes 3, 4, 7 and 11.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presented with fever, joint pains, and headache. Chik sign (image given below) is present on the patient's nose. Which of the following vectors transmits the etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
The given case scenario with fever, joint pain, headache, and Chik sign is suggestive of chikungunya which is transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

Chikungunya presents with sudden onset of fever, crippling joint pain, lymphadenopathy, and conjunctivitis. The fever is typically biphasic with a period of remission after 1–6 days. Nose pigmentation is striking in cases of Chikungunya fever and is termed as Chik sign

No animal reservoir has been identified.

Note: Although Chikungunya is transmitted by both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, A.Aegypti is considered primary vector of transmission for Chikungunya.

chapters.chapter: Miscellaneous Viruses Rubella, Coronaviruses, Prions, Rotavirus, Filovirus, Zika Virus And Nipah Virus

questions.question: A newborn baby has a characteristic rash as shown below. On examination, bilateral pearly white nuclear cataracts are noted, and a continuous murmur is auscultated. What family does the virus implicated in this syndrome belong to?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of bilateral nuclear cataracts, blueberry muffin rash (image), and patent ductus arteriosus(murmur) suggest congenital rubella syndrome. Rubella virus belongs to the family Matonaviridae.

Rubella virus previously belonged to family Togaviridae, but has been recently changed to family Matonaviridae by the International Committee on the Taxonomy of viruses (ICTV), making it the sole genus under the family Matonaviridae.

 Option A: Rhabdoviridae includes Rabies virus.

Option B: Filoviridae includes Marburg virus and Ebola virus.

Option D: Calciviridae includes Norwalk agent.

questions.question: A brain biopsy done at the time of autopsy shows spongiform encephalopathy. Which of the following is unlikely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Spongiform encephalopathy is a feature of prion disease. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is not a prion disease.

SSPE is a rare and chronic form of progressive brain inflammation caused by a persistent infection with the measles virus.

Slow virus diseases are characterized by a long asymptomatic period, often months or years in duration, between the introduction of the infectious agent and the appearance of clinical illness. Examples: AIDS, Kuru, CJD, SSPE, PML

CJD, Kuru, and mad cow disease are classified under slow virus diseases which are caused by prions.

questions.question: Which strain of the Ebola virus has the highest case fatality rate?
questions.explanation:
The Zaire strain has a case fatality rate of 90%

There are five identified Ebola virus strains, four of which are known to cause disease in humans:

1. Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus)

2. Sudan virus (Sudan ebolavirus)

3. Taï Forest virus (Taï Forest ebolavirus)

4. Bundibugyo virus (Bundibugyo ebolavirus).

The fifth, Reston virus (Reston ebolavirus), has caused disease in nonhuman primates, but not in humans.

The Bundibugyo ebolavirus, Zaire ebolavirus, and Sudan ebolavirus have been associated with large outbreaks in Africa. The strain that caused the 2014–2016 West African outbreak belongs to the Zaire ebolavirus species.

questions.question: Which of the following is a leading cause of diarrheal death in children?
questions.explanation:
Rotavirus is a leading cause of diarrheal death among children in the developing world.

Rotavirus infections occur in most children below the age of 5 years and are most frequent between 6-24 months of age. Neonatal infections are common but are often asymptomatic or mild.

Vaccines for rotavirus: RotaTeq and Rotarix, given orally.

Note: Viruses that can cause diarrhoea in children include:

• Rotavirus (most common)

• Norwalk virus

• Adenovirus- types 40 and 41

• Astrovirus

• Coronavirus

• Sapovirus

The image below shows an electron micrograph image of the Rotavirus.

questions.question: An 18-year-old went on an exchange program to Singapore. An adventurous eater, she tried clams and oysters on a cruise ship. 2 days later, she developed fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario describes a case of Norwalk infection. It is the most common cause of diarrhea in older children and adults.

They occur in group settings such as banquet halls, cruise ships, dormitories, and campgrounds, where outbreak sources are usually contaminated food and/or water. Potential sources of contaminated food include shellfish such as clams and oysters, which are contaminated by water.

Clinical features are nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, abdominal pain. Symptoms of gastroenteritis develop 12 to 48 hours after being exposed to norovirus.

The image below is an electron micrograph of Norovirus (Norwalk virus).

questions.question: A 70-year-old lady with recent onset, progressive dementia comes with myoclonus. The brain imaging is shown below. What biochemical component is responsible for this disease?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and imaging suggest a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease(CJD), caused by prions. Prions are composed of protein.

These are infectious protein particles that lack any nucleic acid. They are filterable like viruses but are resistant to agents of sterilization.

Prion proteins have two isoforms:

• PrPSc is the prion protein that causes disease.

• PrPc is the normal prion protein, found in human cells.

Prions cause diseases such as CJD, Kuru, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's.

Laboratory diagnosis of prion diseases:

• Measurement of PrPSc by immunoassay

• Brain MRI

• Brain biopsy

• Stress protein 14-3-3

• Sequencing PRNP gene

• Abnormal EEG

questions.question: A 32-year-old lady is admitted to the ICU with COVID-19. Which of the following statements is false regarding the organism causing it?
options: These viruses have club-shaped peplomers on their surface
It acts by binding to ACE1 and TMPRSS4 receptors
questions.answer: D. It acts by binding to ACE1 and TMPRSS4 receptors
questions.explanation:
The coronavirus spike protein binds to the ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors to enter the human cells.

Coronaviruses are a group of spherical or pleomorphic enveloped RNA viruses having club or petal-shaped peplomers. Coronaviruses are named for the crown-like spikes on their surface.

It spreads through coughing, sneezing, and close personal contact such as touching the mouth, nose.

The virus is highly mutable and so vaccine prophylaxis for all strains is difficult.

Coronaviruses cause upper respiratory tract infections, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), and Middle Eastern respiratory syndrome (MERS). They spread by inhalation of the virus present in droplets or aerosols of respiratory secretions of the patients.

 Basic protective measures against the new coronavirus: (SARS-CoV-2)

• Wash your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds.

• Maintain social distancing- Maintain at least 1 meter distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing

• Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth

• Practice respiratory hygiene- cover your mouth and nose with your bent elbow or tissue when you cough or sneeze, then dispose of the used tissue immediately.

• If you have fever, cough, and difficulty breathing, seek medical care early

• Stay informed and follow the advice given by your healthcare provider

questions.question: A person who comes in contact with a case of coronavirus (COVID- 19) needs to be followed up for __________.
questions.explanation:
A person who comes in contact with a coronavirus(COVID-19) case (confirmed or probable) needs to be followed up for apperance of symptoms of coronavirus for the maximum incubation period of 14 days.

Treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment recommended for COVID-19. People with COVID-19 should receive supportive care to help relieve symptoms. For severe cases, treatment should include care to support vital organ functions.

Basic protective measures against the new coronavirus: (SARS CoV 2)

• Wash your hands frequently for atleast 20 seconds.

• Maintain social distancing- Maintain at least 1 metre distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing

• Avoid touching eyes, nose and mouth

• Practice respiratory hygiene- cover your mouth and nose with your bent elbow or tissue when you cough or sneeze, then dispose of the used tissue immediately.

• If you have fever, cough and difficulty breathing, seek medical care early

• Stay informed and follow advice given by your healthcare provider

questions.question: In a patient undergoing testing for SARS-CoV, a FELUDA test is done. Which of the following statements is false about this technology?
options: It is the acronym for FNCAS9 Editor Linked Uniform Detection Assay
Based on CRISPR gene editing technology
It is slower than RT PCR in detecting SARS-CoV2
It uses CAS-9 protein to bind to the viral signature
questions.answer: C. It is slower than RT PCR in detecting SARS-CoV2
questions.explanation:
FELUDA is faster than RT-PCR in detecting SARS-CoV2.

FELUDA (FNCAS9 Editor Linked Uniform Detection Assay) is a newly approved method based on CRISPR gene-editing technology to identify and target the genetic material of SARS-CoV2.

The CRISPR technology uses a highly specific CAS9 protein to find and bind to the target Covid signature. This is then coupled with paper-strip chemistry to elicit a visual readout on a paper strip.

It is a very affordable, sensitive (96%), and specific (98%) strip test which can detect viral genetic material within 45 minutes.

questions.question: A confirmed case of which of the following viral haemorrhagic fevers was found in India?
questions.explanation:
Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever is a severe form of viral hemorrhagic fever, is caused by Nairovirus species.

It is zoonotic in origin with ticks as vectors. The outbreak was caused due to person-to-person transmission in hospitals.

questions.question: A woman presents with a positive urine pregnancy test, 1 month after taking the MMR vaccine. At the time of receiving the vaccine, she had been advised to avoid conception. What advice do you give her now?
options: Low risk; termination of pregnancy may be considered
High risk of anomalies; serious consideration for termination
questions.explanation:
In this case scenario, the doctor should advise the patient to wait and watch.

The vaccine should not be administered during pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs within 28 days of immunization, the patient should be counseled on the theoretical risks for the fetus.

Studies of over 200 women who had been inadvertently immunized with rubella vaccine during pregnancy showed that none of their offspring developed congenital rubella syndrome. Therefore, termination of pregnancy is probably not warranted.

questions.question: While working at a WHO outreach post in Africa, you conduct an educational program about the Zika virus. What family does this virus belong to?
questions.explanation:
Zika virus belongs to the family Flaviviridae.

It is classified by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV):

• Family: Flaviviridae

• Genus: Flavivirus

• Species: Zika virus

Zika virus is an RNA virus that is transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquito bite and by sexual contact. It causes microcephaly and is associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following features do not support a diagnosis of Zika fever?
questions.explanation:
A petechial rash is not a primary feature of Zika virus infection.

Though petechiae may rarely appear in Zika virus disease it is however not included in the CDC case definition of Zika virus disease. Petechial rash points towards a diagnosis of dengue fever while a maculopapular rash suggests a Zika virus disease.

Zika virus infection is characterized by influenza-like clinical signs including fever, headache, and malaise. A maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, myalgia, and arthralgia usually accompany or follow those manifestations.

The complications of Zika virus are:

• Guillain-Barre syndrome

• Fetal microcephaly in pregnant women.

questions.question: Tropical spastic paraparesis is caused by:
questions.explanation:
is the causative agent of the neurodegenerative disorder HTLV-1-associated myelopathy or tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP).

The condition resembles multiple sclerosis and is associated with progressive weakness of legs and lower body. The patients develop spastic paraparesis or paraplegia, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, and extensor plantar response. The disease progresses slowly and takes the form of thoracic myelopathy.

Other conditions caused by HTLV-1 include:

• Adult T-cell leukemias and lymphomas (ATL)

• Uveitis

• Infective dermatitis

• Arthritis

• Sjögren’s syndrome

questions.question: What family does the Nipah virus belong to?
questions.explanation:
Nipah virus belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae.

Togaviridae contains chikungunya virus.

Flaviviridae contains yellow fever virus, dengue virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, hepatitis C virus, Zika virus

Bunyaviridae contains sandfly fever virus, hantaviruses.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of the fungal cell wall?
questions.explanation:
Chitin is a component of the fungal cell wall.

General characteristics of Fungi:

• They are unicellular/multicellular eukaryotes.

• The cell wall contains chitin, glucan, mannan and other polysaccharides.

• The cytoplasmic membrane contains ergosterol.

• They possess true nuclei with the nuclear membrane and paired chromosomes.

• They divide sexually, asexually or by both.

Raymond Sabouraud is known as the Father of Mycology.

questions.question: Which of the following is a yeast?
questions.explanation:
Cryptococcus is a yeast.

Option A: Candida is a yeast-like fungus.

Option C: Fusarium is a mold/filamentous fungus.

Option D: Talaromyces is a dimorphic fungus.

questions.question: Which among the following is not a sexual spore?
questions.explanation:
Sporangiospore is not a sexual spore. It is an asexual spore.

Fungi can be classified into 4 classes based on sexual spore formation:

Class
Sexual spore
Asexual spore

Glomerulomycetes
Oospores, Zygospores
Sporangiospores

Ascomycetes
Ascospores
Conidia

Basidiomycetes
Basidiospores
Conidia

Fungi imperfecti (Deuteromycetes)
Yet to be identified
Conidia

Fungi imperfecti (Deuteromycetes): These are the fungi whose sexual phases are yet to be identified. Most of the fungi of medical importance belong to this group.

Note: The earlier classification of Phycomycetes, under which Zygomycetes, Oomycetes, and other sub-phyla were present, is now obsolete. Phylum Glomerulomycota has replaced it.

questions.question: Which of the following fungal spores are formed by condensation of the hyphal elements?
questions.explanation:
Arthrospores are asexual spores that are formed along the mycelium/hyphae by segmentation and condensation of hyphae.

Arthrospores are commonly formed by dermatophytes, especially those belonging to the genus Trichophyton. They are also formed by dimorphic fungi like Coccidiodes sp.

questions.question: A young patient presents to the dermatology OPD with a history of itchy hypopigmented patches over her chest for 6 months. A KOH mount is prepared with the skin scraping sample, which on microscopy reveals a characteristic appearance as shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture and the KOH mount preparation showing the spaghetti and meatball appearance suggest pityriasis versicolor.

Pityriasis versicolor is a chronic superficial infection of the stratum corneum caused by Malassezia globosa and Malassezia furfur. The most common site involves the neck, chest, back, and upper arms. The lesions often appear as hypopigmented areas.

The KOH mount reveals fungal hyphae that are short and thick (like spaghetti or banana) and many variously sized spores (like meatballs or grapes) referred to as spaghetti and meatballs or bananas and grapes appearance.

Treatment includes topical azoles or terbinafine for 2 weeks.

The image below shows the hypopigmented lesions of P. versicolour over the chest.

Electron microscopic image of Malassezia furfur

questions.question: Which of the following statements about dermatophytes is true?
questions.answer: B. Microsporum infects skin and hair
questions.explanation:
Microsporum infects only skin and hair, not nails.

Dermatophytes include 3 genera:

• Microsporum: It infects only hair and skin (not nails). The species included in this genus are-

• M. gypseum

• M. canis

• M. nanum.

• Epidermophyton: It infects only skin and nails (not hair). E. floccosum is the only species in this genus.

• Trichophyton: It infects skin, hair, and nails. The species falling under this genus are-

• T. rubrum

• T. mentagrophytes

• T. tonsurans

• T. schoenleinii

• T. violaceum

questions.question: A 23-year-old-lady came to the dermatology clinic with complaints of hair loss and the presence of firmly adherent, black, gritty, hard nodules along the hair shaft as shown. There is no associated pruritis of the scalp. Which of the following could be the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The presence firmly adherent, black, gritty, hard nodules along the hair shaft is suggestive of black piedra. The causative agent of this condition is Piedraia hortae.

Piedra is a superficial fungal infection of the hair shaft. It is of two types:

• Black piedra: It is characterized by firmly adherent, black, gritty, hard nodules along the hair shaft. Scalp hair is most often affected. Hair becomes brittle and breaks easily leading to complains of hair loss. It is caused by Piedraia hortae.

• White piedra: It is characterized by soft, white or light brown transparent nodules that are easily detached from the hair. It affects pubic, axillary, facial hair more commonly than scalp hair. It is caused by Trichosporon beigelii.

Management involves shaving or cutting off the affected hair along with topical antifungals.

questions.question: A 45-year-old diabetic patient presented with complaints of discoloration of his toenail for the past 4 months as shown in the image below. Which pathogen most commonly causes this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of onychomycosis and the pathogen most commonly causing this condition is Trichophyton rubrum. Diabetes increases the risk of onychomycosis.

Onychomycosis refers to nail infections caused by fungi. It can be due to dermatophytes, non-dermatophytic moulds, and candida. Tinea unguium refers to nail infections caused by dermatophytes. This condition may affect toenails or fingernails, but toenail infections are particularly common.

The following photomicrograph of the nail segment in KOH shows T. rubrum fungal hyphae invading nail cells.

The following image is of a lactophenol cotton blue(LPCB) mount showing pyriform shaped microconidia on the hyphae of T. rubrum.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the most commonly used culture media for growing fungi?
questions.explanation:
Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) is the most commonly used culture media for growing fungi. It does not contain taurocholate.

It consists of antibiotics like gentamicin or chloramphenicol to inhibit the contaminant bacteria and also cycloheximide to inhibit the growth of saprophytic fungi. It has an acidic pH of 5.4.

Media used in mycology can be classified as:

• Specific media-

• SDA agar

• Czapek-Dox medium

• Birdseed agar

• Cornmeal agar

• Non-specific media-

• Blood agar

• Brain heart infusion agar

questions.question: A gardener from the sub-Himalayan region presented with multiple ulcerative eruptions along the lymphatics of his hand. A tissue biopsy was taken and sent for culture. Microscopic examination of the organism cultured is shown in the image. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
The presence of multiple ulcerative eruptions along the lymphatics in a gardener from the sub-Himalayan region and the microscopic finding of flower-like clusters of conidia are suggestive of sporotrichosis, caused by Sporothrix schenckii. It is a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation.

The lesions occur following traumatic inoculation of the fungus. A granulomatous nodule is first formed at the site of inoculation that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. The infection can spread via lymphatic channels from the skin and subcutaneous tissue to the lymph nodes resulting in formation of secondary ulcers on the lymph nodes. This condition is known as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. This disease is commonly encountered among gardeners, forest workers and manual labourers.

Clinical presentation of lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis:

questions.question: A farmer developed multiple ulcerative nodules along the lymphatics following a rose thorn prick a week ago. Microscopic finding of the skin biopsy is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows an asteroid body which is characteristically seen in a case of sporotrichosis.

Asteroid bodies are formed due to the deposition of the immune complexes around the yeast cell. It consists of a central rounded or oval basophilic, cigar-shaped yeast cell surrounded peripherally by eosinophilic radiations. Formation of such structures is called the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon.

Note: Asteroid bodies are also seen in sarcoidosis. Those are irregular, star-shaped inclusions seen in multinucleate giant cells.

questions.question: A middle-aged man from south India presented to the OPD with a swelling in his left foot that is unresponsive to antibiotics. On examination, multiple discharging sinuses were noted. The discharge contained brown granules that were soft in consistency. Which of the following is likely the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
A swelling with multiple discharging sinuses with brown granules that is unresponsive to the antibiotics is suggestive of eumycetoma caused by Madurella mycetomatis.

Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand. It can be divided into three types- eumycetomas, actinomycetomas and botryomycosis.

Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the subcutaneous tissue from soil or vegetable sources. Within host tissues, the organisms develop to form compacted colonies (grains) 0.5–2 mm in diameter, the color of which depends on the organism responsible. It results in tumefactions, deformities and draining sinuses discharging these grains or granules.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

• A. Direct Examination: The presence of grains in pus collected from draining sinuses or in biopsy material is diagnostic.

• B. Culture Samples should also be cultured, at both 25–30°C and 37°C, on brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar for actinomycetes and on Sabouraud agar (without cycloheximide) for fungi.

Treatment:

The management of eumycetoma is difficult, involving surgical debridement or excision and chemotherapy. Actinomycetoma on the other hand, responds well to rifampicin in combination with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.

Option A: Actinomadura madurae causes actinomycetoma which would respond to antibiotics.

Option B: Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis which is characterised by lesions along the route of lymphatics.

Option C: Fonsecaea pedrosoi causes chromoblastomycosis which would not have discharging sinuses.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a dimorphic fungus?
questions.explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii is a yeast-like fungus and not a dimorphic fungus.

Dimorphic fungi exist in the yeast form in body tissues and cultures maintained at 37°C, and in the filamentous form in cultures at room temperature(25°C).

Examples of dimorphic fungi include:

• Blastomyces dermatitidis

• Coccidioides immitis

• Paracoccidioides brasiliensis

• Talaromyces marneffei

• Sporothrix schenckii

• Histoplasma capsulatum

• Coccidioides posadasii

questions.question: A 54-year-old man had presented to the clinic with a history of chronic cough. His chest X-ray showed a mass in the left lung with hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the mass was done and findings are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the presence of tiny yeast forms within macrophages are suggestive of Histoplasmosis which is also called Darling's disease. Other names of this condition include Cave's disease and Ohio disease.

The causative agent is a dimorphic fungus called Histoplasma capsulatum. Transmission occurs via inhalation of conidia.

After inhalation, the conidia develop into yeast cells and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. Within macrophages, the yeasts may disseminate to reticuloendothelial tissues, such as the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes.

Biopsy reveals tiny (2-4 microns) oval-shaped yeast cells inside macrophages.

On culture and microscopy, tuberculate macroconidia and hyaline septate mold with microconidia are seen.

It is treated using azole antifungals.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with a recent history of travel to South America was brought to the hospital with fever, enlarged lymph nodes and multiple skin lesions on his face. Tissue sample from the lesion shows the following findings under microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the characteristic pilot's wheel appearance on culture(image) is suggestive of paracoccidioidomycosis caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. It is also called Lutz mycosis/ South American blastomycosis.

Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is a thermally dimorphic fungus that causes a chronic granulomatous disease affecting the lungs, skin, mucosa, lymph nodes. On culture, yeast form is seen at 37° C and the mycelial form at 25° C.

Microscopy of tissue sample reveals thick walled, round, yeast cells with numerous buds attached to each other circumferentially giving the classic mickey mouse or pilot wheel appearance.

Most infections are asymptomatic and few individuals with acute disease present with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and skin lesions.

The below image shows skin lesions in a child with paracoccidioidomycosis.

Treatment:

• Mild/moderate disease: Itraconazole

• Severe disease: Amphotericin B for 2-3weeks followed by Itraconazole.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with low-grade fever and a skin lesion as shown below. He had a history of recent travel to North America. Chest X-Ray reveals consolidation in the right lung with hilar lymphadenopathy. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 37°C shows thick-walled, large (7-20 µ), round yeast cells with a single broad-based bud. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with pulmonary and cutaneous involvement along with a history of travel to North America and the characteristic culture findings suggests the diagnosis of Blastomycosis caused by Blastomyces dermitidis.

Blastomycosis is a chronic infection, characterized by the formation of suppurative and granulomatous lesions, especially, in the lungs and skin.

It is most common in North America and so is also called North Amerian Blastomycosis.

The causative organism is a thermally dimorphic fungus called Blastomyces dermatitidis. Humans are infected by the inhalation of spores in the soil.

Blastomycosis can present in three forms:

1. Pulmonary disease:

• Presents with cough, sputum production, chest pain, and fever

• Hilar lymphadenopathy may be present

• Focal or diffuse consolidation, miliary lesions, or abscess formation may occur.

• Resembles TB and Histoplasmosis

2. Cutaneous disease:

• Involvement of face and exposed parts of the skin

• Skin lesion: ulcerated verrucous granulomas with an advancing border and central scarring. The border is filled with microabscesses and has a sharp, sloping edge. (image in stem)

3. Disseminated disease:

• Multiple skin lesions are the most common presentation

• Highly fatal

• Genitourinary tract (especially prostate) is frequently involved

• Bone involvement resembles chronic osteomyelitis.

It can be diagnosed based on culture findings. Characterictic findings include the presence of thick-walled round yeast cell with a single broad-based bud when cultured at 37°C. (figure of 8 appearance)

Treatment:

• Localised mild/moderate disease - Itraconazole (6 months)

• Disseminated/ severe disease - Amphotericin B

questions.question: A middle-aged man residing in a rural area presents with psychosis, ataxia and convulsions. On further inquiry, you find out there is history of similar complaints in the family members who recently consumed food prepared with grains as shown in the image. What is the poisoning is most likely due to?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette and the presence of dark coloured ergot growing on the wheat as shown in the image are suggestive of ergotism due to Claviceps purpurea

Mycotic poisoning is of two types: Mycetism and Mycotoxicosis

Mycetism:

The fungus itself causes toxic effects.

Examples:

• Claviceps → Ergot poisoning

• Coprine → coprine poisoning

• Inocybe → muscarine poisoning

Mycotoxicosis:

Fungal toxins contaminate food and cause toxic effects.

Examples:

• Aflatoxins: These are a type of mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species of fungi, such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus.

• Fusarium toxins

• Citrinin toxin was first isolated from Penicillium citrinum.

questions.question: The below given image shows result of hair perforation test. The organism likely to show below given appearance is
questions.explanation:
Image shows surface erosion of shaft caused by Trichophyton mentagrophytes.

Hair perforation test:

• Done to differentiate Trichophyton rubrum from mentagrophytes.

• Few strands of human hair are placed in a petridish with 20 ml of distilled water and autoclaved.

• Few drops of sterile 10% yeast extract and a few fragments of the test fungus are added to the hair strands.

• Incubated at 250C for 2-3 weeks.

• Hair is removed and examined microscopically in a lactophenol cotton blue stained wet preparation.

• T.mentagrophytes causes surface erosion of the shaft resulting in wedge shaped appearance of the shaft.

questions.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding Cryptococcus neoformans?
options: It most commonly causes meningitis in AIDS patients
There are 3 serological types based on capsular polysaccharide
Niger seed agar is used to demonstrate melanin production
questions.explanation:
Pathogenic varieties of cryptococcus including C. neoformans and C. gattii are laccase positive. They also have ability to grow at 37° C and these factors are used to differentiate them from non-pathogenic cryptococci.

Cryptococci have been classified into 5 serotypes (A, B, C, D, and AD) based on their capsular polysaccharide:

• Three serotypes fall under Cryptococcus neoformans - A(var. grubii), D(var. neoformans), and AD(a hybrid of serotypes A and D). Although serotype AD is very similar to serotypes A and D, the isolates still comprise a discrete group that can be distinguished.

• The serotypes B and C are now considered a different species - Cryptococcus gattii.

Niger seed agar is a solid medium used for selective and differential isolation of Cryptococcus neoformans from clinical specimens. C. neoformans and C. gattii produces brown colonies on this medium due to the formation of melanin. Melanin is produced by laccase using caffeic acid as the substrate.

The following image shows pigmented colonies of C. gattii growing on niger seed agar.

Cryptococcal meningitis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, is an opportunistic infection seen in individuals with AIDS. Flucytosine and amphotericin B are used in the treatment of this condition.

questions.question:
Which of the following organisms cannot be grown on any culture media?

1. Paracoccidioides brasiliensis

2. Rhinosporidium seeberi

3. Histoplasma capsulatum

4. Pneumocystis jirovecii

5. Rhizopus oryzae
questions.explanation:
Rhinosporidium seeberi and Pneumocystis jirovecii are non-cultivable organisms and cannot be grown on any culture media.

Another example of a non-cultivable fungus is Lacazia loboi. It causes Jorge Lobo's disease which is a chronic subcutaneous mycosis.

Rhizopus oryzae is a mold which is easily cultivable on SDA. Dimorphic fungi like Histoplasma capsulatum and Paracoccidiodes brasiliensis are identified based on their colony morphology on SDA.

Note: Recently, molecular biological techniques have demonstrated that Rhinosporidium is an aquatic protistan parasite. Infections due to Rhinosporidium have been classified under infections due to Protozoa under the ICD 11.

questions.question: A patient with HIV presented complaining of cough and progressively worsening breathing difficulty. Chest X-ray showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The findings of microscopic examination of his bronchoalveolar lavage is given below. Which is the most probable causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture and the GMS stained smear showing the black-colored cysts resembling crushed ping pong balls are suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.

Patients with PCP generally present with fever and cough that is usually non-productive. Chest X-ray is either a normal film if the disease is suspected early, or with diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The classic finding of dense perihilar infiltrate is unusual in patients with AIDS.

Treatment of choice is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole) and pentamidine isethionate. Cotrimoxazole can also be used for prophylaxis in patients having AIDS.

The following X-ray image shows a cyst (arrow) and bilateral lung infiltrates in a patient with PCP:

questions.question: A middle-aged immunocompromised patient presents with complaints of pain during swallowing. She describes it as a burning sensation that radiates to her back every time she swallows. Oral examination reveals creamy white patches on the oral mucosa. The wet mount microscopy of the scraping obtained from the patches is given below. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of odynophagia, creamy white patches on the oral mucosa and the wet mount microscopy showing budding yeasts with pseudohyphae are suggestive of oral candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

It is an opportunistic infection commonly seen in immunocompromised states like AIDS, diabetes etc.

Treatment includes topical azoles or nystatin.

questions.question: A young lady complains of recurrent rhinitis, nasal discharge and bilateral nasal blockage for two years. She has a history of allergic rhinitis. On rhinoscopy, multiple ethmoidal polyps with mucosal thickening and impacted secretions are seen in both the nasal cavities. A tissue biopsy is taken and sent for culture, which on microscopic examination shows the following appearance. What is the most probable organism implicated here?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture and the microscopic appearance is suggestive of fungal rhinosinusitis. The most probable causative organism is Aspergillus fumigatus. It is commonly involved in paranasal sinus mycoses (fungal sinusitis).

The disease has been described to have four types:

• allergic

• non-invasive

• invasive

• fulminant

A possible fifth type called non-invasive destructive type may also exist.

Zygomycetes like mucor and rhizopus are the common agents in fulminant type of fungal sinusitis.

The characteristic microscopic appearance of Aspergillus fumigatus:

• The vesicle is conical.

• Phialides are arranged in a single row.

• Conidia arise from the upper third of the vesicle and are hyaline.

Option B: Aspergillus flavus appears as follows:

• The vesicle is globular.

• Phialides are arranged in one or two rows.

• Conidia arise from the entire vesicle and are hyaline.

Option C: Aspergillus niger appear as follows:

• The vesicle is globular shaped.

• Phialides are in two rows.

• Conidia arise from the entire vesicle and are black.

Option D: Penicillium chrysogenum appear as follows:

• Septate hyphae with branched conidiophores bearing chains of spores(brush or broom appearance).

questions.question: A 68-year-old post-COVID-19 patient presented with a black, foul-smelling nasal discharge and blurred vision. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass eroding the septum and hard palate was visualised. Lactophenol cotton blue mount from the culture is given below. Which of the following statements is false regarding the condition?
options: Iron administration to patients with active infection should be avoided
Posaconazole can be used to treat it
Pulmonary form is the most common
questions.answer: D. Pulmonary form is the most common
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the LPCB mount showing aseptate hyphae branching at right-angles is strongly suggestive of mucormycosis. Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. Pulmonary mucormycosis is the second most common form.

Mucormycosis is an invasive disease caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The disease is often characterized by hyphae growing in and around the blood vessels. It can turn fatal on cerebral involvement and development of speticemia.

Risk factors for the infection include:

• Diabetes (Diabetic ketoacidosis).

• Elevated levels of free iron.

• Defects in phagocytic function.

• Organ or hematopoietic stem transplantation.

Treatment of choice is Amphotericin-B. Posaconazole can be used as an alternative drug.

questions.question: Most common cause of cerebral malaria is:
questions.explanation: Cytoadherence of P. falciparum-infected red cells.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the blood smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

Falciparum malaria infects both young and mature erythrocytes. Binucleate rings (double chromatin) seen in RBCs are common and they resemble stereo headphones in appearance. The rings are often attached to the margins of the red cells and are described as form applique or accole. There may be several rings present within a single erythrocyte.

Hypnozoites are not present in P. falciparum infection.

The peripheral smear finding of P. falciparum malaria are:

• Multiple ring form

• Accole form

• Absent schizont

• Banana shaped gametocytes

• Maurer's dots

The below image shows banana shaped gametocyte:

questions.question: During your rural posting, a patient presents with a high fever and chills. Malaria is endemic in the area so you order a peripheral smear. While examining the peripheral blood smear, you note that the schizont stage is not seen. Which of the following organisms is implicated here?
questions.explanation:
The schizont stage is usually not seen in the peripheral smear of individuals having Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

A mature schizont contains merozoites and hemozoin. This will burst to release merozoites into circulation. The merozoites invade fresh erythrocytes, in which they go through the same process of development called erythrocytic schizogony or merogony.

After the ring form is formed in peripheral blood, the remaining RBC cycle of falciparum occurs in the capillaries of the brain and other internal organs. Hence only the ring form is seen in the peripheral smear.

However, for other Plasmodium species, all erythrocytic stages occur in peripheral blood vessels.

The below image shows the life cycle of Plasmodium spp.

questions.question: Which of the following Plasmodium spp. has the longest incubation period?
questions.explanation:
Plasmodium malariae has the longest incubation period of 28 days.

The incubation period is the interval between the infective mosquito bite and the first appearance of clinical symptoms. The average incubation periods for Plasmodium species are:

• P. vivax: 8-31 days (14 days)

• P. falciparum: 8-14 days (12 days)

• P. ovale: 8-31days (14 days)

• P. malariae: 18-40 days (28 days)

Note: The pre-patent period is the interval between the entry of the parasites into the host and the time when they first become detectable in blood.

questions.question: Which of the following Plasmodium spp. mainly affects the old RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Plasmodium malaria mainly affects the old RBCs.

Options A and D- P. vivax and P. ovale infect young RBCs and reticulocytes.

Option B- P. falciparum infects RBCs of all ages.

The degree of parasitization is not heavy for P. vivax and P. malariae while very high intensity of parasitization is seen in infection with P. falciparum.

questions.question: A microbiologist is examining the slide shown in the following image under the microscope. Which of the following is false regarding this?
options: 'B' is used for determining the species
'A' is air dried rapidly and stained with one of the Romanowsky stains
For 'B' to be considered negative, at least 200 oil immersion fields should be examined
questions.answer: A. 'B' is used for determining the species
questions.explanation:
In the given image 'A' is a thin smear and 'B' is a thick smear. The thin smear is used for determining the species, not the thick smear.

The two types of smears are prepared from the peripheral blood are:

• Thin smear– It is used for detecting the parasites and determining the species. They are air-dried rapidly and stained with Romanowsky stains.

• Thick smear– It is more sensitive and examined under oil immersion microscope. It is more suitable for the rapid detection of malarial parasites. Species identification is difficult. It is recommended that 200 oil immersion fields should be examined before a thick film is declared negative.

The image below shows the thin and thick smears.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the OPD with high-grade fever, chills, and rigors for the past 3 days. A peripheral blood smear revealed the following. Which of the following is false regarding the diagnostic methods used to detect the condition he is likely suffering from?
options: Jaswant Singh Bhattacharya stain is used for peripheral smear examination
HRP-2 antigen test is done for detection of P.vivax
Acridine orange dye is used in quantitative buffy coat method
Rapid diagnostic tests have lesser sensitivity than microscopy
questions.answer: B. HRP-2 antigen test is done for detection of P.vivax
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing ring forms are suggestive of P. falciparum malaria. HRP-2 antigen detection used in rapid diagnostic tests for malaria is specific for P. falciparum.

Jaswant Singh Bhattacharya (JSB) stain is routinely used in India to stain peripheral blood smears for the diagnosis of malaria.

Acridine orange dye is used in the quantitative buffy coat (QBC) method of diagnosis which provides better yield compared to peripheral smears.

Rapid diagnostic tests are based on the detection of antigens using immunochromatographic methods. They are less sensitive than microscopy and also cannot differentiate between species except P. falciparum. The 2 antigens detected are:

• pLDH (parasite lactate dehydrogenase)- pan malarial antigen

• HRP-2 (histidine-rich protein 2)- specific for P.falciparum.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with a 5-day history of fever is brought to the casualty by his son after an episode of seizures. He is diagnosed with malignant tertian malaria. Which of the following complications will you not expect to see in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Metabolic acidosis (and not alkalosis) is a complication of malignant tertain malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

Complications of falciparum malaria include:

• Metabolic acidosis

• Cerebral malaria

• Algid malaria

• Septicemic malaria

• Blackwater fever

• Pulmonary edema

• Acute renal failure

• Hypoglycemia

• Hyperpyrexia

• Severe anemia

• Shock

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient presents with a high-grade fever, headache, and weakness for 5 days. He gives a history of blood transfusion 4 months back. The microscopic examination of the thin blood smear is given below. What is the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the microscopy showing Maltese crosses or tetrads are suggestive of babesiosis caused by Babesia microti.

The definitive host for babesia are ixodid ticks. Man is an incidental, dead-end host.

On microscopic examination, babesia trophozoites appear as intraerythrocytic round or pyriform or ring form. The ring form is the most common and it lacks the central hemozoin deposit which differentiates it from P. falciparum.

Other distinguishing features are the absence of schizonts and gametocytes and the presence of tetrads/Maltese crosses, which are pathognomic of B. microti or B. duncani.

The below image shows Maltese cross appearance of Babesia microti.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Toxoplasma gondii?
options: Oocysts are formed within the intermediate host
The tachyzoites inside the tissue cyst can be reactivated on immunosuppression
questions.answer: D. Human toxoplasmosis is a zoonosis
questions.explanation:
Human toxoplasmosis is a zoonosis. It is transmitted by cats.

Toxoplasma gondii has two types of life cycles:

• Enteric cycle

• Exoenteric cycle

The enteric cycle occurs in definitive hosts such as cats. Exoenteric cycle occurs in intermediate hosts such as humans, mice, rats, etc.

Both asexual reproduction (schizogony) and sexual reproduction (gametogony) occur within the mucosal epithelial cells of the small intestine of the cat. The tachyzoites and tissue cyst represent stages in asexual multiplication, while the oocyst is formed by sexual reproduction.

All three forms, tachyzoites, tissue cyst, and oocyst occur in the definitive host. Only the asexual forms, tachyzoites, and tissue cysts are present in the intermediate host.

Tachyzoites continue to multiply and spread locally by the lymphatic system and blood, while the bradyzoites multiply slowly inside the tissue cyst. The dormant bradyzoites inside the cyst may be reactivated on immune suppression causing renewed infection in the host.

The below image shows the life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii.

questions.question: An HIV positive pregnant woman was brought to the ER after an episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. CECT was done which showed multiple enhancing lesions. A stereotactic biopsy of the cerebral lesions was done and the image is given below. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for her treatment?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing lymphocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils surrounding the toxoplasma bradyzoites which are encased in cysts are suggestive of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Spiramycin is the drug of choice during pregnancy.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic infection commonly found in HIV +ve patients and usually occurs when CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL.

It appears as ring enhancing lesions on contrast enhanced CT. Calcification may also be seen in old lesions.

Sabin-Feldman dye test is a serological test done for the detection of antibodies against toxoplasma. IIF (indirect immunofluorescence), IHA (indirect heamagglutination), and CFT (complement fixation test) are also used for the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis. Dye test remains positive throughout life, while CFT becomes negative soon after acute infection.

ELISA is most commonly used and IgM and IgG antibodies are estimated separately.

Standard treatment is sulfadiazine/pyrimethamine and leucovorin for a minimum of 4–6 weeks. The drug of choice for toxoplasmosis in pregnancy is spiramycin.

questions.question: A Kinyoun-positive oocyst (25 μm) isolated from an HIV patient with diarrhea is shown in the image. What is the likely organism implicated here?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with diarrhea in an HIV patient is suggestive of a coccidian parasitic infestation. Kinyoun-positive oocysts with the size of 25 μm in the image are formed by Cystoisospora.

The below image shows oocysts of Cyclospora cayetanensis in the modified acid-fast stain.

The below image shows oocysts of Cryptosporidium parvum in the modified acid-fast stain.

questions.question: A patient who underwent a renal transplant 3 months ago came with complaints of diarrhea for the last 9 days. The stool sample subjected to Kinyoun staining revealed 4-6 µm structures as shown below. Which of the following is true about the causative organism?
options: It is an obligate intracellular organism
Oocysts are immediately infective after being excreted in stool
Metronidazole is the drug of choice
questions.answer: C. Oocysts are immediately infective after being excreted in stool
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with Kinyoun stain positive oocysts of size 4-6 µm is suggestive of cryptosporidiosis. The oocysts are immediately infective after being excreted in the stool.

Cryptosporidium is a coccidian parasite and implicated in causing traveler's diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The two cryptosporidium species responsible are C. hominis and C. parvum.

The infective form is the oocyst excreted in the patient's feces, which can be acquired through drinking or during recreational water activities. The oocysts are immediately infectious (unlike isospora oocysts, which require maturation), and may cause autoinfection or be implicated in person-to-person transmission. Because of their small size (4-5micron), they is difficult to see using routine staining. Hence acid-fast/Kinyoun's stain is used.

Once ingested, the 4 sporozoites are released from the cyst and attach to the small intestinal mucosa. It causes crampy abdominal pain and non-inflammatory watery diarrhea.

Treatment is mainly supportive, though nitazoxanide has been FDA approved for use in cryptosporidium infection.
