questions.question: A 9-year-old child infected with Toxocara canis is diagnosed to have visceral larva migrans. It is an example of________.
questions.explanation:
Toxocara canis (dog roundworm) infecting a human is an example of an aberrant parasite. It is defined as a parasite that infects a host where they cannot develop further.

Parasites can be classified as:

• Ectoparasites - inhabit only the body surface of the host without penetrating the tissue. The term infestation is often used for parasitization. e.g., lice, ticks, and mites.

• Endoparasite - lives within the body of the host and causes infection.

Endoparasites are further classified as follows:

• Obligate parasites - cannot exist without a host. e.g., Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium.

• Facultative parasites - exist as either parasitic or free-living forms. e.g., Naegleria fowleri.

• Accidental parasites - infects an unusual host. e.g., Echinococcus granulosus infects man

• Aberrant/Wandering parasites - infects a host where they cannot develop further. e.g., Toxocara canis (dog roundworm) infecting humans.

questions.question: Which of the following refers to a host in which the larval stage of the parasite remains viable without further development?
questions.explanation:
A host in which the larval stage of the parasite remains viable without further development is referred to as the paratenic host.

For example, in the lifecycle of Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm), humans are the definitive host. The first intermediate host is cyclops and the second is small freshwater fish. If the small freshwater fish with the plerocercoid larva get eaten by a larger fish, the larva survives in the larger fish. This makes the larger fish a paratenic host.

Host is an organism that harbors the parasite and provides nourishment and shelter to it. It is relatively larger than the parasite.

Types of hosts:

• Definitive host - harbors stages of sexual reproduction of the parasite.

• Intermediate host - harbors stages of asexual multiplication of the parasite.

• Paratenic host - harbors only the larval stage of the parasite which remains viable without further development.

• Reservoir host - harbors the parasite and acts as an important source of infection to other susceptible hosts, especially in endemic areas.

• Accidental host - harbors a parasite that is not usually found in the host.

questions.question: A 46-year-old farmer came to the clinic with cough and chest pain for one week and fatigue for a month. He was diagnosed to have a hydatid cyst in his right lung. Which of the following classes does the causative organism of this disease belong to?
questions.explanation:
The causative organism of hydatid disease is Echinococcus granulosus and it belongs to the class cestodes.

It is a tape-like, segmented worm. It infects man accidentally, giving rise to hydatid cysts.

The image below shows the classification of parasites.

Note: Zoonoses refers to diseases caused by zoonotic organisms. It is not a class of organisms.

questions.question: Which of the following is the smallest cestode infecting humans?
questions.explanation:
The smallest cestode infecting humans is Hymenolepis nana.

Option A: Diphyllobothrium latum is the longest cestode infecting man.

Option C: Heterophyes heterophyes is the smallest trematode infecting man.

Option D: Strongyloides stercoralis is the smallest nematode infecting man.

Also, Fasciolopsis buski is the largest trematode infecting humans.

questions.question: Which of the following parasites has a direct life cycle?
questions.explanation:
Enterobius vermicularis has a direct life cycle.

Parasite requiring a single host to complete its development is said to have a direct life cycle.

Parasites having a direct life cycle are:

Protozoa
Helminths

• Entamoeba histolytica

• Giardia lamblia

• Trichomonas vaginalis

• Balantidium coli

• Cryptosporidium parvum

• Cyclospora cayetanensis

• Isospora belli

• Microsporidia.

• Ascaris lumbricoides

• Enterobius vermicularis

• Trichuris trichura

• Ancylostoma duodenale

• Necator americanus

• Hymenolepsis nana.

Parasite requiring two or more hosts to complete its development is said to have indirect life cycle, e.g. Plasmodium spp.

questions.question:
Match the following:

Patient
Intermediate host

1. A boy from Kolkata with fever and massive splenomegaly

A. Pig

2. A lady from Kerala with bilateral non-pitting pedal edema

B. Sandfly

3. A man with a new-onset seizure and a cyst with a dot sign in MRI brain

C. Human

4. A woman with fever and Maltese cross appearance in peripheral smear

D. Culex mosquito
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option B.

A boy from Kolkata with fever and massive splenomegaly is likely suffering from Kala-azar caused by Leishmania donovani. Its intermediate host is sandfly.

A lady from Kerala with bilateral non-pitting pedal edema is likely suffering from lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. Its intermediate host is the culex mosquito.

A man presenting with new-onset seizures and MRI brain showing cyst with a dot sign is likely suffering from neurocysticercosis caused by ingestion of Taenia solium eggs (Cysticercus cellulose). The intermediate host of Taenia Solium is the pig.

A woman having fever with her peripheral smear showing Maltese cross appearance is likely suffering from babesiosis caused by Babesia microti. Its intermediate host is human.

questions.question: An entomologist who had recently visited Mexico presented to the OPD with fever, fatigue, and an alleged history of contact with the insect given in the image. Which of the following diseases is it a biological vector for?
questions.explanation:
The image shows reduviid bug which is the biological vector for the transmission of Chagas disease. Acute Chagas disease can present as fever with fatigue and a subcutaneous swelling known as a chagoma. It may lead to fatal myocarditis.

Biological vectors not only help in the transfer of parasites but the parasites undergo development or multiplication in their body as well. They are also called true vectors.

Examples of biological vectors are:

• Mosquito - Malaria, filariasis

• Sandfly - Kala-azar

• Tsetse fly - Sleeping sickness

• Reduviid bugs - Chagas disease

• Ticks - Babesiosis

questions.question: Autoinfection is not seen with which of the following parasites?
questions.explanation:
Autoinfection is not seen in infection with Ascaris lumbricoides.

Autoinfection refers to either of the following:

• Reinfection by microbes or parasitic organisms that are present on or within the body. It is also known as internal reinfection. e.g., Strongyloides.

• Self-infection by direct contact with a contagious agent, as with parasite eggs in the infectious state transmitted by fingernails. e.g., Pinworm.

The following are the parasites causing autoinfection (mnemonic: CHEST.C)

• Cryptosporidium parvum

• Hymenolepis nana

• Enterobius vermicularis

• Strongyloides stercoralis

• Taenia solium

• Capillaria philippinensis.

questions.question: A microbiologist is doing research about antigenic variations in parasites. Which of the following parasites will exhibit this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Trypanosoma brucei exhibits antigenic variation within the host. This genetic switch protects them from antibodies.

These trypanosomes exhibit unique antigenic variations of their glycoproteins. There is a cyclical fluctuation in the trypanosomes occurring in the blood of infected vertebrates after every 7–10 days.

Parasites exhibiting antigenic variation include:

• Trypanosoma brucei gambiense

• Trypanosome brucei rhodesiense

• Plasmodium spp.

• Giardia lamblia

 The following image shows Trypanosoma brucei.

The following image shows Plasmodium spp.

The following image shows the trophozoite of Giardia lamblia.

questions.question: You order a peripheral blood film examination while evaluating a patient with pyrexia of unknown origin. Which of the following organisms cannot be detected by this investigation?
questions.explanation:
Stool examination is useful for the detection of Giardia lamblia, not peripheral blood film examination.

Examination of blood is of vital importance for demonstrating parasites that circulate in blood vessels.

Examples of parasites found in the peripheral blood film:

Protozoa
Nematodes

• Plasmodium spp.

• Babesia spp.

• Trypanosoma spp.

• Leishmania spp.

• Wuchereria bancrofti

• Brugia malayi

• Loa loa

• Mansonella spp.

questions.question: A patient has presented to the PHC with fever and chills. You order a rapid diagnostic test to detect HRP-2 antigen. Which of the following diseases is it used to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
HRP-2 antigen detection is used in the diagnosis of malaria.

Malaria antigens detected by the rapid immunochromatographic test are:

• pLDH - positivity is seen in all Plasmodium species

• HRP-2 - positivity is specific for P. falciparum

The below image shows rapid diagnostic test (RDT) kit for malaria.

questions.question: In a patient with a positive Casoni's skin test, which of the following infections will you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Casoni’s skin test is done in patients with hydatid disease.

It is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction (type I).

This test is abandoned now due to non-specificity and has been supplemented by serological tests.

questions.question: A patient presented to the OPD with cough, chest pain, and expectoration of rusty colored sputum. He is diagnosed to have an oriental lung fluke infection. Which of the following parasites is implicated here?
questions.explanation:
Paragonimus westermani is commonly known as oriental lung fluke or Japanese lung fluke. It causes a pulmonary syndrome characterised by cough, chest pain and hemoptysis.

Paragonimus westermani is a trematode. The transmission to humans occurs by eating raw or undercooked crab or crayfish containing metacercariae. The metacercariae excyst in the human gut and young worms migrate to the lungs, where they become encapsulated in lung tissue.

The patient complains of cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. The viscous sputum is speckled with golden-brown eggs.

Treatment: Praziquantel (25 mg/ kg TDS for 1-2 days) is the drug of choice.

The following image shows the life cycle of Paragonimus westermani, the oriental lung fluke.

questions.question: A college student from Mangalore comes to the OPD with intermittent fever, headache, and chills for 1 week. She gives a history of malaria 1 year back for which she had received treatment. Which of the following species you would expect to see in the peripheral smear of this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of malaria relapse and it is caused by Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale species.

In case of P.vivax and P.ovale, two kinds of sporozoites are seen. Some multiply inside hepatic cells to form schizonts while others persist and remain dormant as hypnozoites (resting forms). These dormant forms may get activated and release merozoites, which go on infecting RBCs producing true clinical relapse. It usually occurs after 6 to 12 months of complete cure from the disease.

In case of P.falciparum and P.malariae, the initial tissue phase disappears completely and no hypnozoites are found, hence relapse is not seen.

In Plasmodium falciparum, recrudescence can be seen which is defined as the recurrence of asexual parasitemia. It usually occurs within 8 weeks of treatment and is due to incomplete treatment or drug resistance.

questions.question: A middle-aged woman comes to the clinic with abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue, and weight loss. Stool examination revealed bile-stained eggs. Which of the following organisms may not be implicated in this case?
questions.explanation:
Enterobius vermicularis eggs are non-bile stained and the others are bile stained.

Enterobiasis commonly occurs in young children and is characterised by anal pruritus. The worm may migrate up to the uterus, fallopian tubes and into the peritoneum in adult women. This can lead to:

• Chronic salpingitis

• Cervicitis

• Peritonitis

• Recurrent urinary tract infections.

questions.question: You are examining a wet mount stool sample of a patient with diarrhea. As the eggs are not visible, you concentrate the sample using the saturated salt solution technique. Which of the following eggs will not float in this technique?
questions.explanation:
The eggs of Strongyloides stercoralis will not float in a saturated salt solution.

Concentration methods are used when the parasites in stool are scanty and difficult to identify in routine stool examination. It is of 2 types:

• Floatation methods- the feces are suspended in a solution of high specific gravity and eggs will float up. e.g. saturated salt solution technique, zinc sulfate centrifugal floatation technique.

• Sedimentation Methods - the feces are suspended in a solution with low specific gravity and eggs will sediment at the bottom. e.g. formol-ether sedimentation technique.

questions.question: The life cycle given below is of which of the following:
questions.explanation:
The given life cycle is of Entamoeba histolytica.

Its life cycle includes 2 stages - the motile trophozoite and the non-motile cyst, both of which are seen in the image shown above. The transmission is primarily by the fecal-oral route. There is no animal reservoir.

The ingested cysts differentiate into trophozoites in the ileum which invade the colonic epithelium. The trophozoites penetrate to the submucosal layer and form abscesses which break down to form flask-shaped ulcer.

The trophozoites multiply by binary fission and produce cysts, and both stages are passed in the feces. Trophozoites are rapidly destroyed outside the body. Cysts survive in the external environment and are responsible for transmission.

The most frequent site of systemic disease is the liver.

Note: The genus Entamoeba has four morphologically identical species - E. histolytica, E. dispar, E. bangladeshi, and E. moshkovskii. E. moshkovskii which was initially thought to be non-pathogenic has recently been shown to be a causative agent of non-invasive diarrhea.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed to have amoebic dysentery. Which of the following is the infective form of the protozoan causing this disease?
questions.explanation:
The mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form of Entamoeba histolytica causing amoebic dysentery. It is passed in feces and can remain viable under moist conditions for about 10 days.

The following are the characteristic features of various life stages of Entamoeba histolytica:

The trophozoite is found only in tissues. Its cytoplasm has a ground-glass appearance. The nucleus has a central karyosome with radiating fibrils called linin network giving a cartwheel appearance. Pseudopodia are present which exhibit gliding motility.

The below image shows trophozoite form.

The precystic stage has a large glycogen vacuole and 2 chromatid bars. It secretes a refractile cyst wall to become a cyst.

The cystic stage has a mature cyst with 4 nuclei and no glycogen mass. Chromatid bars disappear.

The below image shows cystic form.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presented with complaints of abdominal pain and 6 episodes of passing foul-smelling dark stool mixed with mucus and blood streaks. There is no history of fever and tenesmus. On examination, vitals are stable and localized tenderness is present in the right iliac fossa. Which of the following is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of amoebic dysentery and the causative agent is Entamoeba histolytica.

Clinical features of intestinal amebiasis:

• Acute intestinal amebiasis- dysentery, lower abdominal discomfort, and flatulence.

• Chronic amebiasis- low-grade symptoms such as occasional diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.

• The amoebic ulcer which is flask-shaped is the typical lesion seen in intestinal amoebiasis. The ulcers are multiple and are confined to the colon. Sometimes, in secondary intestinal lesions, the ulcers are numerous in the cecum, followed by the sigmoido-rectal region.

A granulomatous lesion called an ameboma may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas of the colon which can resemble an adenocarcinoma of the colon.

The most appropriate treatment is intravenous metronidazole.

Option A - Giardia is often asymptomatic, but in some cases can lead to fat malabsorption, dull epigastric pain, and flatulence.

Option C - Campylobacter presents with fever, pain, and watery diarrhea. The stool contains leucocytes and blood.

Option D - Shigella causes bacillary dysentery which is characterised by fever and generalised abdominal tenderness.

questions.question: You received a stool sample of a patient suspected to have dysentery in the microbiology lab. On microscopy, you observe the structures shown in the image. What other findings you will expect to see in this stool sample?
options: RBCs as discrete or in rouleaux
questions.explanation:
The given image is showing erythrophagocytosis (trophozoite with ingested RBCs) and this in the stool sample of a patient with features of dysentery is indicative of amoebic dysentery. The other stool microscopic finding seen in amoebic dysentery is Charcot-Leyden crystals.

The ingested erythrocytes appear as dark inclusions. Erythrophagocytosis is the only characteristic that can be used to morphologically differentiate E. histolytica from the nonpathogenic entamoeba.

Amoebic dysentery:

Clinically, it is insidious in onset with localized abdominal tenderness. Tenesmus, toxicity, and fever are absent.

Under microscopy, RBCs are clumped, yellowish-brown in color. Charcot-Leyden crystals and eosinophils are present.

Charcot-Leyden crystals are diamond-shaped, clear, and refractile structures that may be seen in stool specimens under microscopy and represent breakdown products of eosinophils.

The below image shows Charcot-Leyden crystals:

questions.question: A patient with abdominal pain and mucus in stool is diagnosed to have intestinal amoebiasis. Which of the following is the most common extraintestinal complication of this disease?
questions.explanation:
The most common extraintestinal complication of amoebiasis is hepatic amoebiasis.

In intestinal amoebiasis, most of the trophozoites reach the liver. However, only a small portion of them actually lodge and multiply in the liver cells. Patients usually present with an enlarged, tender liver without detectable impairment of liver function called amoebic hepatitis.

Few patients go on to develop amoebic liver abscess. The center of the abscess contains thick chocolate brown pus (anchovy sauce pus), which is made up of liquefied necrotic liver tissue. It is bacteriologically sterile and free of amoeba. The periphery is made up of nearly normal liver tissue containing invading amoeba.

Complications and sequelae of intestinal amoebiasis:

• Fulminant amoebic colitis

• Toxic megacolon

• Perianal ulceration

• Amoeboma

• Extraintestinal amoebiasis

• Hepatic amoebiasis (most common)- Amoebic hepatitis and Amoebic liver abscess

• Amoebic appendicitis and peritonitis

• Pulmonary amoebiasis

• Cerebral amoebiasis

• Splenic abscess

• Cutaneous amoebiasis

• Genitourinary amoebiasis

questions.question: A 40-year-old man was brought to the casualty with complaints of nausea, vomiting and disorientation. His brother tells you they had recently gone on a camping trip where they had swum in a freshwater lake. On examination, Kernig's sign is positive. A spinal tap is performed and the findings of CSF wet mount microscopy are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and microscopy showing amoeboid trophozoite form with pseudopodia is suggestive of primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. It is caused by Naegleria fowleri.

It is also known as brain-eating amoeba. It occurs in 3 forms: cyst, amoeboid trophozoite and flagellate trophozoite forms.

The infection usually follows swimming in freshwater rivers or ponds. The amoebae invade the nasal mucosa and pass through the olfactory nerve branches in the cribriform plate into the meninges. Incubation period is 2 days to 2 weeks.

Treatment is with intravenous amphotericin B.

Options B & D: Both Acanthamoeba and B.mandrillaris cause granulomatous amoebic meningoencephalitis which is a subacute condition.

Option C: A. cantonensis is the most common cause of eosinophilic meningitis in Southeast Asia. It is a nematode(roundworm).

questions.question: A college student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and corneal ulcers following the use of contact lens. The saline mount preparation of the corneal scraping shows polygonal cysts. What would be the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

Acanthamoeba culbertsoni is a free-living amoeba. It exists as trophozoite form and resistant cystic form. Both these forms are infective. The trophozoite is large and characterized by spine-like pseudopodia (acanthopodia).

Human beings acquire the infection by inhalation of cysts or trophozoites, ingestion of cysts, or directly through traumatized skin or eyes.

It presents as two chronic conditions- acanthamoeba keratitis and granulomatous amoebic encephalitis.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture.

The below image shows the ring lesion seen in acanthamoeba keratitis.

The below image shows cysts of acanthamoeba in lactophenol cotton blue staining.

questions.question: Which of the following protozoan parasites is found in the lumen of the human small intestine?
questions.explanation:
Image 2 shows the trophozoite of Giardia lamblia, which is the only protozoan parasite found in the lumen of the human small intestine. It lives in the duodenum and upper jejunum.

Other protozoan parasites found in the human small intestine do not occur in the lumen but are present in the epithelial cells lining the small intestine. These include:

• Isospora belli

• Cyclospora cayetanensis

• Cryptosporidium parvum

• Sarcocystis hominis

Options A and C: Entamoeba histolytica and Balantidium coli are found in the human large intestine.

Option D: Trichomonas vaginalis is found in the genital tract.

The image given below shows the trophozoite of Giardia lamblia.

The image given below shows the trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica.

The image given below shows the trophozoite of Balantidium coli.

The image given below shows the trophozoite of Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.question: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presented with a chronic history of watery diarrhea. The histopathology of the duodenum is shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the histopathology showing trophozoites of Giardia lamblia in the duodenal wall is suggestive of giardiasis.

Giardia lamblia, also called Giardia duodenalis, is the causative agent of giardiasis. It is the only common pathogenic protozoan found in the duodenum and jejunum of humans.

Infection occurs by the ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated water and food and is transmitted by the faeco-oral route.

It is weakly pathogenic in humans. Secretory IgA and IL-6 are responsible for clearing the infection. Hence, giardiasis usually occurs in immunosuppressed, agammaglobulinemic, or malnourished individuals.

Clinical features:

• Diarrhea

• Fat malabsorption

• Dull epigastric pain

• Belching and flatulence

• Iron deficiency and growth stunting.

• Stool will have excess mucus and fat but no blood.

Detection of antigen by ELISA is more sensitive and specific than microscopy. Entero test is also used in the diagnosis.

Histopathology of the duodenum reveals several heart-shaped or pear-shaped trophozoites with two equally sized nuclei. The small intestinal morphology is usually normal. However, in heavy infections, there may be villous blunting and intraepithelial infiltrates.

Metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide are the first-line agents in the treatment.

The image given below shows a magnified view of the pear-shaped trophozoites of Giardia lamblia.

questions.question: A patient is undergoing the test depicted in the image given below. Which of the following diseases does it help to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
The given image depicts a string test or entero test and is used in the diagnosis of giardiasis.

It is a useful method for obtaining the duodenal specimen in giardiasis.

In this test, a coiled thread inside a small weighted gelatin capsule is swallowed by the patient, after attaching the free end of the thread in the cheek. The capsule passes through the stomach to the duodenum. After 2 hours, the thread is withdrawn, placed in saline, and is shaken. The centrifuged deposit of the saline is then examined for giardia.

questions.question: The findings of the microscopic examination of the wet mount preparation of stool of a patient with diarrhoea is shown below. Which of the following organisms will exhibit this type of motility?
questions.explanation:
The given wet mount preparation of stool shows organisms having falling leaf motility. It is exhibited by Giardia lamblia.

The trophozoite is motile with a slow oscillation along its long axis resembling a falling leaf.

questions.question: A patient came to the gynecology OPD with complaints of foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge and intense itching. The per speculum finding is given below. Which of the following statements is false regarding the causative organism of this disease?
options: It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM or PEM
questions.answer: A. It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the image showing strawberry cervix is suggestive of Trichomonas vaginalis infection. It exists only in trophozoite form.

Trichomonas vaginalis is the only protozoan with one stage in its life cycle ie., trophozoite form (no cyst stage is seen). It is an obligate parasite and cannot live without close association with vaginal, urethral or prostatic tissues.

The common presentation of trichomoniasis is foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge, itching, and dysuria. The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM (cysteine-peptone-liver-maltose) or PEM (plastic envelope medium). The treatment of choice is metronidazole.

T. vaginalis infection in women may lead to infertility, preterm birth and low-birth-weight infants. In men, trichomoniasis has been also associated with infertility through inflammatory damage to the genitourinary tract or interference with sperm function.

The below image shows the trophozoite form of Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.question: A 12-year-old child presented to you with fever, malaise, and weight loss. On examination, you notice the finding shown in the image. In which of the following conditions is this seen?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows posterior cervical lymphadenopathy which is called Winterbottom’s sign. It is seen in West African sleeping sickness.

It is seen in stage I of West African sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.

The table below shows diseases caused by various Trypanosoma species.

Protozoa

Disease

Trypanosoma brucei gambiense

West African sleeping sickness

Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense

East African sleeping sickness

Trypanosoma cruzi

Chagas’ disease/South American trypanosomiasis

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding Trypanosoma?
options: Tsetse fly is the vector for both T. rhodesiense and T. gambiense
Humans are the reservoir for T. rhodesiense
questions.answer: D. Humans are the reservoir for T. rhodesiense
questions.explanation:
Humans are the reservoir for T. gambiense, not for T. rhodesiense.

The table below shows characteristic differences between West African and East African trypanosomiasis.

Characteristics

West African trypanosomiasis

East African trypanosomiasis

Parasites causing myocarditis include:

• Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense

• Trypanosoma cruzi

• Toxoplasma gondii

• Echinococcus granulosus

• Trichinella spiralis

questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents to the OPD with fever and malaise for the past 4 months. On examination, the following ocular finding is noted along with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the image showing Romana's sign is suggestive of Chagas disease.

It is caused by T. cruzi. Reduviid bugs are vectors for Chagas disease.

Inoculation of T. cruzi in conjunctiva causes unilateral, painless edema of periocular tissues in the eye is called Romana’s sign. This is classically seen in acute Chagas disease that lasts for 1 to 4 months.

The following image shows a patient with Romana's sign.

Acute Chagas disease is also characterised by the presence of chagomas which are subcutaneous lesions occurring at the site of inoculation.

Chronic Chagas disease is characterized by megaesophagus, megacolon, and myopathy.

Shown below is an image of the Reduviid bug.

questions.question: Which of the following is used for the culture of Trypanosoma?
questions.explanation:
NNN (Novy, McNeal, and Nicolle) medium is used for the culture of Trypanosoma brucie and cruzie. It is also used for the culture of Leishmania.

The other media used in the culture of Trypanosoma are Weinman's medium and Tobie's medium.

Options B, C & D: Boeck and Drbohlav medium, Craig’s medium and NIH polygenic medium are used for the culture of E.histolytica.

questions.question: The given life cycle belongs to which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
The given life cycle belongs to Trypanosoma cruzi.

T. cruzi is the causative organism of Chagas disease or South American trypanosomiasis. They are intracellular parasites.

It passes its life cycle in two hosts- the definitive host is the man and the intermediate host (vector) is reduviid bug or triatomine bugs.

Metacyclic trypomastigotes are the infective forms to the man that are found in feces of reduviid bugs. Transmission occurs when mucus membranes, conjunctiva, or wound on the surface of the skin are contaminated by feces of the bug.

Inside the definitive host, the trypomastigotes differentiate into intracellular amastigotes. The amastigotes multiply by binary fission and differentiate into trypomastigotes, which are then released into the bloodstream. These are the infective stage for triatomine bug. No multiplication occurs in this stage.

Inside the triatomine bug, the trypomastigotes are transformed into epimastigotes and then into metacyclic trypomastigotes in the hindgut which are excreted in feces.

Note: Amastigote forms resemble the Leishmania spp. and hence they are frequently known as Leishmanial forms. They are found in muscular tissue, nervous tissue, and reticuloendothelial system.

questions.question: The given life cycle belongs to which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
The given life cycle belongs to Leishmania donovani.

The definitive hosts are man, dog, and other mammals and the vector/intermediate host is female sandfly. Promastigotes are infective forms to man.

L. donovani exists in 2 forms:

• Amastigote form- in humans and other mammals

• Promastigote form- in the sandfly and artificial culture

When the infected sandfly bites a person, infectious promastigotes are released into the host dermis along with the sandfly saliva, which potentiates parasite infectivity.

Amastigote form (as shown in the image below) is also known as Leishman-Donovan (LD) body. It is an intracellular form found inside macrophages, monocytes and reticuloendothelial cells. It contains a kinetoplast which consists of a parabasal body and a blepharoplast. Flagellum is absent.

Promastigote form (as shown in the below image) is present in the midgut of the female sandfly. The kinetoplast lies transversely near the anterior end. A single flagellum is seen. It is the infective form of Leishmania donovani for humans.

questions.question: You are performing the following diagnostic procedure in a patient having fever for the past 2 weeks to find the causative organism. Which disease are you most likely testing for?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows bone marrow aspiration and it is most commonly done to diagnose Kala-azar.

The microscopic demonstration of amastigotes from bone marrow is the gold standard for the diagnosis of Kala-azar

Generally, the sternal marrow is aspirated by puncturing the sternum at the level of the 2nd or 3rd intercostal space, using a sternal puncture needle.

Other samples collected are peripheral blood, splenic aspirate, and enlarged lymph node.

In kala-azar:

• Most common specimen collected for microscopy- bone marrow aspirate.

• Most sensitive method- splenic aspirate.

Option B: Schistosomiasis is typically diagnosed by stool examination for parasite eggs.

Option C: Toxoplasmosis is usually diagnosed based on serologic testing.

Option D: Chagas disease is diagnosed by peripheral blood smear examination, culture and examination of aspirates from lymph nodes and chagoma.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy from Delhi presented to the OPD with the finding seen in the image. It is diagnosed to be an oriental sore. Which of the following causes this?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows cutaneous leishmaniasis and is caused by Leishmania tropica complex. It is also called oriental sore/Delhi boil/Bagdad boil/Aleppo button. It is seen mainly among children in endemic areas.

Old world Leishmania tropica complex includes 3 species:

• L. tropica

• L. major

• L. aethiopica

New world Leishmania tropica complex includes 3 species:

• L. mexicana complex

• L. braziliensis complex

It begins as a raised papule that grows into a nodule which then ulcerates over some weeks. The margins of the ulcer are raised and indurated. The ulcer is usually painless unless secondary bacterial infection occurs.

questions.question: A medicine resident is evaluating a patient with abdominal pain and diarrhoea. The stool wet mount finding is given below. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the trophozoite form of the Balantidium coli. Living trophozoites/cysts are yellowish or greenish in color on wet mount.

Balantidium coli occurs in two stages:

• Trophozoites are oval in shape and contain two nuclei. There is the presence of cilia over the entire surface and are larger around the mouth. Its anterior end is narrow and the posterior end is broad. At the anterior end, there is a groove leading to the mouth (cytostome). Posteriorly, there is a small anal pore (cytopyge).

• Cysts are smaller, round with a micronucleus, a macronucleus and many contractile vacuoles.

questions.question: What is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of kala-azar?
questions.explanation:
The rapid dipstick test is the method of choice for the diagnosis of kala-azar.

The following tests are used for the laboratory diagnosis of kala-azar:

• Rapid diagnostic tests - rK39 and dipstick test strip.

• Parasitological diagnosis - demonstration of LD bodies on microscopy is confirmatory

• Surveillance purposes - Aldehyde test of Napier

• Serological diagnosis - Rapid dipstick test, direct agglutination test, ELISA, indirect fluorescent antibody test

• Assessing immune status - Leishmanin (Montenegro) test

• Induration of ≥ 5 mm is considered positive

• Usually becomes positive 4-6 weeks after onset of cutaneous leishmaniasis

questions.question: Which of the following cestodes requires only one host?
questions.explanation:
Hymenolepis nana requires only one host for its development. Man serves as the host for H. nana.

Usually, cestodes complete their life cycle in 2 different hosts except:

• Hymenolepis requires only 1 host, man.

• Diphyllobothrium requires 3 hosts

Parasite requiring a single host to complete its development is said to have a direct life cycle.

Parasites having a direct life cycle are:

Protozoa
Helminths

• Entamoeba histolytica

• Giardia lamblia

• Trichomonas vaginalis

• Balantidium coli

• Cryptosporidium parvum

• Cyclospora cayetanensis

• Isospora belli

• Microsporidia.

• Ascaris lumbricoides

• Enterobius vermicularis

• Trichuris trichura

• Ancylostoma duodenale

• Necator americanus

• Hymenolepsis nana.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child is brought to your clinic with complaints of diarrhea and abdominal pain for the last 4 days. Stool microscopy is shown below. The eggs present in the stool float in a saturated solution of salt. Which of the following can you use to treat her?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the egg seen on stool microscopy are suggestive of infection with Hymenolepis nana. A single dose of praziquantel (25 mg/kg) is the drug of choice.

The Hymenolepis nana eggs have a thin colorless outer membrane and inner embryophore enclosing the hexacanth oncosphere. The space between two membranes contains yolk granules and 4-8 thread-like polar filaments arising from two knobs on the embryophore. The eggs float in saturated salt solution and are non-bile stained.

Hymenolepiasis occurs more commonly in children and is usually asymptomatic. In heavy infections, they present with nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and irritability. Sometimes pruritus may occur due to an allergic response.

The image given below shows the egg of Hymenolepis nana.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presented to the ER with complains of abdominal discomfort, indigestion, nausea and diarrhea after consuming measly pork. Stool examination reveals round eggs as shown in the image below. Which of the following statements is true regarding the causative organism?
options: Eggs are not infective to man
The eggs do not float in saturated salt solution
questions.answer: C. The eggs do not float in saturated salt solution
questions.explanation:
Development of the given symptoms following the consumption of measly pork is suggestive of intestinal taeniasis caused by Taenia solium (pork tapeworm). The eggs of Taenia solium do not float in the saturated salt solution.

The eggs of T. solium are infective to man and pigs. The eggs of T. saginata are infective only to cattle and not to man.

The adult worm of Taenia solium is usually 2-3 meters long and the scolex has dagger-shaped hooks.

Man is the definitive host. The intermediate host is usually pig, but occasionally it can be man.

The below image shows the life cycle of T. solium.

questions.question: While examining a patient with right upper quadrant pain, you note the abdomen is soft with localised tenderness present. CT abdomen findings are given below. Based on these findings, you post the patient for a PAIR procedure. Which of the following is not used in this procedure?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and CT findings are suggestive of hydatid disease of the liver. Hypotonic saline is not used as a scolicidal agent for the PAIR procedure (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, and Re-aspiration) which is the treatment of choice in the early stages of this condition.

Computed tomography (CT) scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cyst. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa.

In PAIR the steps involved are:

• USG or CT guided puncture of the cyst

• Aspiration of the cyst fluid

• Injection of scolicidal agent

• Re-aspiration of fluid after 5 minutes

The following agents can be used as scolicidal agents:

 Scolicidal agent

Complications associated with it

Cetrimide

Acidosis

95% Alcohol

Cholangitis

Hypertonic saline

Hypernatremia

Sodium hypochlorite

Hypernatremia

Hydrogen peroxide

The below image depicts the PAIR procedure.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presented to the OPD with a history of progressive breathlessness and cough for 3 months. A chest X-ray was done which showed a cavitary lesion in the lower lobe of the right lung. Wedge resection of the lesion was done and the histopathology image is given below. What is the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the histological slide showing the hydatid cyst are suggestive of infection with Echinococcus granulosus.

The hydatid cyst wall consists of 3 layers:

• Pericyst- the outer dense fibrous capsule that is formed as a result of host inflammatory response.

• Ectocyst- the intermediate layer consisting of acellular, chitinous, laminated hyaline material.

• Endocyst- the inner germinal layer that is cellular and consists of a number of nuclei embedded in protoplasmic mass and is extremely thin. It is the vital layer of the cyst and it is the site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.

The clinical features of hydatid disease of lung are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis and chest pain. Treatment includes wedge resection or lobectomy and administration of albendazole.

The below image shows the histology of hydatid cyst.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms does the given life cycle belong to?
questions.explanation:
This is the life cycle of Diphyllobothrium latum. It is also known as fish tapeworm or broad tapeworm.

The 3 hosts of Diphyllobothrium latum are:

• Definitive host- man, dog, and cat.

• First intermediate host- freshwater crustacean

• Second intermediate host- freshwater fish.

The infective form to humans is the third stage plerocercoid larvae. It possesses a rudimentary scolex.

The adult worm lives inside the small intestine and lays operculated eggs. These freshly passed eggs contain an immature embryo surrounded by yolk granules. This hexacanth embryo with 6 hooklets inside the egg is called oncosphere.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presented to you with complaints of tingling and numbness in her legs. On examination, her hands appear as shown in the image, ankle reflex was absent and Romberg's test was positive. Which of the following is most likely implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with cutaneous hyperpigmentation and features of subacute combined degeneration are suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency. This can be caused by Diphyllobothrium latum.

The anemia develops because the tapeworm absorbs a large quantity of vitamin B12 and interferes with its ileal absorption leading to vitamin B12 deficiency. This can also lead to megaloblastic anemia (Bothriocephalus anemia).

In severe cases, patients may exhibit neurological features of vitamin B12 deficiency like:

• Tingling and numbness

• Bilateral lower limb weakness

• Bilateral hypertonia

• Sensory ataxia (Romberg's positive)

• Absent deep tendon reflexes.

It is treated with parenteral vitamin B12 supplementation.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms most commonly causes Katayama fever?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, Katayama fever is most commonly caused by Schistosoma mansoni.

It is an immune complex mediated disease caused by antibodies to the schistosomulae, adult worms, and eggs. This acute illness consists of fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and allergic manifestations.

The diagnosis is by the demonstration of the eggs in feces.

Praziquantel is effective in the treatment. Glucocorticoids are given to suppress hypersensitivity reactions.

Instances of Katayama fever are rarer in infections with Schistosoma haematobium compared to S. mansoni.

*Note: Katayama fever is most commonly caused by S. japonicum and S. mansoni. But, among the given options, S. mansoni is the most common cause of Katayama fever.

questions.question: A 20-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with complaints of fever, intermittent abdominal pain, and burning micturition. He gives a history of swimming in a freshwater lake 10 days back. Urine microscopy shows the following. Which of the following is the causative agent?
options: Schistosoma species cannot be determined based on egg
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture and image showing an egg that is non-operculated with the terminal spine at one pole are suggestive of infection with Schistosoma hematobium.

Species differentiation of schistosoma can be done based on the location of the spine as follows:

• Terminal spine- Schistosoma hematobium

• Lateral spine- Schistosoma mansoni

• Rudimentary lateral spine- Schistosoma japonicum

The image below shows egg of Schistosoma mansoni. Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein.

Adult worms of S. japonicum live in the superior mesenteric vein draining the ileocecal region. They are also seen in the intrahepatic portal venules and hemorrhoidal plexus of veins.

The image below shows an egg of Schistosoma japonicum.

 Adult worms of S. hematobium live in the vesical and pelvic plexus of veins.

 The below image shows the life cycle of S.hematobium:

questions.question: A 50-year-old fisherman presented with complaints of blood in the urine. A diagnostic cystoscopy was done and the microscopic view of the biopsied specimen is given below. Which of the following is most likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing keratin pearls are suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder. It is associated with Schistosoma hematobium infection.

Chronic schistosomiasis presents as painless hematuria, dysuria, and proteinuria. Fibrosis may cause obstructive uropathies like hydronephrosis and hydroureter. It has been associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Such malignancy is detected in a younger age group as compared to transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder.

The following parasites cause malignancies:

• Schistosoma hematobium- bladder carcinoma

• Clonorchis sinensis and Opisthorchis viverrini- bile duct carcinoma

questions.question: Which of the following organisms does the given life cycle belong to?
questions.explanation:
The given life cycle belongs to Clonorchis sinensis. It causes clonorchiasis (Asian liver fluke infection).

The hosts for Clonorchis sinensis are:

• Definitive host- humans

• First intermediate host- snail

• Second intermediate host- fish

Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish containing the encysted larvae (metacercariae). In the duodenum, metacercaria will undergo excystation and migrate to bile ducts to develop into adult worms. The eggs containing miracidia are excreted in human feces which are then ingested by snails. Miracidium hatches out in the midgut of the snail. Inside the snail, sporocyst develops into 1st and 2nd generation redia and then to cercariae. The cercariae now penetrate the fish and develop into metacercaria (infective form).

Chronic clonorchiasis is strongly associated with cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.question: A wet mount examination of the stool sample of a patient with abdominal pain and diarrhea is given below. Which of the following parasites is he likely infected with?
questions.explanation:
The given image showing an operculated egg (egg having a lid-like structure on its end) in the stool sample is suggestive of Fasciola hepatica infection.

The eggs of Fasciola hepatica are large, ovoid, operculated, and bile stained. They contain an immature larva (miracidium) and do not float in the saturated salt solution.

The following are the parasites with operculated eggs:

• Fasciola hepatica

• Fasciolopsis buski

• Fasciola gigantica

• Paragonimus westermani

• Opisthorchis felineus

• Clonorchis sinensis

• Gastrodiscoides hominis

• Diphyllobothrium latum

Eggs of Schistosoma japonicum, Enterobius vermicularis, and Ancylostoma duodenale are non-operculated.

questions.question: Which of the following parasites is ovoviviparous?
questions.explanation:
Strongyloides stercoralis is an ovoviviparous parasite.

Nematodes are classified as follows:

• Oviparous - lay eggs:

• Unsegmented eggs: Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichuria

• Segmented eggs: Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus

• Eggs containing larva: Enterobius vermicularis

• Viviparous - produce larvae. e.g., Trichinella spiralis, Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi

• Ovoviviparous – lay eggs containing fully formed larvae that hatch immediately. e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient presented with complaints of diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 1 week. The stool microscopy revealed the following. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the stool microscopy showing the rhabditiform larva of S. stercoralis are suggestive of strongyloidiasis. The most appropriate treatment for this condition would be ivermectin.

Strongyloidiasis is caused by Strongyloides stercoralis. It is generally a benign and asymptomatic condition. In some cases, there may be cutaneous, pulmonary, and intestinal manifestations.

questions.question: An 8-year-old child was brought with complaints of perianal itching which is worse in the night. The scotch tape method demonstrates eggs as shown in the image given below. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of perianal itching and the scotch tape microscopy showing the eggs are suggestive of infestation with pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis).

The eggs of pinworm are plano-convex in shape, colorless, non-bile stained, and float in the saturated salt solution. Eggshell is double layered and relatively thick, though transparent.

Since pinworms are not released in feces, the diagnosis cannot be made by conventional fecal ova and parasite tests. NIH swab method and the scotch tape method are used for the collection of specimens.

The NIH swab (National Institutes of Health, USA) consists of a glass rod, at one end of which a piece of transparent cellophane is attached with a rubber band. The cellophane part is used for swabbing by rolling over the perianal area. It is returned to the test tube and sent to the laboratory. The cellophane piece is detached, spread over a glass side, and examined microscopically.

The image given below shows the NIH swab.

In scotch tape method, the tape is firmly pressed against the anal margin, covering all sides. The tape is transferred to a glass slide with sticky side down. Then a drop of toluene is added for clearing and examined under the microscope.

The below image shows the life cycle of Enterobius vermicularis.

questions.question: Which of the following helminthic infections that is commonly transmitted by soil, is characterized by the egg in stool as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).

The characteristic features of whipworm eggs are:

• Eggs are barrel-shaped in the middle with a projecting mucus plug at each pole containing an unsegmented ovum. The plugs are colorless.

• They float in the saturated salt solution.

• It has a triple shell, the outermost layer of which is stained brown.

They are commonly transmitted by soil. The eggs passed in the stool are unembryonated. Microscopic identification of the eggs in a stool specimen is diagnostic of whipworm infection.

In moderate infections of 20 adult worms or less, the worms are confined to the caecum and ascending colon. The symptoms include epigastric and lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea (rarely bloody), vomiting, flatulence and distention, weight loss, and increased blood and iron loss.

In heavy infections of 200 adult worms or more (trichuriasis dysentery syndrome), the worms are in the distal colon and rectum. The symptoms include bloody diarrhoea with profuse mucus, abdominal pain, tenesmus, weight loss leading to cachexia, severe anemia, and rectal prolapse. On examination, clubbing may be present. Blood investigations may show moderate eosinophilia.

Chronic infection leads to growth retardation and nutritional deficiencies. Around 0.005 ml of blood is lost per day per worm. In heavy infections, as much as 4 to 5 ml can be lost per day per worm.

Treatment is mebendazole or albendazole.

questions.question: A college student came to the OPD with fever and muscle aches. He tells you he had consumed smoked pork at a party 2 weeks back. Following this, he had developed abdominal cramps and diarrhea which had resolved on their own. CBC revealed eosinophilia and the muscle biopsy showed the following finding. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and muscle biopsy showing larvae are suggestive of trichinellosis. It is caused by Trichinella spiralis.

Trichinella spiralis is known as the pork worm since the infection is acquired by consuming raw or undercooked pork. The initial infection presents with diarrhea and abdominal pain. In the later phase of the infection, the larvae move from the intestines into the circulation and migrate into muscles where they are encysted. This causes symptoms like fever and myalgia.

These larvae are calcified in about 5-6 months. Eosinophilia caused by parasitic infection also comes down after 6 months.

Detection of spiral larva in muscle tissue is done by performing a muscle biopsy. Deltoid, biceps, gastrocnemius, or pectoralis muscles are usually selected for biopsy.

 Other parasites that can be demonstrated in a muscle biopsy are:

• T. solium

• T. cruzi (amastigote)

 The image below shows Trichinella spiralis larvae within the muscle.

questions.question: In a patient with a positive Bachman intradermal test, which of the following infections will you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Bachman intradermal test is used for the diagnosis of trichinellosis.

In this test, 1:5,000 or 1:10,000 dilution of the trichinella larval antigen is injected intradermally. An erythematous wheal appears in positive cases within 15-20 minutes. The test remains positive for years after infection.

questions.question: A 9- year-old boy was brought to the casualty with fever and colicky abdominal pain. An erect X-ray abdomen showed multiple air-fluid levels. Stool examination revealed the following egg. Which of the following is false about the organism causing this condition?
options: Egg containing L1 larva is infective
questions.answer: D. Egg containing L1 larva is infective
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of ascariasis caused by Ascaris lumbricoides. Embryonated egg containing the L3 larva is the infective form.

Man is the only natural host. There is no intermediate host. The infection is acquired via the consumption of food or water contaminated with eggs. The eggs hatch after reaching the duodenum to release the larvae. These penetrate the intestinal mucosa and enter the portal vessels. From the liver, larvae reach the systemic circulation, lungs and then reach the small intestine to produce symptoms.

Clinical features:

Due to the migrating larvae:

• Fever

• Dry cough

• Asthmatic wheezing

• Loeffler's syndrome

Due to the adult worm:

• Asymptomatic

• Nutritional effects - protein-energy malnutrition, Vitamin A deficiency

• Toxic effects - urticaria, angioedema due to hypersensitivity

• Mechanical effects - colicky abdominal pain, volvulus, and intestinal obstruction

• Ectopic ascariasis - acute biliary obstruction, pancreatitis, and obstructive appendicitis.

The life cycle of Ascaris lumbricoides is given below.

questions.question: What is the most common cause for visceral larva migrans?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause for visceral larva migrans is Toxocara canis. It occurs most commonly in children and presents as fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pneumonitis.

Larva migrans is generally seen when human infection occurs with nonhuman species of nematodes. It can be classified into cutaneous or visceral types, depending on whether the larval migration takes place in the skin or in deeper tissues.

Visceral larva migrans is caused by the migration of nematode larvae that are acquired via the oral route. Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the migration of nematode larvae (most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense) that are acquired via skin penetration.

Patients having visceral larva migrans may develop neurological disturbances (neural larva migrans) and endophthalmitis (ophthalmic larva migrans).

Differences between cutaneous larva migrans and visceral larva migrans:

Cutaneous larva migrans
Visceral larva migrans

Tissue involved
Skin
Various organs of the body like the liver, lungs, and eyes

Infecting Organism
Mostly by non-human nematodes
Mostly by non-human nematodes (mainly by dog and cat)

Portal of Entry
Penetration of skin
Ingestion of infected eggs

Eosinophilia
Mild
Persistent high

Serodiagnosis
Not developed
Well developed

Treatment
Thiabendazole
Diethylcarbamazine and prednisolone

questions.question: A middle-aged woman comes to the OPD with complaints of weakness for the past 3 months. She is diagnosed to have microcytic hypochromic anemia. The stool microscopy reveals the following. What is the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of iron deficiency anemia and the stool microscopy showing the egg is suggestive of infection by Ancylostoma duodenale.

Eggs of both Ancylostoma duodenale (old world hookworm) and Necator americanus (new world hookworm) are identical.

The hookworm eggs are oval or elliptical in shape, colorless, and non-bile stained. It has a thin transparent hyaline shell membrane. The ovum is segmented with 4 to 8 blastomeres. There is a clear space between the segmented ovum and eggshell. Eggs float in the saturated salt solution.

Humans are infected when filariform larvae in moist soil penetrate the skin or subcutaneous tissue. The larvae are then carried in the venous circulation to the heart and lungs, where they may cause mild transient pneumonitis or bronchitis. They migrate up the respiratory tract to the pharynx, are swallowed, and reach the small intestine producing epigastric pain, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

A. duodenale or N. americanus ingest blood, secrete anticoagulants, and interfere with the absorption of iron, B12, and folic acid. This leads to iron deficiency anemia and protein-energy malnutrition resulting from blood loss.

The average blood loss of the host per worm per day is 0.2 mL with Ancylostoma duodenale and 0.03 mL with Necator americanus.

questions.question: A patient presented to the OPD with dry cough, low-grade fever and wheezing. He is diagnosed with Loeffler’s syndrome. Which of the following parasites does not cause this?
questions.explanation:
Loeffler's syndrome is an eosinophilic inflammation of the lung caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, Strongyloides stercoralis and Necator americanus. Enterobius vermicularis does not cause Loeffler’s syndrome.

It is associated with pneumonia characterized by dry cough, low-grade fever, wheezing, urticaria, and eosinophilia.

Parasites causing Loeffler’s syndrome are:

• Migrating larva of:

• Ascaris lumbricoides

• Strongyloides stercoralis

• Ancylostoma duodenale

• Necator americanus

• Echinococcus granulosus

• Cryptosporidium parvum

• Eggs of Paragonimus westermani

• Entamoeba histolytica

• Trichomonas tenax

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman had gone on a trek in the Amazon rainforest. A month later she presented to the OPD with the following lesion which was painful and pruritic. Her systemic examination was normal. Which of the following organisms is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing serpiginous skin lesions are suggestive of cutaneous larva migrans or creeping eruption or ground itch. This is most commonly caused by Ancylostoma braziliense.

Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by non-human hookworms like Ancylostoma braziliense and Ancylostoma caninum. It is acquired via direct skin contact with soil contaminated by dog or cat feces. The larvae remain confined to the outer layers of skin, as they are unable to penetrate the basement membrane of the human skin.

It presents as erythematous, pruritic papules at the site of entry and serpiginous tracks in the epidermis. The symptoms begin to appear within the first two weeks of the patient’s return from a tropical or endemic country. The larval track progresses at approximately 1 cm/h with cutaneous lesions only progressing a few millimeters to a few centimeters daily.

Diagnosis is based mainly on clinical features.

The treatment includes:

• Thiabendazole topical application

• Albendazole 400mg/day X 3 days or

• Ivermectin 200mcg/kg single dose stat

The differences between cutaneous larva migrans and visceral larva migrans are:

Cutaneous larva migrans
Visceral larva migrans

Tissue involved
Skin
Various organs of the body like the liver, lungs, and eyes

Infecting Organism
Mostly by non-human nematodes
Mostly by non-human nematodes (mainly by dog and cat)

Portal of Entry
Penetration of skin
Ingestion of infected eggs

Eosinophilia
Mild
Persistent high

Serodiagnosis
Not developed
Well developed

Treatment
Thiabendazole
Diethylcarbamazine and prednisolone

Note: A rapidly moving lesion (10cm/hr) produced by Strongyloides stercoralis is known as larva currens (running larva). It occurs as an otherwise asymptomatic lesion in immunocompetent individuals. In immunocompromised, hyper-infestation syndrome occurs with paralytic ileus and secondary Gram-negative sepsis.

questions.question: Which the following filarial worms are non-pathogenic to humans?
questions.explanation:
Mansonella ozzardi is generally non-pathogenic to humans.

Option A: Onchocerca volvulus infection may manifest as skin nodules or onchocercoma which are formed as a result of fibroblastic reaction around adult worms deep in the subcutaneous tissues. Microfilariae cause lesions in the skin and eyes.

Options B and C: In lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria and Brugia), the typical manifestations are caused by the adult worms blocking lymph nodes and vessels. Microfilaria (larval form) are responsible for allergic manifestations seen in occult filariasis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man came to the hospital with complaints of progressive swelling of his legs. On examination, you note bilateral non-pitting edema of the lower limbs with thickening of the overlying skin. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.answer: C. Night blood test for worms
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis). The best next step would be to test the night blood for worms since the filarial species is nocturnally periodic (between 10 pm and 4 am) in India.

Lymphatic filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi.

Elephantiasis is a delayed sequel to repeated lymphangitis, obstruction, and lymphedema. Repeated leakage of lymph into tissues first results in lymphedema, then to elephantiasis.

Diethylcarbamazine is the drug of choice.

Option A: PCR is negative in chronic filariasis.

Options B & D: Lymphangiography and lymphoscintigraphy may be used to demonstrate abnormal lymphatic urinary fistula leading to chyluria in chronic filariasis.

questions.question: A child from Bihar is brought to the AIIMS ER with a high-grade fever. On examination, bilaterally enlarged, tender inguinal lymph nodes are present. The peripheral smear examination finding is shown in the image. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing sheathed microfilaria with two nuclei at the tail tip is suggestive of infection with Brugia malayi.

Acute infection may manifest as acute adenolymphangitis which is characterized by high fever, lymphatic inflammation (lymphangitis and lymphadenitis) and transient local edema. The most commonly affected lymph nodes are inguinal nodes followed by axillary nodes which become enlarged, painful and tender.

The following are the characteristic features of microfilaria of Brugia malayi:

• Smaller in size compared to microfilaria of W. bancrofti.

• Shows kinks and secondary curves.

• Cephalic space is longer.

• Carries double stylets at the anterior end.

• Nuclear column appears blurred in Giemsa-stained films.

• Tail tip carries 2 distinct nuclei, one terminal and the other subterminal.

The below image shows the microfilaria of Brugia malayi.

questions.question: A patient from Kerala has presented to your OPD with fever. A magnified view of peripheral blood smear is shown below. Which of the following is false regarding the organism seen?
options: DEC provocation test is used to demonstrate microfilaria during the day
Second stage filariform larva is the infective form
Microfilaria is the major diagnostic form
Filarial stage of adult worms are responsible for disease
questions.answer: B. Second stage filariform larva is the infective form
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with a peripheral smear showing sheathed microfilaria with a pointed tail free of nuclei is suggestive of Wuchereria bancrofti. The third stage filariform larva is the infective form.

Wuchereria bancrofti infection is usually asymptomatic. The symptoms are due to obstruction of lymphatics by the filarial stage of adult worms.

The lymphatic vessels of the male genitalia are most commonly affected in bancroftian filariasis, producing episodic funiculitis, epididymitis, and orchitis. Adenolymphangitis of the extremities is less common.

Hydrocele is the most common sign of chronic bancroftian filariasis, followed by lymphedema, elephantiasis, and chyluria. The swelling involves the whole leg, the whole arm, the scrotum, the vulva, or the breast.

DEC provocation test is used to demonstrate microfilaria during the day.

The image below shows the life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti.

The image below shows the difference between microfilaria of various filarial nematodes.

questions.question: A 54-year-old farmer from Assam presented with the finding shown in the image. He had also developed a painless swelling in his elbow 2 years back which has gradually been increasing in size. Which of the following is the drug of choice to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and image showing sclerosing keratitis are suggestive of onchocerchiasis (river blindness). The drug of choice is ivermectin.

It is caused by Onchocerca volvulus. It is also known as convoluted filaria or blinding filaria.

The vector is blackfly (Simulium species) which breed in fast-flowing rivers, and therefore the disease is most common along the course of rivers. Hence, it is also called river blindness.

The usual presentation is formation of a subcutaneous nodule or onchocercoma. It is a firm non-tender nodule arising from bony sites like scalp, elbow, ribs, and iliac crest. It is associated with pruritus and rashes.

The microfilaria in the eyes cause photophobia and gradual loss of vision. The most severe manifestation is sclerosing keratitis and chorioretinitis which causes blindness. It is the 2nd major infective cause of blindness in the world after trachoma.

Suramin and diethylcarbamazine (DEC) were used earlier but are not used nowadays. DEC destroys microfilariae but usually causes Mazzotti reaction consisting of pruritus, rash, lymphadenopathy, fever, hypotension, and occasionally, eye damage.

Note: Onchocerciasis is not endemic in India but sporadic cases have been reported from North-Eastern India.

questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents to your clinic with photosensitivity, redness, and watering of the eyes for the last 2 days. She shows you this photo of a swelling in her hand that had arisen 2 weeks back but disappeared in just 3 days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing Calabar swelling is suggestive of loiasis caused by Loa loa.

Calabar swellings are temporary foci of inflammation that appear as Loa loa wanders through the subcutaneous tissues. They are up to 3 cm in size and are also called fugitive swellings because they disappear in a few days only to reappear elsewhere.

Loa loa is transmitted by the bite of Chrysops species (deerflies). The infective form is the third stage microfilaria. After entry into human skin, it grows into an adult worm.

The ocular manifestations occur when the worm reaches the subconjunctival tissue during its wanderings. They include:

• Granuloma in bulbar conjunctiva

• Painless edema of the eyelids

• Proptosis.

The image below shows Calabar swelling.

The image below shows a live, adult Loa loa in the anterior chamber of the eye.

questions.question: Which of the following is also known as Weingarten syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is also known as Weingarten syndrome.

Tropical eosinophilia occurs as a result of hypersensitivity reaction to microfilarial antigens and not directly due to lymphatic involvement. It is a manifestation of occult filariasis (Meyer's-Kouwenaar syndrome).

Clinical features of occult filariasis include massive eosinophilia and hepatosplenomegaly.

Synonyms of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia include -

• Weingarten syndrome

• Pseudo-tuberculosis of the lung

• Eosinophilic pseudo-leukemia

• Tropical eosinophilic asthma

• Frimodt-Moller and Barton's syndrome

questions.question: Which of the following is known as serpent worm?
questions.explanation:
Dracunculus medinensis is known as serpent worm.

It is a viviparous nematode.

This has been eradicated from India and all of the southeast Asian region in the year 2000.
